en: Preface to the *Cānlin Bǎoxùn*.

This book has been widely circulated in the region north of the Yangtze River and is highly esteemed in the Wu region. Yet, among the monastics of Min and Yue, eight or nine out of ten have neither seen nor heard of it.
If one wishes for the Zen groves to flourish and the Way of the Dharma to prosper, how could this be possible? I—[the author]—...
In the past, while traveling on pilgrimage to Yunqi, I beheld this collection as if I had obtained a most precious treasure. I have cherished it for many years;

though I have been unable to practice its teachings with full vigor, I have nonetheless not dared to neglect it for even a moment. This anthology begins with the Elder Mingjiao and concludes with the Great Master Lanyan.
Among its three hundred pieces, every word flows from the bitter hearts of these venerable masters, and their language—
It is said that [this teaching] is luminous and upright, direct and concise; it truly serves as a model for all ages.

Nevertheless, to synthesize the *Yi* (Changes) and put it into practice is indeed difficult. What is valued is the pruning of the flowery to take the substantial, urgently remedying the currency of the Semblance Age, crushing the heterodox to support the orthodox, and restoring the true doctrine of antiquity.
Once the winds of decadence have subsided, the Way of primal simplicity will be realized.
It is complete. Yet, how could the defects of oral and aural transmission—the perverse and groundless doctrines—have arisen?
Therefore, I have often wished to publish it for the common benefit of all; however, I regret that my purse was empty and I could not accomplish the task.

Consequently, I have gathered together like-minded colleagues to carve the woodblocks for circulation, which will be of great benefit to the regions of Min and Yue. Should a monk of fiery temperament happen to strike against it...
A single word or half a phrase, when brought forth, shall cover heaven and earth. Why worry that the Zen groves will not flourish or the Way of the Dharma will not prosper?

Not only will my own wish be fulfilled, but it will also not betray the great intention of the patriarchs of antiquity—who emitted the Great Jewel Light from their mouths to illuminate the world—nor the fundamental aspiration of the Zen groves throughout all time.
Spring of the Jiashen Year of the Chongzhen Reign (1644). The seventy-third monk, Ruyou, bows his head and records this preface to the *Combined Commentary on the Jewel Teachings of the Chan Forest*.

These *Jewel Teachings* have existed for a long time. As for this "Combined Commentary," why was it produced? Lately, I have observed that the style of Chan has flourished and its Dharma-transformation has spread widely.
Practices have gone astray and false interpretations have spread; the true cause has sunk into oblivion. The mountain forests lack a master, while the cities abound in devious ends.
Cunning flattery arises unchecked, and thorny weeds run rampant. Among them, some borrow from monasteries to purchase power and status, or rely on bribery to sell their reputations.
They mock those who are upright and straightforward for not being conversant with worldly affairs, and thus indulge their partiality and arrogance, wandering about without restraint. It is as if...
As for these corrupt customs, where are the exemplary models for future generations? To what can we turn as a bulwark against the decadence of the final age?
Few indeed would escape the reproach of the great venerable masters such as Mingjiao Song and Yuanrong Ne.

How much more so for one who trains talented individuals, emulates the sages of antiquity, whose virtue and speech are firmly established, and whose instruction in the principles of the Dharma is diligent—yet who now fears that those with infirm feet will find no way to the physician’s gate, and those of dull faculties...

In the workshop of the Master of Many Furnaces (Duobei), when pearls are hidden among fish eyes and jade is covered by common stones, how could one prevent tiles and rubble from filling the void, or allow only the feeble mules to roam the wilds?
Nevertheless, even a fragment of excellence or a mere inch of skill may be recorded for superior judgment; yet who knows that rotten seeds and scorched sprouts might also be selected?
Generally speaking, those who draw near seek conformity, and those on narrow paths settle for mere acceptance, failing to consider the standards of measurement.

Master Lin upholds and supports the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it is no wonder that his discernment regarding the precious instructions is so profound. Layman Jinghui has had the opportunity to observe this from the sidelines.
One day, he brought this collection to Huiyun and consulted with me, saying, "This may serve as a mirror for those who are currently mired in corruption.
He then entrusted it to Elder Mu, leaving it to the various quarters to examine and critique it.
Preface to the Combined Commentary on the *Cān-lín bǎo-xùn* (Precious Instructions for the Zen Forest), compiled by the Abbot of Wulin Huyun Chan Monastery, Shi Xingsheng,
on the third day before the eve of the New Year in the Jichou year of the Shunzhi era.
An ancient worthy once said: "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish.

Now, as for those whose achievements cover all living beings and whose fame flows through successive generations—generals and ministers are considered the pinnacle of such glory—and yet they still seem to find no worth in these roles, then is this not what is meant by a "great man"?
Is he not one who is complete in both moral virtue and wisdom?
Wind! You have distanced yourself from the traces of the vulgar and base, embodying a lofty and brilliant magnificence.

You uphold solitary and extraordinary integrity, such that above you are sufficient to accord with the Buddha-mind, and below you are sufficient to rescue all sentient beings. You stand firm as a model for gods and men, illuminating both past and present.
Yet, as the time since the Sage has grown ever more distant and the human heart has become chiseled and debased, those who preside over affairs look only to their own convenience.
In pursuit of worldly sustenance, practitioners followed the tide and became mired in secular society; as the Buddha-dharma declined, it gradually took on the appearance of a vast river flowing away.
It was for this reason that the two great beings of Miaoxi and Zhuanan composed their "Precious Instructions.

Indeed, these two masters lived at a time when Cheng Hao and Zhu Xi were championing the clarification of Confucian learning; they themselves maintained a dignified bearing and decorum, and what they discussed was the rectification of the mind and the cultivation of sincerity.
I consider that what you have distinguished concerns the interests of both the public and the private.

As for those who treat the followers of Śākyamuni as if they were actual enemies, yet when one examines the list provided here—beginning with Mingjiao Yongsheng and extending to the various great masters of venerable standing—one finds their realization was transcendent and their practice authentic;
they did not merely succeed in fortifying their own sectarian boundaries, but were also able to ensure their meritorious achievements were like those of the Duke of Zheng.
Lord Zhao Qingxian’s literary reputation was like that of Su Zizhan and Huang Lüzhi; his mastery of the Way was like that of Hu Kanghou and Zhang Zishao.
Among the other eminent officials and great scholars, numbering no fewer than several hundred families, there were none who did not pay their respects and offer their sincere devotion.
"Entering the marketplace with hands hanging down"—even Chengzi followed this by sighing, "The ritual and music of the Three Dynasties are all contained herein.

Zhuzi also remarked, "I wish you would point toward the nature and mind; your words transcend both existence and non-existence. Although he intended to refute him, in the end there was no flaw or opening to be pointed out.
This was not merely due to the subtle penetration and realization of the various venerable masters, but also because of the *zong* (the lineage/principle).

The vigor of his character was sufficient to seal his mouth. Thus, when it came to the moment of acting upon affairs, he revered morality and virtue, sharpened his integrity, distanced himself from fame and glory, and suppressed the pursuit of profit and sustenance;
his brilliance and uprightness were truly such that they could deeply win over the hearts of others.
If one were to instead pursue power and influence, chase after profit and fame, or harbor arrogance and conceit, turning their back on and despising teachers and friends,
thereby shattering the Great Way and disrupting the ancient regulations— though their name might be loftily titled "Master of Knowledge" (Jñānin), yet when examining their actual substance,
they would engage in acts that even the vulgar would be ashamed to perform. How could such a person succeed in propagating the Buddha-seed and upholding the Dharma?
The True Dharma ensures that the worthy and noble men of the world will have nothing to criticize regarding its legacy.
Should the world at present be deluded by it, would one not feel inward shame when reflecting upon it in the clear stillness of night? Therefore, these two masters composed this compilation.
It supports what is declining and revives what is in decay; it is fully compatible with the various chapters of the Confucian *Jinsilu* (Records of Near Reflection).
It is truly a mirror for the Buddhist gate and a model for monastics. Although this work has been circulated, it has long suffered from omissions and defects.

Thus, Master Shan of Eastern Wu provided a supplement to the preceding sections, while Master Jian of Yunqi appended the phonetic glosses and meanings at the end. This may indeed be called a complete version.
Thus it is. Although the phonetics and meanings were complete, the text circulated as a single independent work, making it inconvenient to consult.

Therefore, I, along with my younger brother Cheng Shu, have pruned its redundancies and supplemented what was incomplete, establishing this definitive version. I have appended annotations beneath each respective entry to facilitate reading.
I only wish that those who aspire to be great men [mahāsattva] will, from the stage of self-cultivation (*śaikṣa*) up to—
For those who have left the mundane world to become human beings, it would be well to take this single volume daily into one’s hands as a "leather-and-string" reminder [of vigilance].
This preface to the *Chanlin Baoxun* (Precious Instructions for the Chan Forest) was composed by the lay practitioner Zhang Wenjia, style name Zhongjia, of Net-Hui in Wulin,
during the summer of the Gengyin year.
Regarding these "Precious Instructions": formerly, when Miaoxi was clearing away the thatch at Zhuanan in Jiangxi, they were compiled together.

During the Chunxi era, while I was traveling at Yunju, I obtained them from the elder monk Zu’an. Alas, due to the passage of time, they have been damaged by insects; the beginning and end are incomplete.
Later, I encountered [these works] in various records and biographies. After accumulating them for ten years, I had only about fifty pieces.
I then further selected the "Bequeathed Words" (yiyu) of the various elders from Huanglong down to Fozhao and Jiantang, editing and categorizing them into three hundred pieces.
Although these were acquired at different times, I did not arrange them according to chronological order. My general aim was to enable students to eliminate their preconceived biases.

It benefits both self and others, striving solely for the Way, Virtue, Benevolence, and Righteousness. Its literary style is elegant, leisurely, and plain, devoid of any traces of arrogance, extravagance, abstraction, or eccentricity;
it is truly capable of assisting one’s long-term strategy for entering the Path. Furthermore, I intend to carve this into woodblocks to facilitate its wide dissemination.
Should there be like-minded scholars who, upon seeing it once, grant their hearts’ assent, I shall do so even if I die of old age.
The hills and valleys are sufficient for my aspirations. Written by the śramaṇa Jingshan of Eastern Wu.
"Miaoxi, Miaoxi" refers to Chan Master Dahui Pujo Zonggao of Mount Jing in Lin’an Prefecture.
He was the son of the Xi family of Ningguo in Xuanzhou, Jiangdong. He was a successor of Chan Master Foguo Keqin, belonging to the fifteenth generation under Nanyue.
At thirteen, he entered the school of secular learning but took no pleasure in worldly classics. He went to Zen Master Huiji at Huiyun Monastery on Mount Dongshan.
At seventeen, he shaved his head and donned the monastic robes. Later, he entered the ancient Yunmen Monastery to the west of Yunju.

At the old site, he cleared away the brambles and constructed a hermitage, remaining there for twenty years. Later, traveling through Huxiang and eventually to Mount Yangshan, he met Chan Master Zhuan-an Gui.
Together they composed over a hundred verses on ancient cases (songgu). This *Baoxun* (Precious Instructions) is the collection made at that time.
Chan Master Zhuan-an Shigui of Longxiang in Wenzhou was the son of the Shi family of Chengdu Prefecture.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Foyan Qingyuan and belonged to the fifteenth generation under Mount Heng.
"Chūmō" (Clearing the Thatch): "Chūmō" means to cut grass; it refers to clearing away thatch grass to construct a hermitage for a secluded life.
"Shunji": the era name of Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty.
The lineage and clan of Master Zu’an are unknown.
As for Master Huanglong Hui, the National Teacher of the Longxing Prefecture: he was the son of the Zhang family of Xinzhou and succeeded Shichuang Chuyuan;
he belongs to the eleventh generation below Nanyue.
Fozhao resided at Yuyang Monastery in Mingzhou, which was the Fozhao Monastery in Qingyuan Prefecture.
Chan Master Foguang Fozhao Zhu’an was a native of the Peng family of Linjiang County. He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Dahui Zonggao and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Heng.
He received his tonsure under Chan Master Ji of Huaguang Monastery on East Mountain in his home prefecture. Later, during the Chunxi era of Emperor Xiaozong...
In the eleventh month of the third year of the Xih era, an imperial edict summoned him to enter Xuande Hall to discourse on Chan.
In the fifth year of the Chunxi era, he was granted the title "Fozhao," which spread throughout the realm, causing the school's teachings to flourish greatly.
Chan Master Jiange Xingji of Guoqing Temple in Taizhou was a native of the Yang clan of that same prefecture.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jingyuan of Huguo Temple and belonged to the sixteenth generation under the lineage of Mount Heng.
"Eastern Wu" refers to the name of the administrative district of Suzhou in Eastern Wu. "Śramaṇa" is a contraction of a Sanskrit term;
its full form is *śramaṇaka*, which means "diligent in cessation. This signifies being diligent in practicing wholesome dharmas and personally extinguishing all evils.
"Jingshan" (淨善) is the personal name of the author of this preface. Junior students must not pronounce both characters together; it should be read as "Upper Jing, Lower Shan.
This is the first volume of the *Combined Commentary on the Jewel Instructions of the Chan Forest*, collated by the layman Zhang Wenjia (style name Zhongjia), known as Net-hui of Hulín.
Master Mingjiao Song said: "Nothing is more honorable than the Way; nothing is more beautiful than virtue.
Where the Way and virtue abide, even a commoner is not in straits. Where the Way and virtue do not abide, even one who rules the world is not successful."
Bo Yi and Shu Qi were men who starved to death in the past; yet when their names are compared to others today, everyone feels joy.
Jie, Zhou, You, and Li were sovereigns of men in the past; yet when their names are compared to others today, everyone feels indignation.
Therefore, the student’s concern is that the Way and its Virtue are not fully realized within his person;
it is not a concern that power and status do not reside with him (*Xianjin ji*).
Chan Master Mingjiao Qisong of Furi Monastery in Hangzhou, whose courtesy name was Zhongling, styled himself "The Hidden One."
Zi was the son of the Li family of Tanjin in Tengzhou. He succeeded Dongshan Xiaocong and belonged to the tenth generation of the Qingyuan lineage.

He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and received full ordination at thirteen. At nineteen, he began his travels to seek teachers. He constantly carried a single scroll of an Avalokiteśvara image and daily recited the sacred name one hundred thousand times;
this was his regular practice. There were no secular scriptures or books that he did not examine thoroughly. He composed the *Yuan*... [text continues]
The treatise consists of over one hundred thousand words, demonstrating that the Way of Confucianism and Buddhism is a single, unified system.
It was submitted for imperial review by Wang Sù, the Director of the Longtu Pavilion serving as Governor of Kaifeng, along with Ouyáng Xiū and Chéng Shīmèng.

Upon reading it, Emperor Rénzōng expressed great admiration and commendation, ordering its inclusion in the Imperial Canon through the Bureau of Editorial Revision. It is titled *Fǔjiào piān* (Treatise on Assisting the Teachings) in three fascicles, and the author was granted purple robes.
"Square-robe" (*fāngpáo*) is a designation for the "Clarifier of the Teaching.
In its original Sanskrit, the correct name for *heshang* is *upādhyāya*. Transmitted from Khotan, it was translated as *heshang*;

transmitted to this land [China], it was translated as "Power-Born" (*lìshēng*). This means that those who have left the household life grow and flourish in the Dharma by virtue of their teacher's power.
The body produces the wealth of merit and nourishes the life-force of wisdom; therefore, it is called "born of power.
When the mind of the Way penetrates, it is called the Way; furthermore, the perfection of its name is termed the Way—namely, the subtle and wondrous Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
In Confucianism, this is the subtle Way of "sincerely holding to the Mean."
Virtue that rectifies the person is called "de" (virtue). This refers to the establishment of one's character. Monks possess precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
Confucians possess filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness—all of these are termed "virtue."

"King" (Wáng; the final syllable is pronounced with a departing tone). Generally, whoever possesses the world is addressed by people as "King. Furthermore, one who personally presides over the four seas is called a "King.
Boyi and Shuqi were the two sons of the Lord of Gouzhu. Gouzhu is the name of a state; their surname was Motai.
The family name was Ji. His eldest son, Boyi, was named Yun and styled Gongxin; his younger son, Shuqi, was named Zhi and styled Gongda.
They were posthumously titled Boyi and Shuqi respectively. When their father was about to die, he left a testament to establish Shuqi as his successor.

Shuqi considered fraternal succession to be paramount, thinking, "If I occupy the position, it would be unjust. Boyi considered his father’s command to be supreme, thinking, "If I occupy the position, it would be unfilial."
The two men fled together. The people of the state installed the second son as their ruler.
Hearing that Chang, the Chief of the West, was skilled at caring for the elderly, they said, "Why do we not go and submit to him? When King Wen passed away, King Wu went forth to attack Zhou.

The two men struck the horse's head and remonstrated, saying, "The father has died and remains unburied, yet you have already taken up arms; can this be called filial piety? To use a subject to usurp [the throne]..."
"Your Majesty, can this man be called loyal? His attendants wished to execute him, but Grand Duke Tai said, 'This is a man of righteousness,' and he supported him and led him away.
After King Wu had pacified the world and the Zhou became the sovereign, Bo Yi and Shu Qi felt ashamed [of the new regime] and would not eat the grain of Zhou.
They subsequently went into hiding on Mount Shouyang, where they gathered *wei* sprouts to eat, until they eventually starved to death.
Jie of Xia, named Lügui, was the son of Emperor Fa. According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who harms many people and kills excessively is called "Jie.
He was licentious and unrighteous. He obtained a woman of the Shi clan named Meixi and constructed towers of jade and terraces of precious stone to indulge his pleasures to the utmost.
He created a wine-pool where boats could be navigated and a mound of dregs that could be seen for ten li. Longfeng offered loyal remonstrance, but Jie would not follow it.
He was killed. King Tang of Yin possessed great virtue. Yi Yin assisted Tang in attacking Jie. Jie was defeated in battle and fled to the state of Sanzong.
Tang pursued and attacked him there, banishing Jie to Nanchao, where he died.

Shang Zhou’s name was Xin; he was also called Shou. He was the son of Emperor Yi. According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who "harms righteousness and diminishes goodness" is called Zhou.
He obtained the lady Da Ji of the Su clan and doted on her excessively. He established a wine moat and a forest of meat, ordering men and women to pursue one another therein in the nude.
He constructed the Palace of Eternal Night and employed the "frying-grid" punishment. He disemboweled pregnant women and castrated men.
He constructed the Deer Terrace (Lùtái), which was completed after seven years. He cruelly harmed the loyal and virtuous;
his minister, Shù Bìgān, exhausted his loyalty in remonstrance and subsequently had his heart torn out and died. The Grand Preceptor Jīsǐ feigned madness and became a slave.
His elder brother, Wéizǐ, departed to avoid the loss of righteousness. Later, King Wǔ raised an army to attack him, defeated him, and ascended the Deer Terrace. [He] covered...
He threw himself into fire and died.
Zhou You (Zhou You) was named Gongnie; he was the son of King Xuan. According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), "obstructing and preventing so that there is no passage" is called *You*.

His governance was likely tyrannical toward the people, which led to Mount Qi collapsing of its own accord and the rivers and mountains running dry. He obtained a woman from the state of Bao, named Bao... [The text ends here].
It seemed as though he favored her; consequently, he demoted Queen Shen and the Crown Prince Yijiu. Lady Bao Si did not enjoy laughing.
[The King] raised fires on Mount Qiang to mock and amuse Lady Bao Si so that she would laugh. Later, Lord Shen became enraged and summoned the Qunrong, who killed the King at the foot of Mount Li.
King Zhou Li’s name was Hu; he was the son of King Yi. According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who slays the innocent is titled "Li.

The king acted without the Way, being extravagant, arrogant, and tyrannical. The people of the state slandered him, so the king appointed the Minister of Guard (Wei Wu) to monitor such slanders, ordering that anyone who slandered him be executed.
Duke Shao remonstrated with him, saying: "To block the mouths of those below while allowing the faults of those above to ascend will surely bring ruin to the altars of the land."
Ji was filled with anxiety, but the King would not listen. The people of the state rebelled against him, and the calamity reached the King himself. The King then fled into exile at Zhi.
As the Crown Prince was still young, the two dukes, Zhou and Shao, acted in harmony and cooperation to manage the affairs of state; therefore, this period is called the "Shared Regency" (Gonghe).
The twenty-two pieces of the *Xiaoya* were all the virtuous governance of Wen, Wu, Cheng, and Kang; by this time, they had all been completely abolished.
Mingjiao said:
"The learning of the sages and worthies is certainly not something that can be mastered in a single day. When the daylight is insufficient, one must continue it with the night."
Accumulated over months and years, it will naturally be accomplished. Thus it is said: "Study to gather [knowledge], and inquiry to discern it.

These words mean that study cannot be made manifest without inquiry and discernment. Yet, among those who study today, there are rarely any who utter a single word of inquiry or discernment to others.
I do not know how they hope to assist their fundamental nature or achieve the benefit of daily renewal (from the *Jiupeng ji*).
The Sage is called "sage" because his spiritual intelligence clearly and penetratingly discerns; furthermore, "sage" implies correctness, for he instructs others through correct teaching.
The Worthy is called "worthy" because they transcend the ordinary and approach the level of the sage.
Regarding the phrase "accumulating learning through inquiry and debate": this means that if a person does not apply themselves to learning, they will have no means [to achieve their goals].
One must comprehend the various principles so that they become one's own.

If one studies without inquiry, there will be no means to distinguish among these various principles, such that their categories might fall into disorder and one may not know how to choose between the refined and the coarse, or the fundamental and the derivative. This is derived from the text of the second line of the hexagram Yi (Threatening) in the *Book of Changes*.
"Bì" means to supplement and "bǔ" means to assist.
The inscription on King Tang’s basin says: "If one renews oneself today, let one renew oneself day after day, renewing oneself ever anew.
Thus, for the student therein, it refers to advancing in their studies and cultivating virtue so as to become ever renewed—like bathing the body to wash away old defilements.
...to cleanse themselves and renew themselves. Mingjiao said:
"When Grand Historian Sima Qian read the *Mencius*, upon reaching the passage where King Hui of Liang asks, 'How can I benefit my state?
he unconsciously set down his scroll and sighed deeply: 'Alas! Benefit is truly the beginning of disorder. Therefore, the Master [Confucius] rarely spoke of benefit. He constantly...

This is to prevent it at its source. The "source" refers to the beginning. If those who honor the poor and humble are themselves corrupted by the pursuit of profit, how can they distinguish right from wrong?
Now, for those in public office, if they seek profit unjustly, the law will fall into disorder. For those in private life, if they seek profit through deception, affairs will fall into disorder.
When affairs are in disorder, people contend with one another unequally; when the law is in disorder, the people resent and do not submit. Thus, there arises rebellion, strife, and contention.

Those who disregard death act upon this very principle. Is this not, then, a sharp beginning to disorder? Furthermore, the sages and worthies strictly cautioned against pursuing profit and held benevolence and righteousness as supreme.
Yet in later generations, there were still countless instances of those who relied on profit to deceive one another, wounding social customs and subverting the teachings;
how much more so when one openly proclaims and practices the way of seeking profit. To desire [this] from Heaven...
To rectify the customs of the lower classes so that they are neither decadent nor coarse—how could this be achieved? (From the *Xianjin ji*). Grand Historian:
surnamed Sī-mǎ, given name Tán; he served as the Grand Historian. His son, named Qiān, succeeded him in his father’s office.
Because he honored his father, he was referred to as "Gōng" (Grand). He was a native of Lóngmén during the Western Han.
Mencius’s name was Ke; his courtesy name was Ziyu. He was a native of the state of Zou. He composed the *Book of Mencius* in seven chapters.
King Hui of Liang was Marquis Huan of Wei. His capital was Daliang, where he usurped the title of King. His posthumous title was Hui.

According to the *Records of the Grand Historian*, in the thirty-fifth year of King Hui’s reign, he offered humble etiquette and generous gifts to summon men of talent, and thus Mencius arrived in Liang.
The King asked, "Old man, you have come from no less than a thousand li away; how can you benefit my state?
Mencius replied, "Why must Your Majesty speak only of 'benefit' (li)? There is simply benevolence (ren) and righteousness (yi).

When the King questioned his meaning—referring to such matters as strengthening the military and enriching the state—Mencius’s response was that he did not regard wealth as the benefit, but rather regarded righteousness as the true benefit.
"Rarely speaking of profit" means that such instances are few. He rarely spoke of profit, destiny, and benevolence. The principle of destiny is subtle; the Way of benevolence is vast;

and profit is harmful to righteousness. It is said that the Sage feared students would become mired in profit, extinguishing the public good with private gain, and that by coveting profit they would violate righteousness and sink into the base and debased; therefore, he rarely spoke of it.
The honorable and the poor alike revere [this teaching]. The Son of Heaven is honored; the common people are poor.
From the Son of Heaven down to the commoners, all are equally afflicted by the disease of greed for profit; what difference is there between them?
It is a malady. It is a spreading affliction.
It is a predatory seizure.
Mingjiao said: "Of all the evils committed by people, there are those that have form and those that are formless. As for the formless..."
Evil is that which harms others. Evil with form is that which kills people. The evil of killing is small; the evil of harming is great.
Thus, within the midst of feasting and recreation there may be poisoned chalice; amidst talk and laughter there may be spears and halberds;

within the inner chambers there may be tigers and leopards; and within the neighboring lanes there may be barbarians. Unless one is a sage or a worthy who cuts it off before its sprouting and guards against it—
Regarding matters of ritual and law, is its harm not indeed extreme? (From the *Huxi Guangji*).
It is said that visible evils are small, while invisible evils are great. The treatise states: "Visible evils come from a specific source; [invisible evils do not]."
An enemy that can be resisted may be countered; however, an insidious evil that has no manifest form arrives unpredictably, and its harm is not trivial.

This is why the evil of killing a person is small, while the evil of harming a person is great. Killing a person is spoken of in terms of outward traces; harming a person is spoken of in terms of the heart.
Although the trace may be that of killing, the transgression may be excused; yet when one harbors a cruel heart that harms the principles of righteousness, the calamity is grave.
It is extremely so. Therefore, evil that has form is manifest and visible; evil that lacks form is obscure and unfathomable.
Because it is visible and knowable to people, [the former] is regarded as light and small;
because it is neither seen nor known by people, [the latter] is regarded as heavy and great.
"Yóuyàn" (Wandering Banquet) means "leisure. It is a banquet where guests and hosts rejoice together in tranquility.
"Zhèn" is the name of a poisonous bird; its shape resembles a rooster, its color is purple-green, and its neck is eight inches long.
It feeds on snakes and vipers. Its feathers, when passed through food and drink, kill a person who consumes them.
The *ge* and *mao* are both weapons of war. The *ge* is a leveled-headed halberd, six feet six inches long. The *mao* is two zhang long;
its shape is like a hook. Both are instruments for inflicting injury upon others.
The main chamber at the rear of the hall is called the *táng*; the innermost, secluded part is called the *ào*.
Five neighboring households constitute a *líng*; twenty-five households constitute a *xiàng*.
*Róng* and *dí* refer to the Western Rong and Northern Di tribes.
Ritual (*li*) is the patterned refinement of the principles of Heaven and the norms of human affairs. "Law" (*fa*) refers to systems, institutions, and regulations.
The *Zuo Zhuan* states: "It is stored within the profound and the obscure, yet it manifests at the moment of sudden crisis."
Were it not for sages establishing ritual as a defense, the human race would have perished long ago.

Mingjiao said: "When the Great Awakened Master Liaan was residing at Yuwang Monastery, two monks were disputing over offerings without ceasing, and the administrators were unable to resolve the matter.
The Great Awakened one summoned them and rebuked them, saying: 'In the past, when Lord Bao presided over Kaifeng, there was a citizen who...'"
The hundred taels of white silver that Chen entrusted to me has been lost. I have now returned it to his family, but his son will not accept it.
I hope you, sir, will summon his son and restore it to him. The Duke sighed in wonder and immediately summoned the son to speak with him.

The son declined, saying, "During my late father's lifetime, there were no private deposits of white silver in another household. The two men persisted in their refusal for a long time, until the Duke had no choice but to yield.
He entrusted the city temples and monasteries with the performance of rites for the deceased to offer merit on their behalf. I witnessed this with my own eyes;

even those mired in worldly toil can thus disregard wealth and admire righteousness, yet you, as a disciple of the Buddha, lack integrity and shame to such an extent that I have consequently expelled you according to the rules of the monastic community (*Xihu Guangji*).
Chan Master Huailian of Yuyang Monastery in Mingzhou, known by his courtesy name Qizhi, was a native of the Chen family of Zhangzhou, Fujian.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Hetan Huacheng and belonged to the fourteenth generation of the Qingyuan lineage.

In the first month of the second year of the Huangyou era of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at the Jingshi Jingyin Chan Monastery in the capital. On the tenth day of the second month...
On the ninth day, he was summoned for an audience at Huacheng Hall, where the Emperor questioned him on the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
His responses were so well-suited to the imperial will that he was granted the title Chan Master Dajue. He returned to reside at Guangli Temple on Mount Aśoka.
Lord Bao’s name was Zheng; his courtesy name was Xiren; his posthumous title was Xiaosu. He served as an Imperial Censor by nature, being stern and severe, never once showing a smile.
During his tenure as Governor of Kaifeng, there was a commoner named Li Jue’an who had a son of tender years.
Because he was ill, [Jue] entrusted one hundred taels of white silver to Zhang Huiming. When Jue’an passed away, Huiming returned it to his son.
The son would not accept it; on one hand, he thought that since he had received a person’s deposit, it ought to be returned;
on the other hand, he thought that his father had made no such deposit and thus he should not accept it. Each simply exhausted his own sense of conscience.
It was entrusted to San’ya.
When Dajue Liai first traveled to Mount Lu, Chan Master Yuntong Ne saw him at once and expected him to be a man of great capacity.
Someone asked how he knew this. Ne replied, "This man is centered and impartial; whether in motion or stillness, he maintains dignity."
He was dignified and austere. Furthermore, his mastery of the Way and his integrity were such that his words were concise yet exhaustive in their principles.
Among ordinary people, few who possess such natural endowment fail to become accomplished vessels (from the *Jiupeng ji*).
Chan Master Juren of Yuan Tong Lu Shan, whose courtesy name was Zhongmin, was the son of the Jian family of Zizhou in Western Sichuan.
He was a dharma successor of Ziyong of Yanqing, the tenth generation in the lineage of Qingyuan. By nature he was eminent and heroic; he could recite from memory anything he saw once.

He left home at the age of eleven and received full ordination at seventeen after completing his recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Later, he traveled to Xiangzhou, where he attained a profound and secret realization.

The Essentials of the Mind. Later, he traveled to Mount Lu, where his reputation for the Way grew daily more esteemed. Cheng Shimeng, the Prefect of Nankang Commandery, submitted a memorial requesting that he reside at Yuan Tong Temple.
He was central and impartial, upright and not deviant.
"Venerable" (*zun yan*) means venerable and worthy of respect; "dignified" (*yan*) means majestic and awe-inspiring.
"Righteousness" (*yi*) and "meaning" (*yi*) are synonymous.
"Concise speech" (*yan jian*) implies sincerity and trustworthiness; "exhausting the principle" (*jin li*) refers to the luminous clarity of the essence of the Way.

At the beginning of the Huángyòu era of Emperor Rénzǔ, a small envoy bearing silver seals was dispatched, carrying a decree written on one chi of fine silk, summoning Yuántōng Nè to reside at the Great Monastery of Xiàocí.
Nè declined on the grounds of illness and did not rise to the call; instead, Dàjué submitted a memorial in response to the imperial edict.

Some said, "The Sage Emperor honors and exalts virtue and morality, and his grace extends even to the springs and rocks. Why does the Master so stubbornly decline? Nè replied, "I have unworthily joined the ranks of the monastic community..."
Lun. My hearing and sight have grown dim; I am fortunate to dwell in peace beneath these woods, eating vegetables and drinking water.
Even Buddhas and patriarchs would not do such things, let alone others. As the ancient sages said, "It is difficult to dwell long beneath a great name.

Throughout my life, I have practiced the principle of contentment and have not burdened myself with fame or profit. If one grows weary of it in the heart, when will there ever be enough? Therefore, to the east—
Sūshō once said: "To know contentment is honor; to know sufficiency is wealth; to avoid fame is to preserve one's integrity;
to begin well and end well—this was attained by Yuántōng" (from his *Xíngshí*).
"Renzu" refers to Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty. "Huangyou" is the name of his reign era.
"Yindang" refers to silver ear-rings. During the Qin and Han periods, minor eunuchs wore silver ear-rings with left-side *mao* (sable fur) plumes;
Emperor Ming changed these to gold ear-rings with right-side *mao* plumes. Those who entered and exited the palace to transmit imperial edicts were all exclusively eunuchs.
"Chichi" refers to the "one-chi board" (尺一板) used during the Han dynasty to convey imperial edicts.
As for the restoration of the Bianjing temples, following the destruction of monasteries during the Tang dynasty, the two streets (of the capital) were restored during the Jianlong era of Taizu.
The *Zhishi* (Cessation and Observation) belongs to the Nanshan Vinaya school; it is merely a scholastic study of the commentaries and sub-commentaries of Cien and Xianshou.
Those among scholars who possessed transcendent intelligence all grew weary of names, forms, causes, and effects.

At that time, the Tiantai *Zhi guan* and the Dharma-dhātu Chan school had not yet spread. Since the Chunhua era (the reign title of Emperor Taizong), the Venerable of Siming, Zunsui, the Master of Repentance of Tiantai, [emerged].
He traveled southeast and established his seat there. In the practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, he took the mind as the core principle; his eye of wisdom illuminated the world.
The scholars Yang Yi and Chao Hui further elucidated his teachings. At this time, the Imperial Messenger Li Yunning petitioned to offer a residence in Bianzhou for his use.
He established a Chan monastery and was granted the plaque name "Shifang Jingyin Chan Monastery.

The Emperor took a keen interest in the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and issued an edict for the Three Departments to deliberate on the matter, summoning a man of the Way to serve as abbot. Ou-yang Hsiu and Ch'eng Shih-meng petitioned for the invitation of Chan Master Yuan-t'ung Nê.
The Emperor personally held the imperial decree and sent it down to Chiang-chou; however, Nê claimed he suffered from cataracts and deafness.
He went [to the capital]. The Emperor respected him all the more and permitted him to nominate a successor. Wön-ŭn nominated Taegak to respond to the imperial decree;
thus, the world’s worthies and sages were found through Wön-ŭn.
*Saṃghārāma* is translated as "Garden of the Assembly. A "garden" refers to a place where things grow;

the disciples of the Buddha cause the sprouts of the Path to grow, proceeding toward the attainment of the fruits of sainthood and being able to bring benefit and happiness to all living beings; therefore, it is called the "Garden of the Assembly."
The head of a banner is called a *jing*. It is used to signal those who have performed meritorious deeds;
it also signifies reverence (*qin*) and respectful honor.
To decline firmly means to refuse and not accept. Three declines constitute the ritual limit (*jie*); one decline constitutes courtesy (*li*); two declines constitute [the intermediate stage].
"Qian. "Three refusals" means a firm refusal.
"Lan" (濫) means to be improperly included among the miscellaneous.
"Fànshū" (飯蔬) refers to eating; "shū" (蔬) means coarse food. The mind of the Sage is a complete unity of the heavenly principle (*tīnlǐ*). Although...
Even when one is in the extremity of distress, joy is nonetheless present everywhere.
Such a person regards unrighteous wealth and honor as mere floating clouds—whether they exist or not—and remains utterly unmoved in their heart.
The nature of things is fundamentally like space; it is difficult to name and difficult to characterize. Although gold dust is precious, when it falls into the eye, it becomes a source of irritation.
The ancient sages pointed to Fan Li as an example of one who was entangled in worldly attachments.
"Yan" means "satisfaction.
Dongpo’s surname was Su, his given name Shi, and his courtesy name Zizhan. He was a native of Meishan. He received the Dharma from Chan Master Changcong of Donglin.
His official career reached the rank of Hanlin Academician. He once engaged in spirited exchanges and poetic duels with Foyin, and built a residence in Huangzhou.
Because he lived to the east of the city, he was called the Layman Dongpo.
Master Yantong Ne said: "The life of a cripple depends on his staff; without the staff, he falls. The life of a ferryman depends on his boat."
If one loses their boat, they will drown. Generally, those who dwell beneath the forest trees have nothing of their own to rely upon;
those who rely on external power for their importance cannot avoid the calamity of falling and drowning the moment they lose what they rely upon (from the *Lushan Yalu*).
"Lame" means being unable to walk. "To rely upon" (*xié*) is a term for having something to depend on. Yuantong Ne said:
"In the past, the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang established monastic groves and instituted rules and regulations, desiring to remedy the corruption of the Dharma during this age of semblance.
Yet he did not realize that scholars of this age of semblance would steal those very rules and regulations to destroy Baizhang’s [legacy]."

In the remote antiquity, though people dwelt in nests or caves, everyone disciplined themselves; after the era of Great Sages, though there are lofty halls and vast mansions, everyone neglects themselves.
Thus it is said: "Safety and peril depend on virtue; rise and fall depend on destiny.
If virtue can be sustained, what need is there for monasteries? If destiny can be relied upon, why employ rules and regulations? (From *Yelù*)
Baizhang Dazhi Chan Master Huaihai of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou was a native of the Wang family of Changle in Fuzhou.
He was a dharma heir of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi and the second generation descendant of the lineage of Nanyue.
A "congregation forest" (conglin) is the place where the assembly of monks resides; it is the site where practitioners settle their minds to cultivate the Way.
Grass that does not grow in disorder is called a "thicket" (cong); trees that do not grow in disorder are called a "forest" (lin). This signifies that within it there are rules and standards.
The compass is for circular objects; the square is for rectangular objects. These are the models and standards of the monastic community (chōrin).

To misappropriate the compass and square for public purposes while placing them in private service constitutes the meaning of "stealing from one's own office" (kanshu jidō). Furthermore, to commit villainy by exploiting the Dharma is likewise a transgression.
"An assistant supervisor acts as a thief. This means that by following the rules and regulations, one instead brings harm to the monastic community.
In ancient times, those who dwelt in nests or caves had no monasteries;
they lived in nests during the summer and in caves during the winter, governing themselves according to the established codes and laws.
Regarding security and peril, prosperity and decline: for those with virtue, the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) flourishes daily;

for those without virtue, the community falls into daily peril. This is destiny; this is the times. It is said that security and peril depend on the person, while prosperity and decline depend on the times.
If the abbot lacks virtue and moral character, the community will soon be abandoned. Even if he possesses virtue and moral character, if it is not the right time, he cannot succeed by force.
One may take this up and practice it. The *Huashu* of Master Tan says: "If virtue can be carried forth, why necessarily expand one's stores of grain and silk?
If numbers can be relied upon, why necessarily expand one's armor and weapons?"
Yuantong said to Dajue: "The ancient sages cultivated their minds before thoughts had sprouted and guarded their emotions before they were disordered. This was because preparation prevents calamity;
thus, one sets up double gates and strikes the wooden clappers to await violent guests, taking this from the hexagram Yù (Preparation).

When a matter is prepared for in advance, it is easy; to act upon it at the last moment is certainly difficult. Among the worthies and sages of antiquity, there were those who harbored lifelong anxieties."
That there is not a single morning of distress lies truly in this (from the *Jiuping ji*).
To govern is called "governing" (*zhi*); to settle the mind is called "governing. To cultivate and rectify one's affairs while applying one's effort is called "governing.
When affairs possess order and principles and their efficacy has already been manifested, it is therefore called "governed."
The hexagram *Yù* (Thundery Joy), composed of *Dì* (Earth) below and *Léi* (Thunder) above, carries the meaning of peace, harmony, and joyful delight.
Yang [Xi] said: "Once the paths of the rivers and roads are open, violent guests will arrive; this is why there is no other method than to provide defense. Thus, he takes the image from *Yù*:
by setting up double gates to ward them off and striking wooden clappers to alert them, violent guests will have no way to enter. As for the two yin lines...

The two yang lines above represent the image of double gates. The single yang line at the bottom represents the image of striking the wooden clapper. The three yin lines within represent the image of joy and ease.
Furthermore, it is said that "Yù" (Ease/Indulgence) signifies indolence; one strikes the wooden clapper to awaken others from such indolence.
The character for *tuò* (柝) is pronounced *tuō*. It is made by hewing wood; it is struck during night patrols. Master Dàjué Liǎn said:
"Jade is not fashioned into a vessel unless it is carved; a person does not know the Way unless they study. What is present allows one to know the past;
what comes after allows one to know what preceded. That which is good may serve as a model; that which is evil [may serve as a warning]."
This is the rule. Examining the predecessors of old, those who established themselves and achieved renown in their time rarely did so without accomplishing it through study and inquiry (Jiǔfēng jí).
The two lines beginning with "Jade is not polished" are from the "Xueji" (Record of Learning) chapter of the *Liji* (Book of Rites).
The two lines beginning with "What is currently... are from Han Yu’s memorial in response to Emperor Shunzong of Tang.
The good is that by which one’s own virtuous mind is inspired; the evil is that by which one’s wayward ambitions are chastened.
The Great Awakened One said:
"The principle of the wondrous Way was once embodied by the sages in the *Yi* (Book of Changes). When the Zhou dynasty declined, the legacy of the former kings—"
When the Dharma was destroyed and rites and righteousness had perished, then strange words and heterodox arts emerged sporadically to disorder the customs.

Upon our Śākyamuni’s entry into the Middle Kingdom, he demonstrated the primary truth (*paramārtha*) to people in its pure essence, yet from beginning to end he established compassion to transform sentient beings;
this was also a means of responding to the times. Since the birth of the human race, when the original simplicity had not yet dispersed, there were the Three Sovereigns.

Their teachings were concise and plain; this was the Spring. When the apertures of the emotions were daily being excavated, the teachings of the Five Emperors became detailed and ornate; this was the Summer.
As the times and the world changed, human emotions shifted accordingly; thus, the teachings of the Three Kings became dense and rigorous; this was the Autumn.

Regarding the proclamations and oaths of the Shang and Zhou dynasties, scholars of later generations have often been unable to understand them, yet to the people of those times, they were as clear as listening to [a familiar conversation].

If one follows this without deviation, how would the customs differ from those of the present? Yet when it comes to the ritual offerings of the Qin and Han dynasties, there is nothing they will not resort to.
Therefore, for those in the world who cannot bear [this] and wish to hear [the truth], the Buddha, the Tathāgata, then appeared.
First, one must examine this through the principle of human nature and destiny. Winter is one of the four seasons of Heaven, which circulate to generate and sustain all things.
The Sage establishes his teachings so that they mutually support one another to transform and perfect the world; it is precisely like this.
Yet, when these reach their ultimate limit, all inevitably suffer from defects. These defects are merely superficial traces;

it must be that sages and worthies arise in the world from time to time to rescue them. Since the Qin and Han dynasties, more than a thousand years have passed, and social customs have become increasingly decadent and thin.
The teachings of the sages were established as three distinct pillars, yet they have come to disparage one another;
the Great Way has become desolate and few return to it—this is truly lamentable (Letter in Reply to Minister Sun Xunlao).
The wondrous spirit is unfathomable; its profound mysteries are difficult to know. Words cannot express it, and analytical discernment cannot comprehend it;
therefore, it is called "wondrous" (miao).
It is that which is entrusted or manifested; it is extraordinary and strange.
"Reaching up to" (dai ji) means to arrive at.
"Śākyamuni" is translated here as "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren). This signifies that he transforms sentient beings through the benefits of benevolence and virtue;
his essence is pure and singular, without admixture.

The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is not existent; the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is not non-existent. Being neither existent nor non-existent is called the Middle Way, the ultimate truth.
"To show" means to manifest; it is like heaven and earth manifesting the myriad phenomena to humanity.
Compassion consists of kindness, which can bestow happiness, and pity, which can extract one from suffering.
As for the birth of the people, they descended from Heaven; that is, when the Yin and Yang united in sexual intercourse, they were born as human beings through the transformation of the primal qi.
"Pure and simple" means being sincere and not hypocritical.
"The Three Sovereigns" refers to their majesty. "Great" (Dà) signifies that the Dao is as vast as Heaven; "Heaven" is a designation for the ultimate greatness.
Because they were resplendent, no one could oppose them. [These were] Tàihào (the Lord of Great Brilliance), Fúxī; Yán dì (the Lord of the Flaming Fire), Shénnóng; and Huángdì (the Yellow Emperor).
The Xiong clan was able to broaden their Way; thus they were called the Three Sovereigns (Sanhuang). They were adept at employing the principles of governance according to the times.
During the era of the Three Sovereigns, customs were simple and pure, and the people were honest and unadorned; they administered affairs by tying knots in cords.
To draw lines on the ground to create a prison is to lack the state where wealth is abundant without competition and the people submit naturally without restrictive commands.
"Sin" (竇) refers to a hole or cavity;

if one does not carve out the heart so that it possesses the free roaming of Heaven (*tianyou*), then the six cavities will contend with one another—this is called "carving the emotions" (*zaocqing*).
The Five Emperors were those who practiced "shendì" (examination and discernment). This refers to examining and discerning the myriad things; it was a title for those who ruled over the world.
They were: Shao Hao, the Lord of Metal Heaven; Zhuanxu, the Lord of High Yang; Di Ku, the Lord of High Xin; and Di Yao, the Lord of Tao Tang.

Emperor Shun of the Youyu clan presided over the altars of soil and grain and brought peace to the people; his conduct accorded with the Way of the Sovereigns, and thus he is numbered among the Five Emperors.
He was adept at employing benevolence and trustworthiness.
Examining the records of the era of the Five Emperors, it was then that the atmosphere gradually opened; institutions were first established and laws were formulated.

The Five Canons became earnest and the Five Rites were complete; the Five Robes were distinguished and the Five Punishments were comprehensive. Thus, the legal codes, rituals, and music were fully manifested.
The Three Kings were those toward whom the world turned. They were Xia Yu, whose clan name was Si; Yin Tang, whose clan name was Zi;
and Zhou Wen Wang, whose clan name was Ji. Confucius said, "They were those who skillfully employed wisdom and courage."
During the era of the Three Kings of Mithila, the position of the "Nine-Five" (the throne) was not transmitted to descendants by bypassing the worthy;
rather, ritual, music, literature, and the systems of punishment and law reached their full perfection at this time.
*Gao* (Edicts) and *Shi* (Oaths) are titles of chapters in the *Shangshu*. Examples include the "Zhonghui’s Edict" and the "Edict of Tang" from the Shang dynasty;

and the "Kang Edict," the "Jiu Edict," the "Gan Oath," the "Tang Oath," and the "Tai Oath" from the Zhou dynasty. An oath is a solemn agreement. To clarify this covenant to the feudal lords, it is said:
"If I, your sovereign, commit a transgression, do not hold the myriad regions accountable. If the myriad regions commit a transgression, the guilt lies with me."
As for "I" (Zhen-gong):
"Buddha" is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Awakened. This means awakening oneself and awakening others, such that one's practice of awakening is perfected.
The Tathāgata comes from the path of suchness. "Suchness" refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*); "coming" refers to initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*).
Because the initial and the original are non-dual, he is called the Tathāgata.
That which is bestowed by Heaven upon the life-principle and destiny is called "destiny" (*ming*); that which is received by things is called "nature" (*xing*). As for the nature...
All these are termed "principles" (*li*). Although their names differ, the principle is one and the same.
They alternate and interact with one another.
As for the traces of decline, they are like the unworthiness of Danzhu and Shangjun, or the lack of kingship in Jie, Zhou, You, and Li. Regarding the Law...
The decline of the teachings at the gates and the disorder of the state's administrative regulations are both termed "corrupt traces" (*bieji*).
"Mimi" means gradual and progressive decline; furthermore, it implies a process of disintegration that extends and continues.
The Three Cauldrons were fashioned by King Yu. They have three legs and two ears; they are vessels for harmonizing the five flavors.
The cauldrons are divided into three legs, with one mouth facing heaven and another mouth [facing the earth]; this represents the Way of the King.
"Di-zi" means to revile, reproach, and slander.
Sun Xunlao, the Secretary of the Institute for the Compilation of Writings and Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, asked for instruction from Dajue, saying:

"Since the Three Dynasties, successive sages have inherited one another; government has been harmonious with the people, and the Way and its tradition have continued unbroken. Yet, Buddhism was not included [among them]."
The future was yet to come. From the end of the Zhou and Ji dynasties through the changes from Qin to Han, the nets of law and the nests of punishment overspread the skies and fell upon the wilds;

yet they did not reform themselves because the Buddha-dharma had already arrived. Throughout the four seas, factions divided and divergent doctrines emerged one after another, reaching their height from the Tang dynasty through the Five Dynasties.
Amidst the myriad affairs and ten thousand state machinations, where order and chaos were never constant, what was the purpose of upholding the teachings of the Buddha?
Furthermore, there are those who wear grass garments and eat from trees, dwelling in crags and drinking from mountain streams; these do no more than seek their own private perfection.
Others possess fame yet act contrary to their reputation, assuming a guise that is not true. As the transformative influence of the teachings has not yet reached them, corruption arises.
However, the Master must surely have a discernment regarding this; we await his explanation. This "Treatise on the Sublime Way" is the Master’s response.

The Great Awakened One said: "Now, one who acts as a leader of a region and wishes to practice the Way they have attained to benefit others must first subdue themselves and bestow kindness upon all things, lowering their heart toward everyone.
Only then, regarding gold and silk as mere refuse and soil, will the fourfold assembly honor and turn to them. (Letter to the Monk Xu of Jiuxian).
This means to eliminate one's own selfish mind.
Regarding the fourfold assembly—the two groups of householders and the two groups of those who have left the home life—the Great Awakened One said:
"There were those among the predecessors who possessed the talent for intelligence yet lacked concern for their own safety or security, such as Shimen Cong, who dwelt at..."
O worthy Shun, these two cases may serve as a warning. Thus, it is truly difficult to discern the fixed karma of human life;
yet, if one examines its origins in detail, how could one fail to recognize that it stems from the fault of negligence and lack of reflection? Therefore it is said:
"Calamities lie hidden in the subtle and manifest themselves through what people neglect. Viewed in this light, one ought all the more to exercise caution and reverence. (From the *Jiupeng ji*)
He was intelligent and his learning was unconfused; thus he was called "Cōngmíng" (Intelligent and Wise).
Regarding Shìmén Cōng of Gǔyǐnshān Shìmén Sè in Xiāngzhōu: Chan Master Yùncōng succeeded Shǒushān Niàn Chánshī.
He was the ninth generation under Nányuè. After he attained the Dharma, while he was residing at Shìmén, the Governor of Xiāngzhōu...
He was flogged and humiliated out of personal malice. Upon his return, the assembly of monks welcomed him by the roadside.

The head monk stepped forward to inquire after him, saying, "The Governor has unjustly and cruelly insulted you, Master. The Master pointed to the ground and said, "A pile of bones rises from level earth.
As soon as he spoke, a pile of bones surged up at his hand. When the Governor heard of this, he sent men to scrape it away, but it surged up again just as before.
The Prefect’s entire family perished in Xiangzhou.
As for Chan Master Yunju Xiaoshun of Nankang County’s Qixian Monastery, his courtesy name was Laofu.
He was a descendant of Huo of Ruizhou and a tenth-generation successor in the lineage of Qingyuan. He resided at Qixian on Mount Lu during the reign of Emperor Huai.

The official was stationed in Nankang, where there were many instances of corruption. Emperor Shun could not bear that the property of the Sangha (changzhu-wu) should be used to solidify his position through personal ties;
consequently, he was slandered by others. When the Prefectural Governor questioned him about returning to secular life, the people stripped him of his robes.

Dajue had previously entered Shun’s chamber, so he went to the capital to visit Dajue. Dajue yielded the main quarters to Shun and resided in a side room. Emperor Renzong [several times... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

The Emperor issued an edict for him to enter the palace to inquire about the Way, yet [Xiao] ultimately did not speak of the matter of Shun. One day, by imperial decree, Jingci Temple was ordered to provide a meal for monks;

there he saw Dajue serving Shun with great reverence. Upon his return, he reported this to the Emperor. The Emperor summoned him for an audience and sighed, saying, "His Daoist resonance is extraordinary and magnificent;
he is truly a man of realization from the mountains and forests. He then wrote upon a fan: "Bestowed upon Xiao Shun," and permitted him to remain as a monk as before.

He resided again at Xiqian, where he was further granted purple robes and a silver bowl. On the day Shun resigned from Xiqian, two strong men carried his sedan chair as far as the gate of Luohan Temple;
the two men said to one another, "Now he is no longer the Elder of our monastery."
"There is no need for a long-distance escort; leave the sedan chair and return. After Shun had returned, he sent someone to comfort him, saying, "What you did at that time was correct.
Just set your mind at ease; there is no need for suspicion or fear. Upon entering the monastery and ascending the hall, he said:
"Without cause, I was slandered and unjustly met with misfortune; for more than half a year, I lived as a layman. Today I return once more to Sanxia Temple. Several...
"Much joy, how much anger?"—the particle *u* here functions as a term of inquiry or hesitation;
it expresses a sense of humility and reticence, such that one does not dare speak with direct certainty, yet still asks: "Is it so?
*In-mi* (隱微) means "hidden and obscure" above, and "minute matters" below; it refers to the fact that the beginning of an affair is not worth worrying about, yet calamity [may arise].
What is hidden and obscure is deeply cause for concern. For that which is manifest is easily seen by others, and thus one may act upon it;
whereas that which is hidden is difficult for others to know, and therefore one must be cautious and not negligent.
Master Yunju Shun, whose courtesy name was Laofu, while residing at Qixian on Mount Lu, suffered an unjust and violent assault due to the private resentment of the local magistrate, Official Huai.
The people stripped him of his robes, and he traveled to the capital to seek out Dajue. Upon reaching Shan yang (present-day Chuzhou), he was detained by snow at an inn.
One night, a guest arrived through the falling snow accompanied by two servants; upon seeing Laofu, he recognized him as an old acquaintance.
Having changed his clothes, he prostrated before him. The old man questioned him, and the guest replied, "In the past, while following Master Dongshan, I was a laborer who carried loads to Hanyang;
I am Song Rong, your former servant. The old man conversed with him about their shared past, and the guest sighed for a long time.
At dawn, he prepared a meal and presented five taels of white silver. He then called for a servant, and the guest said, "This boy shall go back and forth to the capital."

The number of cities passed through was great, and the hardships encountered along the way were fully detailed. Since the Master’s journey was certainly not undertaken with ease, I, an old man, was able to reach the capital by virtue of this;
from this, I gain even greater insight into the character these two men maintained throughout their lives (from the *Jiuping ji*).
To suffer injustice is to encounter agonizing pain;
to be met with transgression and violence is to be contrary to principle. These phrases appear in Mencius, Chapter "Li Lou.
"The people wear the robes of laymen" refers to the clothing of those who have returned to secular life.
He recounted events from the past.
Regarding the carriage of the Son of Heaven: that which has wheels is called a *liǎn* (palanquin), while that which lacks wheels is called a *yú* (litter).
The Great Awakened One said, "Old man Shun, by nature you are simple and straightforward; you do not understand matters such as weighing, balancing, or the accumulation of wealth. Day after day...

His fixed daily recitations never underwent even the slightest alteration. Although tasks such as lighting lamps and sweeping the floor were performed by him personally, he once remarked, "The ancients had the precept that if one does not work for a day, one shall not eat for a day;
what kind of person am I? Though I am advanced in years, my resolve has only grown firmer.

Someone asked, "Why do you not have your attendants perform these tasks for you? The old man replied, "I have endured the vicissitudes of cold and heat, and my rising and sitting have been irregular."
I do not wish to weary you.

"Fu" (賦) refers to the endowment. That which is evenly distributed and spread forth is called "fu"; it signifies that which Heaven has bestowed as nature upon humanity, being uniform and without partiality.
"Scale" (quan-heng) refers to the upper weight (the counterweight) and the lower beam of a balance.
"Merchandise" (huo) refers to goods that are transformed into objects through wealth;
"accumulation" (zhi) refers to the gathering and storing of wealth and treasures. Furthermore, "殖" (zhi) also refers to what is appropriate for merchandise.
"One day without work, there is no Baizhang Monastery. This monastery was situated on the summit of Mount Nanyue.
Master Dazhi labored daily to repay the offerings provided to him. When someone urged him to stop, he said, "I have no virtue to spare from burdening others.
The community could not bear it and hid his tools; when they searched everywhere and could not find them, he refused to eat. Thus, there is [the saying]: "One day without work..."
The saying, "If one day you do not work, do not eat for that day," has spread throughout the world. The conduct of past masters was for the most part like this.
It is something to be emulated; it is something to be practiced.
Shun Laofu said: "To transmit and uphold this Way, what is most precious is that all things be true.

To distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and to eliminate deluded sentiments, is the reality of governing the mind. To recognize cause and effect and clarify sin and merit is the reality of one’s conduct.

To propagate the Way and virtue and welcome those who come from afar is the reality of presiding over a monastery. To assess talents and appoint officials is the reality of employing people. To examine speech..."

To act and determine what is permissible constitutes the true essence of seeking out the worthy; if one does not maintain this reality but merely displays empty fame, it is of no benefit to principle.

Therefore, in a person’s conduct, sincerity and integrity are paramount. If one maintains this without wavering, then even amidst the level and the perilous, one can remain consistent—both matters will be tranquil (from the *Ershi Tantan’an Ji*).
To transmit from generation to generation is called *chuan* (transmission). To grasp and maintain with earnest devotion is called *chi* (retention).
To uphold one's integrity so that one’s resolve does not change is called *cao* (steadfastness). To practice and tread the path without negligence is called *li* (practice).
The *zhuchi* (abbot) abides in moral virtue and maintains the teachings so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Furthermore, he dwells in the ultimate truth, upholding it without loss.
"Huàn" means to display for sale. "Yú" means to change.
"Yí" refers to the upper part being level and even, while the lower part is steep and uneven.
It signifies the attainment of principle.
Shun Laofu said to Master Fushan Yuan: "In pursuing the unsurpassed, wondrous Way, one becomes even more steadfast when at one's limit, and even more vigorous as one grows old.
One must not conform to worldly customs by covetously seeking fame and profit, thereby losing the supreme virtue within. For jade is prized for its purity and luster;
thus, vermilion and purple cannot alter its substance. The pine stands out in the cold of winter; frost and snow cannot wither its integrity."
Thus we know that integrity and righteousness are the greatest virtues in the world. Only you, sir, possess a character worthy of admiration; how could you not exert yourself?
As the ancients said: "The soaring wings fly alone; solitary wind has no companion. This is indeed fitting for you (from the *Guǎnglù*).
Master Fayan Yuanjian of Mount Fushan in Shuzhou, known as Master Yuanlu, was a native of the Wang clan of Zhengzhou.

He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xiao of Xie County. Once, while traveling through Sichuan with Daguanying, Xue Datou, and a group of seven or eight others, they encountered several instances of trouble.
The Master resolved these matters through his wisdom; because he was skilled in administrative affairs, the group referred to him as "Lugong" (the Recorder).
"Only then will it become even more firm"— these were the words of Ma Yuan. "Not falling from the ambition for the azure clouds"—
how could one not recognize the heart that remains resolute even at white hair?
If one assumes an improper appearance merely to accommodate others and seek personal ease, this is not true integrity.
What the mind and heart direct is called "will" (*zhì*); it consists in being cautious and not pursuing external objects.
"Substance" (zhi) refers to one's fundamental nature. "Manifestation" (biao) refers to endurance.
"Integrity and righteousness" (jieyi) means possessing steadfast character while one's actions accord with moral principle.
"Dignity" (biaozhi) means to stand out; it describes the ultimate state of being transcendent, eminent, and towering.
The *Yi* says of self-strengthening: "The way of the gentleman is to be active and vigilant all day long, striving with vigor and never ceasing.
This is like the soaring flight of powerful wings above and the vigorous flapping of feathers below.
Master Fushan Yuan said: "The ancients attended their teachers and chose their friends with such diligence that they did not dare to be idle day or night.

Even when performing menial tasks such as tending the hearth or carrying grain for grinding, they never shied from labor. While I was at Yechian, I personally witnessed this through my own experience."

However, if one harbors even a slight regard for profit and harm, or a mind that calculates gain and loss, then one will resort to equivocation and indulgence to such an extent that there is no limit.
Furthermore, if one’s own person is not upright, how can one possibly study the Way? (The Dharma Words of Attendant Yue)
"Lushen" (陸沈) means to sink without water; it refers to being hidden when one ought to be manifest, sinking among the multitude so as not to wish for others to know one.
Master Guisheng of Guangjiao Monastery in Yexian, Ruozhou, was the son of the Jia family of Jizhou.
He succeeded Master Nian of Shou Mountain, the ninth generation under Nanyue. His tenure as abbot was austere and rigorous; the monastics feared him.
When Fushan Yuan and Tianyi Huai heard of his lofty reputation, they went specifically to visit and consult him. It happened to be a time of bitter snow and cold;
he rebuked them with shouts and drove them away, even splashing water on the ground until their robes were soaked. Other monks...
The master became angry and left. Only Yuan and Huai remained; they adjusted their robes and sitting mats and sat back down as before.

When the master returned, he scolded them, saying, "If you do not leave immediately, I shall beat you. Yuan stepped forward and said, "We two have come from thousands of miles away specifically to study the Chan of the Master.
How can we leave merely because you splashed us with a ladleful of water? The master laughed and said, "You two..."

When Yuan came, he insisted on practicing Chan meditation; however, he subsequently went to register as a resident monk and was appointed as the head cook (*dianzuo*). The community grew weary of his austere and simple lifestyle.
One day, while Xuansheng had gone out to the manor, Yuan stealthily took the keys and retrieved oil and flour to prepare a five-flavor congee.

Just as it was nearly finished, the Master suddenly returned. After the meal, the Master went to the kitchen, and Yuan arrived. The Master said, "You have stolen the oil and flour; this constitutes embezzlement."

Changzhu said, "I actually took oil and flour; I pray you will punish me. The Master ordered that his robes and bowl be appraised and returned to him, then struck him thirty blows with a staff and drove him out of the monastery.
His fellow practitioners urged him to reconsider, but the Master would not consent. A friend said:
"If you will not allow me to return home, I beg only this: let me join the assembly to listen to the Dharma. The Master did not grant permission.

One day, as the Master went out into the street, he saw [the monk] standing before a guesthouse for travelers. The Master said, "This is the corridor of the monastery's gate quarters; you have been here for a long time."

"Has Yuan ever returned the shop money? he asked. "Have the accounts calculated and whatever remains owed collected? Yuan showed no sign of distress; instead, he went to the market with his alms bowl to beg for the funds to repay it.
One day, as the Master was walking out into the street, he saw Yuan holding his bowl. Upon returning, he said to the assembly, "Yuan’s true intent is to practice Chan.
He then sent him back to his quarters and, ascending the hall before the assembly, formally bestowed the robe upon him as a Dharma heir.
"To follow those who conspire for good and oppose those who do not—how could there be any fixed standard of impartiality?
This is from the *Xiaoya* (Minor Odes).
"To seek peace through mere indulgence and expedient tolerance"—this is from the *Liji* (Book of Rites).
Master Yuǎn said: "Between heaven and earth, there are indeed things that grow easily;

yet if one exposes them to the sun for a single day and subjects them to the cold for ten days, it is not seen that they can grow. The unsurpassed, wondrous Way is brilliantly manifest within the space between the heart and the eyes, and thus it is not difficult to see.
It simply requires firm resolve and diligent practice; its realization may be awaited whether sitting or standing."
Perhaps one may believe for a single day and yet doubt for ten days; one may be diligent in the morning and yet weary by evening.
It is not merely that these things are difficult to perceive before one's eyes; I fear that one might turn their back on them for the rest of one's life. (Written by Chan Master Yun).
"Bào yīn" means "exposed to the sun.

Master Yuǎn said: "Among the essentials of monastic administration, nothing precedes the careful examination of what to adopt and what to reject. The ultimate point of adoption and rejection is determined within;
the germination of safety and peril is determined without. However, safety is not the safety of a single day, nor is peril the peril of a single day."
All things arise from gradual accumulation; this must be examined. By abiding in the Way and its Virtue, one accumulates the Way and its Virtue;

by abiding in ritual and righteousness, one accumulates ritual and righteousness; by abiding in exploitation and oppression, one accumulates resentment. When resentment accumulates, those both within and without become estranged and turn away.
When ritual and righteousness accumulate, those within and without become harmonious and joyful. When the Way and its Power accumulate, those within and without are moved and submit.
Therefore, when the Way, its Power, ritual, and righteousness are pervasive, both within and without rejoice; when oppression and resentment reach their extreme, both within and without grieve.
Such movements of grief and joy bring forth the responses of calamity and fortune.
To exploit, plunder, and harm others;
"inner" refers to one's own followers, while "outer" refers to the fourfold assembly.
To have the grace of one's benevolence spread everywhere is called "pervasive. They grieve [at his actions], daring to be angry yet not daring to speak.
Master Yuǎn said: "There are three essentials for a *zhuchi* (abbot): benevolence (*rén*), clarity (*míng*), and courage (*yǒng*).

The benevolent person practices the Way and virtue, promotes transformation and instruction, brings peace to those above and below, and brings joy to those who come and go. The clear-sighted person observes propriety and righteousness, recognizes safety and peril, discerns the worthy from the foolish, and distinguishes right from wrong.
The courageous person acts with decisiveness, makes judgments without hesitation, eliminates the treacherous, and removes the sycophants. To be benevolent yet lacking clarity—"
If there is a field that is not plowed, it is like having intelligence but lacking courage. If there are seedlings that are not weeded, it is like having courage but lacking benevolence;
one knows how to reap but does not know how to sow. When these three are complete, the forest flourishes; if one is missing, it declines; if two are missing, it is in peril.
Third, if there were not even one [of these], then the Way of sustaining and upholding [the Dharma] would perish (from the "Two Matters" letter sent to Master Jingyin).
