Regarding the three essentials, Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty was advised by Sima Guang, who said: "Benevolence, intelligence, and courage. The commentary states:

"The benevolent person is pure in accordance with the principles of Heaven; they sever all evils and possess not the slightest trace of selfish desire. The intelligent person illuminates the nature of physical phenomena and distinguishes [between right and wrong]."

Regarding right and wrong, they harbor not a single moment of doubt. The courageous, upon seeing what is righteous, will surely act upon it; hearing of what is good, they will surely transform themselves;
they do not retreat or shrink from anything.

To transform others through the Way and instruct them is called "teaching" (jiao). To personally practice it from above so that it moves like the wind among those below is called "transformation" (hua).
"Flattery" (nin) refers to talent in eloquence used for skillful compliance and service.
"Weeding" (yun) refers to hoeing; "reaping" (yi) refers to harvesting.
Master Yuan said: "The wise and the foolish, the worthy and the unworthy, are as different as water and fire; they cannot share the same vessel, nor do they exist at the same time.
This is simply their inherent nature. The virtuous and wise are pure, refined, upright, and sincere; they deliberate according to the Way, its Virtue, benevolence, and righteousness.

In their speech and actions, they only fear not conforming to human feelings or failing to accord with the principles of things. As for those who are unworthy, they are treacherous, perilous, deceitful, and sycophantic."
Arrogant toward themselves and displaying their own abilities, they indulge in desires and seek only profit, disregarding everything else.

Thus, when a monastery gains a worthy person, its virtue and morality flourish and its regulations are established, eventually forming a successful seat of the Dharma. Yet, if even one unworthy person is placed among them, they will stir up the crowd and bring disorder to the assembly.

Both within and without the realm are ill at ease. Though one may possess great wisdom and ritual propriety, what use are they? Such is the difference between the wise and the foolish, the worthy and the unworthy, the superior and the inferior.
How can one not exercise discernment? (A Letter from Venerable Huiru Fang)
The wise, the foolish, the virtuous, and the unworthy all receive the qi of purity and harmony. Those who possess clear and sharp talent and discernment are called "wise.

Those who receive the qi of turbid dregs and conflicting impurities, being stubborn, dull, and ignorant, are called "foolish. Those who receive the most perfectly harmonious qi of Heaven and Earth [are the virtuous].
Those who are compassionate, frugal, gentle, and kind are called "worthy. Those who possess a temperament of chaotic yin and yang, being fierce, treacherous, and depraved, are called "unworthy.
This is a matter of absolute principle, like the mutual exclusion of light and darkness, or the impossibility of incense and skunk coexisting.

Deceitful flattery—those who are deceitful flatterers do not resemble the superior man (*junzi*). They claim that their speech is as refined as that of the sages and worthies, yet their conduct does not match that of ordinary people.
From the very beginning of birth, one's inherent lot and destiny were determined; thus, purity and turbidity were already fixed, resulting in the distinction between the wise and the foolish.
This is their differentiation.
To be of a single, pure color in the formation of one's character is called "pure" (chun); to be gentle and capable of sagehood is called "exquisite" (yi).
"Satiety and desire" (shi-yu) refers to superior greed; it is that which the lower emotions find pleasing and crave.
The main ropes that bind everything together are called the "net-veins" (綱); the various meshes are called the "net-arteries" (紀). A net relies upon its net-veins and net-arteries;
a ruler relies upon his ministers as limbs. These are the great standards of regulation.
"Superior" refers to excellence; "inferior" refers to weakness. "Wu" means "how.
Master Yuanyang said:
"The abbot resides above and ought to receive those below with humility and courtesy; the administrators reside below and must exert themselves to the fullest."
Thus they serve their superiors. When those above and below are in harmony, the way of maintaining the monastery (zhuchi) flows unimpeded.

If those in superior positions are arrogant and self-important, while those in subordinate positions are negligent and aloof, such that the sentiments between superior and inferior do not communicate, then the way of maintaining the monastery is blocked.

When ancient masters maintained a monastery, they were at leisure and had no pressing affairs; they would engage in relaxed discussion with their students on all manner of topics, reaching every possible depth of inquiry.
For this reason, even a single word or half a phrase recorded in biographies is still cited to this day. What is the cause of this?

First, it is to ensure that the sentiments of those above reach those below, so that the Way remains free from obstruction. Second, it is to allow for a prior assessment of whether the capacities and natures of students are sufficient.
In all matters of advancing and retreating, he acted with perfect propriety; naturally, those above and below were harmonious and solemn, and both the distant and the near turned to him in reverence.
It was through this that the flourishing of monastic communities was brought about (from the Letter to Qing Huayan).
"From' (從) and 'rong' (容) are pronounced with the *qi* (恭) and *qie* (切) finals respectively; they denote being relaxed and unhurried.
'Yong' (雍) and 'su' (肅) denote harmony and reverence.
Master Yuanyang said to Daowu Zhen: "If one's study has not yet reached the Way, yet one flaunts what one has seen and heard, and races about with intellectual acumen and understanding..."
Those who seek to overcome others through the sharpness of their speech and eloquence are like a latrine smeared with vermilion and lacquer;
it does nothing but increase its stench (from the *Xihu jiwen*).
Daowu Zhen, the Chan Master Zhen of Daowu Monastery in Tanzhou, was a successor of Chan Master Shishuang Yuan.
He was the tenth generation descendant of Nanyue;
he was renowned for his bold and unrestrained self-confidence.
*Dan-huo* (丹雘) is a general term for mineral pigments and colors. The *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) states that there is much *dan-huo* beneath Mount Jizu.
The *Shuowen jiezi* (Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters) states: "Huo (雘): beautiful."
Master Yuan said to the senior seat-holder Yan: "The mind is the sovereign of the single body and the root of the myriad practices.

If the mind does not attain wondrous awakening, deluded emotions arise spontaneously. Once deluded emotions arise, one’s vision of principle is not clear. When the vision of principle is not clear, right and wrong become confused and disordered.

Therefore, to govern the mind, one must seek wondrous awakening. Upon awakening, the spirit becomes harmonious and the breath tranquil; the countenance becomes reverent and the expression dignified. Regarding delusion...
Thoughts and emotions are all melted away into the true mind. By using this to govern the mind, the mind becomes naturally numinous and wondrous.
Thereafter, one guides beings and points out their delusions; who would not follow such transformation? (From the *Fushan Shilu*)
Wuzu Yan, Chan Master Fayan of Wuzu in Qizhou, was the son of the Deng family from Mianzhou.
He succeeded Chan Master Baiyun Yuan and belonged to the thirteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage.
The mind-mind is the treasury of spiritual intelligence; it is empty yet luminous, penetrating and transparent, that which possesses all principles and responds to myriad affairs.
It is said that the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable dharma-gates are all established by means of this single mind.
"Respectful" (*jing*) means harmonious and joyful.
"Dignified" (*zhuang*) means solemn and majestic. "Spiritual" (*shen*) refers to the numinous. That which cannot be measured by yin and yang is called the spiritual.
Furthermore, it is the essence of yang. Master Wuzu Yan said: "In these times, those among the monastic community who study the Way do not have their reputations spread abroad; this is not because—"
That which people distrust is generally due to their holy life (*brahmacarya*) being impure and their conduct lacking sincerity.

They often seek fame, reputation, profit, and sustenance through expedient means, extensively flaunting their outward ornaments; consequently, they are censured by those with discernment. Thus, they obscure what is essential and subtle;
even if they possess the Way and its Virtue like the Buddhas and Patriarchs, those who hear or see them will doubt and not believe them. You all, on another day...
If there are those who cover their heads with sprouts, they should encourage themselves by this (from the letter of Fojian to Foguo).
A scholar is given the title "De" (Virtue);
"di" means to be precise and verified, and "dang" means to be central and upright.
To hear the sound of departing is called "hearing," as the sound manifests externally.
To desire profit and wealth is called "profit" (li); that which is delighted in by such profit is called "nourishment" (yang).
Taking a handful of thatch to leave the mundane world and become a person for others is what constitutes a "thatched hut" (cao-an).
"Exert yourself and apply yourself with diligence.
The Patriarch Yan said: "When my late teacher first resided at Yangqi, the old house had broken rafters that barely shielded against wind and rain. It happened to be the end of winter;
snow and sleet filled his bed, and he had no place to stay. Disciples offered their sincere devotion, wishing to provide funds for repairs, but the teacher declined."
He said to them: "Our Buddha has spoken thus: 'In this age of the *kṣaya-kalpa*, high cliffs and deep valleys shift and change without constancy;

how can one expect everything to be perfect and as one desires? Seek contentment for yourself. You have left the household life to study the Way, yet your practice is not yet stable, and you are already forty or fifty years old.
How could you afford the leisure to concern yourselves with grand dwellings? They ultimately did not comply. The next day, he went up...
The Hall Master said: "Yangqi has just settled in; the walls of his hut are thin and sparse. The entire bed is strewn with snow-white pearls. He shrinks his neck and sighs in secret.
Suddenly he recalls the ancients who dwelt beneath the trees. (From the *Guanglu*)
Chan Master Fange of Yangqishan in Yuanzhou was surnamed Yang and was the son of the Leng family of Yichun.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Ciming Yuan and the tenth generation descendant of Mount Heng.
"Mo" does not share the same pronunciation as "mù. "Xiàn" refers to the falling of sleet mixed with snow.
"Luáng" conveys a sense of urgency or lack of leisure. This means that although there is sleet and snow, one does not allow the suffering of the cold to disturb the mind.

"Jue" (詎) means "how could it be? "Shifengwu shi" (事豐屋事) refers to the matter of a grand mansion; it signifies a fondness for luxury. Li Jinggong of the Song dynasty, whose name was Han, served as Chancellor.

He maintained an extremely frugal lifestyle and resided in a humble alleyway. His official residence had no double gates. When his family members urged him to renovate it, Han said: "I am supported by the state's bounty..."
Abundant emoluments, security, honor, and the fulfillment of one's desires— since human life cannot be guaranteed from morning until evening, what use is there in laboring for magnificent dwellings?
Tomorrow is another day.
Dwelling beneath trees, the disciples of the Buddha’s precepts take but one meal at midday and lodge for a single night under a tree;
they cultivate the body to avoid fame, remaining unshakable even when faced with a moment of great crisis.
The Patriarch Yan said: "A monk guards the city of his mind and upholds the precepts, contemplating them day and night and practicing them morning and evening.
His practice does not exceed his contemplation, and his contemplation does not exceed his practice. Having its beginning and completing its end, it is like a farmer who has well-defined boundaries."
Their transgressions will be few.
The "city of the mind" refers to that within which dwells the Dharma King of Perfect Enlightenment, the gathering place of ten thousand virtues; hence it is called the city of the mind.
Only when one ensures that the crown [of the head] is not encroached upon and that one is not shaken by external conditions and circumstances can one advance upon the Path.
"Excessive thinking leads to error. To learn without reflecting results in confusion; to reflect without learning results in peril. The Patriarch Yan said:

"What is called a 'congregation' (conglin) is a place for forging both sages and ordinary people, a ground for nurturing and developing talent, and the source from which transformation and education emerge.
Although they dwell together in large numbers, they are led and harmonized, each having their own lineage of teachers. Now, in various quarters..."
He did not strive to uphold the laws and regulations of the former sages; his likes and dislikes were biased, and he frequently altered others according to his own views of correctness.
How could later generations have anything to take as a model from him? (From the *Tantan ji*, two matters).
To mold soil is called *táo* (pottery); to cast metal is called *zhù* (foundry).
*Gé* means to reform or change.

Yuanzu said: "In benefiting sentient beings and transmitting the Way, the primary concern lies in finding the right person; yet the difficulty of knowing people has been the ailment of even the sages and philosophers."
One may listen to their words but cannot yet guarantee their conduct; one may seek their conduct but fears overlooking their talent.

Unless one has previously associated with them and fully understood their background from beginning to end—probing their aspirations and actions, and observing their capacity and ability—then those who preserve the Way while concealing their utility will remain unknown.
As for those who peddle their reputation and polish their appearance, their hypocrisy cannot be tolerated; even if they remain hidden and secretive, their true nature will eventually be revealed.
The Source and its Flow. Now, the principle of observing and investigating with detailed listening is certainly not something that can be mastered in a single morning or evening.
This is why after Nan-yueh Huai-jang met the Great Mirror (Hui-neng), he still served him for fifteen autumns; and when Ma-tsu met Huai-jang...

We have also followed one another for over ten years. Thus we know that at the time of the transmission between former sages, it was certainly not something that those of shallow virtue dared to uphold.
It is like water from one vessel being poured into another; only then can one truly succeed to the grand regulations. It is like the weeds of one's own household;
this is the clear and verified principle of careful observation and detailed listening. How could it permit the use of clever words, insincere expressions, or fawning behavior?
"To be fawning and yet chosen—this is indeed a cause for illness and anxiety.
The Sage said: "Do not worry that others do not know you; worry rather that you do not know others. (From Yuanwu’s Writings)
"Listen to their words and observe their conduct"—this is how I first observe people. I listen to what they say and take it as a sign that they possess virtue;
yet I fear they may be able to speak but unable to act, so I must certainly observe their actual conduct.
Nanyue Rang, Zen Master Huairang of Nanyue in Hengzhou. He was the son of the Du family from Jinzhou and succeeded the Sixth Patriarch, Dajian Chan Master [Huineng].
Dajian, the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, was a native of Yuanyang—that is, Zhuozhou. He was of the Lu clan.
The Master’s son was born before his father moved to reside in Xinzhou in Lingnan. Later, Huineng was born, who succeeded the Fifth Patriarch, Grand Master Hongren.
Mazu of Jiangxi, Chan Master Daoyi, was the son of the Ma family from Shifang County in Hanzhou.
He succeeded Chan Master Nanyue Huairang as his dharma heir. He left home to become a monk at Luohan Monastery. His appearance was extraordinary: he walked like an ox and gazed like a tiger;
he could extend his tongue past his nose, and there were two wheels beneath his feet. He was a man of the Tang dynasty during the reign of Emperor Dezong.

It is certainly not the case that one who is inferior can surpass their teacher; only one who is fit for transmission may do so. To see oneself as equal to the teacher is to diminish the teacher’s virtue by half.
The grand regulations and great Dharma—meaning to weigh the Buddhas and Patriarchs and to serve as a model for humans and devas—are no trivial matter.

Regarding the phrase "the master of the household plants the grass": the master of the household selects a son of virtuous character to succeed to the family enterprise, ensuring that the ancestral legacy is not lost or neglected.
As for "planting the grass," it is like a farmer planting a field; he assesses the fertility of the soil before sowing his seed.

"Artful speech and a commanding countenance"—the term "commanding" (ling) here implies excellence. Speech is the sound of the mind issuing from the mouth; it should issue forth when it ought to issue.
The countenance is the manifestation of the mind appearing on the face; it should appear when it ought to appear. Thus, the Heavenly Principle (tianli) is preserved within.

Yet, if these issues forth improperly into the external world—artful speech like a reed organ, sweet words like sweet wine, and a display of respectful demeanor that is merely superficial—then one has strayed.
They adorn their appearance, striving only to please the ears and eyes of others, while the virtue of their fundamental mind is entirely forgotten.
They cultivate external habits of flattery and formal decorum; their movements are light and frivolous, yet they possess no genuine virtue within.

To bend one's body with flattery and seek favor through sycophancy is called *chān* (flattery). To curry favor by being compliant and seeking to please others is also flattery. The Patriarch Yan said:
"The great handle of the abbot lies in both benevolence (*huì*) and virtue (*dé*). These two must be practiced together; to neglect either is unacceptable.

in his relations with those below, he does not treat them with vulgar familiarity. He knows the subtle. The subtle is the minute movement [of a thing]; it is the first manifestation of good fortune or misfortune."
Master Huitang Xin studied under Master Yuegong Hai at Baofeng. Yuegong was profoundly enlightened in the deep principles of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and was peerless on the sea [of the Dharma].
Whenever Huitang heard a single phrase or a single word from him, he felt as though he had obtained a most precious treasure, his joy beyond measure.
Among the monks, there were those who spoke privately in criticism. When Huìtáng heard of this, he said, "I shall strike at their strengths to sharpen my own weaknesses;
what cause for regret is there in that? Yīng of Shǎowǔ remarked, "Master Huìtáng’s brother in the Way is revered by the Zen monks as a paragon of learning."

If one still considers it strength to surpass others through one's own venerable virtue, and feels shame for what one has not yet seen or heard, then those who cause the monastic community to expand itself while remaining narrow toward others will have a standard by which to emulate;
how could this be anything less than a small but significant benefit? (From *Lingyuan Shiyi*)
Yuan Shu, walking alone, said to Xie Zhuang: "If there were no one like me in Jiangdong, you would walk alone.

This refers to "striking and sharpening" (kòu lì): the former means taking [from another], while the latter means polishing. It means taking what others have in surplus to compensate for one's own deficiencies.
Xian said to Zengzi: "The wealth of the lords of Jin and Chu does not satisfy me. They rely on their wealth, while I rely on my benevolence;
they rely on their rank, while I rely on my righteousness. Why should I have any dissatisfaction? *Mian* means resentment or regret; it implies a sense of deficiency.
It is powerful and victorious; it is joyful.
From the broad, one becomes narrow; from the expansive, one becomes smaller than others.

It produces the scriptures and classics as models and standards of conduct, causing people to rely upon and practice them, so that all the great officers and the people of the state may [attain this].
"There is that which one should emulate. This is from Mencius. Huìtáng said:
"The essentials of being a *zhùchí* (abbot) should consist in adopting what is far-reaching and great, while setting aside what is immediate and minor.
If a matter is not yet resolved, one should consult those who are mature and experienced; if doubts still remain, one should further question those who possess true insight. Even so...

There is still much that remains unfinished, yet it has not reached an extreme. Should the abbot happen to indulge his private whims and act solely for his own gain, and one day fall victim to the schemes of a petty person, to whom shall the blame be attributed?
Therefore it is said: "Deliberation lies in the many; decision lies with the one.
Through deliberation by the many, one may observe the ultimate consequences of benefit and harm; through decision made by oneself, one can bring order to the monastic community.
Regarding this matter of right and wrong (in his letter to Caotang), Huìtáng did not accept the invitation to reside at Wúshān.
Chén Yíngzhōng of Yánpíng sent a letter urging him, saying: "In ancient times, those who held the position of abbot had no formal office;
those of virtuous character were selected to dwell there. One who assumes such a responsibility must surely awaken others to this Way."
These people will ultimately not allow themselves to be changed by power, status, fame, or profit. Today, however, students have not yet clarified the Great Way;

each pursues divergent doctrines and flows into the realm of names and forms, eventually being moved by sounds and colors. Thus, the worthy and the unworthy are intermingled and cannot be distinguished.
This is precisely the time for those who are mature and experienced to take compassion to heart and take the Way upon themselves, to block and turn back [the tide].

To cross the river is certainly not difficult. However, as for withdrawing to seek tranquility and making ease one's primary concern—this is merely what those who seek their own solitary perfection prefer;
it is not what the monastic community expects of you (from *Lingyuan Shiyi*).
Chen Yingzhong of Yanping County: Chen Liaoweng, whose given name was Fan and courtesy name Yingzhong, was styled the Layman of Huayan.
He compared impure rice—meaning broken grains mixed with fine rice—to the relationship between gentlemen and petty men.
They become so intermingled that they cannot be distinguished.
Regarding "compassion" (*cèyǐn*), Mencius said: "The heart of compassion is the sprout of benevolence. "Compassion" (*cè*) refers to the intensity of one's sorrow;
"pity" (*yǐn*) refers to the depth of one's pain. This is precisely the heart of mercy and the inability to bear [the suffering of others].
It means to dam the hundred rivers and turn the myriad currents so they flow into the sea. As Han Yu stated in his "Exposition on the Advancement of Learning":

"Daming the hundred rivers to flow eastward; turning back the wild waves that had already collapsed. This refers to entering the marketplace and extending one's hand, engaging with sentient beings to benefit their lives.
"Mì" means tranquility.
One day, Huìtáng saw that Huánglóng had a look of displeasure, so he asked him about it in advance.
Huánglóng said, "I have not yet found someone to serve as the *jiānshōu* (storekeeper). Huìtáng then recommended Fùsì Gǎn. Huánglóng said, "Gǎn is still impetuous; I fear he will cause trouble."
When people discussed this, Huìtáng said, "Attendant Huà is somewhat upright and prudent.

Hónglóng remarked, "Although Huà is upright and prudent, he is not equal to Zhuāngzhǔ Xiù, who possesses both great capacity and loyalty. Língyuán once asked Huìtáng, "Hónglóng appointed one person as a supervisor (*jiānshōu*)."
"Why such excessive anxiety? Huìtáng said, "Those who possess a state or a family have never failed to take this as their foundation;
how could it be that only Huánglóng did so? Even the former sages once warned against it. (This refers to Dàméi Xiù, Shuānglǐng Huà, and Gǎn Tièmiàn—the three of them. From Tōngān’s Wall Record.)
He paid homage to the Vice-Abbot, Chan Master Cigan of Fuyan on Mount Nanyue. He was the son of the Du family from Tongzhou and succeeded Chan Master Huanglong Nan.
He served as the transformation attendant for Chan Master Bi of Shuangling in Longxing Prefecture, who had received the Dharma from Huanglong Hui.
Chan Master Nan.
"Lian" (Integrity) means to be upright and honest without partiality.
Chan Master Huixiu of Daomiao in Tanzhou, whose courtesy name was Xiuzhuang: he was the son of the Ying family of Yingshou Prefecture and succeeded Huang [Xianbei].
As for Master Longchan:
to have measure means to accommodate all streams;
to have loyalty means to serve one’s superior with total sincerity.
Chan Master Lingyuan Weiqing of Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture was the son of the Chen family of that prefecture.
He was a successor of Huanglong Zuxin.
Huitang said to Imperial Secretary Zhu Shiying: "When I first entered the Way, I relied upon my own [confidence] and thought it would be very easy; however, upon meeting Huang..."
Master Long first placed his teacher behind him and withdrew to reflect upon his daily activities. He found that they contradicted the fundamental principle in countless ways.

Thereupon, he applied himself to practicing it with vigor for three years; even amidst freezing cold and humid heat, his resolute will did not waver. Only after this did he attain accord with the principle in every matter.
Now, even his coughing, spitting, and swinging of arms are the very meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West (from the *Zhangjiang ji*).
The Grand Secretary Zhu’s name was Xianmu and his courtesy name was Shiying. Having attained the rank of Grand Secretary, he sought the Way from the Chan Master Nanshan of Huanglong.
Relying on and taking pride in his own clever intelligence, he held the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs in low esteem.
The upper part is a spear; the lower part is a shield. In ancient times, people sold these two items together, each praising its own excellence.
A wise man said: "I shall buy your spear and then pierce your shield. If it either penetrates or does not penetrate, you will have no defense.
This is used as a metaphor for internal contradiction.
Qi Daye: "The intense heat of the sultry summer surpasses [ordinary] heat.
Zhu Shiying asked Huìtáng: "When a gentleman unfortunately commits even a slight transgression, people are so busy pointing their fingers and naming him that they cannot stop.
Yet, a petty person creates evil all day long and does not consider it so. What is the reason for this? Huìtáng—
It is said: "The virtue of a gentleman is comparable to fine jade. If a flaw exists within, it must manifest on the outside;

thus, those who see it marvel at its uniqueness and cannot help but point it out. As for the petty man, everything he does daily is nothing but transgression and evil—so what further need is there to speak of him? (From the *Zhangjiang ji*).
Huìtáng said: "The Way of the Sage is like Heaven and Earth nourishing the myriad things; there is nothing that is not fully provided for within the Way.

The Way of ordinary people is like the rivers—the Yangtze, the Yellow, the Huai, and the Ji—and the mountains, valleys, hills, and gullies, or the plants, trees, insects, and creatures, each merely exhausting its own capacity.
They do not realize that beyond this, there is nothing that is not fully provided for. How could the Way be two? It is realized through attaining it."
Regarding the question of whether there are differences of small and great between the shallow and the deep (in response to Zhang Wujin’s letter):
"Rivers" refers to the various streams that flow into the sea; "hills" refers to large mounds of earth.
"Kunzhuye," Huìtáng said, "that which has long been neglected cannot be perfected quickly; long-standing corruption cannot be eliminated all at once; one should not linger too long in leisure;
human sentiments cannot always be perfectly balanced; and calamities cannot be evaded by mere expediency. One who acts as a true spiritual friend must understand these things."
"Regarding these five matters, one may engage with the world without weariness" (Letter to Master Xiang).
Huìtáng said: "The former master’s deportment was grave and dignified; those who saw him felt awe and reverence. When monks requested leave for personal affairs, he would often sternly refuse them.
Only when he heard that someone was attending to their elderly parents did his countenance become serene and his expression reveal a sense of profound respect as he fulfilled his filial duties."
He sent him off with these instructions. His love for his parents was as respectful and filial as this (as stated in the letter to Xie Jingwen).
Huìtáng said: "In the past, the former master Hóngzōng of Huánglóng lived together with the Venerable Yúnyǐngyuè of Yúnfēng at Fènglín in Jīngnán during the summer retreat."
Yue was fond of debate. One day he engaged in a heated argument with some monastics, while the Master was reading a sutra as usual, appearing as though he neither heard nor saw anything.
Subsequently, Yue went to the Master’s desk and, glaring at him, rebuked him, saying, "Are you here practicing the 'measuring' of a spiritual friend?
The Master bowed his head in apology and continued reading the sutra as before. (The above is recorded in the *Lingyuan Shiyi*).
Chan Master Yunfeng Wenyue of Nanyue was a native of the Xu family of Nanchang.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Daoyu Shouzhi and belonged to the eleventh generation of the Nanyue lineage.
Master Huanglong Nan said: "In the past, I traveled through Hunan with Wen Yue. We saw a monk carrying his travel bag on his back as he journeyed.
Wen Yue was struck with wonder and frowned; then he scolded him, saying: 'This is something from your own inner chambers that you refuse to set down.
Instead, you burden others by making them carry it for you—is this not far too much toil? (Linjian Lu)
*Cu’è* (蹙頞) refers to knitting the brows and pressing the nose together.
*Guīwù* (閨物) refers to the emotional perceptions within the breast of a woman; it is also an object of private indulgence.
*Hàng* (夯, pronounced xiǎng) refers to the posture of bearing a heavy load.
Huanglong said: "The success of an abbot depends on winning over the assembly; winning over the assembly depends on understanding human sentiments.

The Buddhas of the past have said that human sentiment is the field of merit for the world, for it is from this that the Way of principle arises. Thus, the fortune or misfortune of an era, and the increase or decrease of affairs, must depend upon human sentiment.
When sentiment is either open or obstructed, fortune and misfortune arise; when affairs are either substantial or meager, there is increase or decrease."

The benefit reaches its ultimate point. Only the Sage can penetrate the sentiments of the world. Therefore, in the differentiation of the hexagrams of the *Yi*, when Qian is below and Kun is above, it is called Tai;
when Qian is above and Kun is below, it is called Pi. As for the taking of symbols, when the upper is diminished and the lower is augmented, it is called Yi.
When the lower is diminished to benefit the upper, it is called "Diminution" (Sǔn). Now, Qian represents Heaven and Kun represents Earth.
For Heaven to be below while Earth is above is certainly a reversal of their proper positions; yet it is nonetheless called "Threatening Peace" (Tài), because the upper and lower interact.

For the host to be above while the guest occupies the lower position is certainly consistent with propriety; yet it is nonetheless called "Obstruction" (Pǐ), because the upper and lower do not interact. This is so.
When heaven and earth do not interact, the myriad things cannot flourish; when human sentiments do not interact, all affairs fall into discord.
The principles of diminution and augmentation are likewise derived from this. Now, those who occupy positions of authority can restrain themselves to enrich those below;

the subordinates will surely be joyful and serve their superiors. Is this not what is called "augmentation"? Conversely, when those above hold the subordinates in contempt and act with self-indulgence, the subordinates will surely...
To harbor resentment and rebel against one’s superior—is this not what is meant by "diminution"? Therefore, when the superior and the subordinate interact, there is prosperity (*tai*);

when they do not interact, there is stagnation (*pi*). He who diminishes himself is benefited by others; he who benefits himself alone is diminished by others. Is the attainment or failure of one's emotional state not a matter of great consequence?
The former sages once used the analogy of man as a boat and emotion as water: water can carry a boat, yet it can also overturn it. When water follows the boat...

If one floats with the current, they will sink if they oppose it. Thus, when a monastic leader wins the hearts of the people, the institution flourishes; when they lose the hearts of the people, it falls into ruin.
If they win them entirely, there is total prosperity; if they lose them entirely, there is total decay. Therefore, shared goodness brings abundant blessings, while shared evil brings severe calamity.

Goodness and evil follow their own kind, as orderly as beads on a string. The rise and fall of an institution mirror its conduct, as clear as gazing at the sun. This is the fundamental principle of successive generations.
The Guī (Turtle) [is a letter to Huangbo Sheng].

The hexagram Fǒu (Obstruction) signifies being closed and blocked. "The great goes out and the small comes in" means that the Yang lines go out to dwell outside, while the Yin lines come in to dwell inside.
The Yin energy does not ascend; the Yang energy does not descend. When these two energies do not interact, the myriad things are not produced;
heaven and earth are blocked and obstructed. In terms of human affairs, the ruler does not bestow trust upon his ministers, and the ministers do not offer trust to the ruler.
When those above and below do not interact, human sentiments are blocked and obstructed. In terms of the individual, that which is external is the Yang energy...
It is dispersed and lacks harmony. That which is within, the yin qi, clings and is not regulated. Yin and yang do not unite; qi and blood do not circulate;
the exterior and interior lose their proper measure. This is the hexagram of the seventh month.
The hexagram Tai signifies "thorough penetration. "The small goes out and the great comes in": the "small" refers to Yin; it moves outward and dwells outside.

The "great" refers to Yang; it comes inward and dwells within. As the Yang energy descends and the Yin energy ascends, the two forces intersect, whereby the myriad things are transformed and produced.
Thus, Heaven and Earth are in thorough penetration and harmony. In terms of human affairs, the "great" is the ruler and the "small" is the minister. The ruler...
By advancing sincerity, one entrusts the subordinates; by advancing loyalty, the ministers serve their sovereign.
When the wills of those above and below are communicated, the court is harmonious and prosperous. Yang represents the gentleman, while Yin represents the petty man.
When the gentleman comes and resides within, and the petty man goes and resides without, human relations are harmonious and prosperous. This is the hexagram of the first month.
The Hexagram Sun: Mountain over Lake, the hexagram Sun. Sun means "diminution" or "reduction.

In terms of human affairs, those above take from the people to enrich themselves, while those below diminish their own resources to serve their ruler; inevitably, this leads to the depletion of both the high and the low.
Therefore it is called "Diminution" (Sun).
The Hexagram Yi (Increase) consists of Wind and Thunder. Yi means to augment and increase. Xun represents wind; Zhen represents thunder. When thunder rages, the wind blusters;
these two elements assist one another, which is why they constitute increase. In terms of human affairs, this refers to those in high positions bestowing [favor].
Its moisture extends downward; those below advance their sincerity to serve those above. This is a mutual augmentation of both.
Therefore it is called *Yì* (Increase).
*Shù* means "the multitude. *Pàn* means "to rebel," "to turn back," or "to turn one's back."
"Stringing together pearls" means to thread them on a string; it signifies that they continue in succession without interruption. They follow one after another like pearls strung together.
Regarding the observation of the sun, it is said to be the source of arising and ceasing; its reality lies in diminution and increase, gain and loss. Therefore, it is called "observing the sun."
The *yuánguī* (tortoise) lives for a thousand years; it measures one chi and two cun in length. It possesses foreknowledge of future good and ill fortune, as well as calamities and blessings.
The Yellow Dragon said to Lord Jing: "In all matters undertaken with a focused mind, one must always ensure that the path ahead is wide open, allowing everyone else to pass through;
this is the way a great man applies his mind. If it is narrow, treacherous, and impassable..."
"He alone causes others to be unable to act; furthermore, there is not even a place for his own feet to stand" (*Zhangjiang ji*).
Lord of Jing (Jing Gong) was surnamed Wang, named Anshi, styled Jiefu, and a native of Linchuan.

In the third year of the Xining era of Emperor Shenzong of the Song dynasty, he was appointed as Chancellor and enfeoffed as the Duke of Jing. In the fourth month of the summer of the seventh year, there was no rain; Anshi resigned.
In the second month of the eighth year, he was appointed as Chancellor for the second time. In the twelfth month of the ninth year, he retired from office.
He went to seek the Way from Chan Master Nanyuan of Huanglong.
Huanglong said: "In all your speech and silence, your actions and conduct, you claim that above you do not deceive Heaven, and outwardly you do not deceive others; inwardly..."
"Not to deceive one's own heart" can truly be called "attaining it. Yet, one must still remain cautious and reverent even in the solitude of private and hidden moments.
Only when there is not the slightest trace of self-deception can it be called "attaining it. (Letter in Reply to Lord Jing)
"Conduct" (*jǔcuò*) refers to the actions taken in response to circumstances. "Below," it means to establish and bestow [virtue].
To "dwell alone in the hidden and subtle": "alone" refers to a place unknown to others, known only to oneself.
"Hidden" refers to the dark and secluded; "subtle" refers to minute matters.

This means that within the profound darkness, even minute and subtle affairs—though their outward traces have not yet manifested—have already begun to stir in their incipient state (*ji*). Although others do not know of them, one alone knows them.
Upon reaching this point, one must be even more cautious and reverent.
Huanglong said: "The office of an elder is a vessel for the Way and its virtue.

When the former sages established the monasteries, set forth the regulations, and instituted titles and positions, they selected those monks endowed with the Way and virtue, designating them as 'elders' (zhǎnglǎo), intending that they put their Way and virtue into practice, rather than merely usurping this title in vain.
Our late master Ciming once said: 'It would be better to die old while guarding the Way...'"
To dwell in mountain valleys is not as good as practicing the Way and leading the assembly within the monastic groves (sōngnim).
Is it not because one who properly maintains the office of an elder preserves the moral virtue of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? (In a letter to Ch’wigwan Chin).
Huanglong said to the recluse Pan Yanzhi: "The study of the sages and worthies cannot be accomplished in a moment;
it must rely upon accumulation. The essentials of accumulation are solely diligence and devotion. One must eliminate personal indulgences and practice without weariness.
Only then can one expand and fulfill this, thereby exhausting the subtleties of the world" (*Longshan Guanglu*).
The hermit did not value holding office; he delighted in himself through the Way.
His name was Pan Yanzhi, his courtesy name was Yanzhi, and his style was Qingyi Jushi.
He sought the Way from Chan Master Nanhua Huanglong Nan.
In moments of haste and urgency, during times of mere expediency,
one should expand upon the meaning of "guǎng" (廣). Furthermore, it is derived from the sense of "stretching" (張) and "filling" (滿).
When Pan Yanzhi heard that Huanglong’s method of the Way was strict and profound, he asked for its essentials. Huanglong said, "If the father is strict, the son will be respectful.
Today's discipline and instruction are tomorrow's model. It is like leveling the various terrains: that which is high is lowered, and that which is low is leveled.
When he ascends a mountain a thousand fathoms high, I shall go with him; when he is weary,"
"Reaching down to the depths of the Nine Abysses, I am likewise there with them. When skill is exhausted and delusion is ended, they simply rest of their own accord.
It is further said: "To nurture and nourish is how spring and summer bring forth life;
to frost and snow is how autumn and winter bring things to fruition. How could I wish to remain without words? (Linjian Lu)
When his father Yan Maoyuan went on a military campaign against Jiaozhi, he instructed his sons and nephews with a letter, saying: "Do not covet personal indulgences;
apply yourselves diligently to your studies and duties. His sons and nephews followed this advice and did not dare to disobey. Thus we know that Zijing was made so by the strictness of his father.
Lung-wa said: "The Way of the world prizes hitting the mean. Both excess and deficiency are unacceptable;
one must level them down, seeking to diminish what is in surplus and augment what is insufficient, striving to accord with the Middle Way."

*Xiūyù* (姁嫗): The first character is pronounced with the *qǔ* rhyme group; the second is pronounced with the *yù* rhyme group. When the Yin and Yang attain harmony, they cover and nourish the myriad things.

To speak of this in terms of vital energy (*qi*), it is called *xiū*; to speak of it in terms of physical form, it is called *yù*. *Xiū* should be written as *xù* (煦), as found in the *Líjì* (Book of Rites).
Within the chamber of Huanglong were three "gateless barriers" (guānyǔ). Among the monastics, few were able to harmonize with their mechanism.

Even when there was a response, he would merely sit upright with eyes closed, showing no sign of approval or disapproval. When Yan repeatedly pressed him for further clarification, Huanglong said, "Those who have already passed through the barrier."
He flung his arms about and departed. He went to ask the customs official whether he might pass; this was one who had not yet penetrated the barrier (*Linjian lu*).
Regarding the "Three Barrier Sayings," Huanglong asked Longqing Xian: "Everyone has their own karmic affinity (*jìngyuan*);
where is your reverend’s affinity? Xian replied: "In the morning I ate white congee; by evening I felt hungry again. Furthermore: [text continues].
A questioner asked, "How is my hand compared to the Buddha’s hand? Xian replied, "Playing the lute under the moon. He asked again, "How is my foot like a donkey’s foot?
Xian replied, "The heron standing in the snow is not the same color [as the snow]. For over thirty years, there was no one who could grasp his essential point.
Should anyone attempt to respond, he would simply close his eyes and sit upright. For this reason, the monastic community called him... (the Master).
These are the Three Barriers. The Master himself composed a verse on them: "Where the conditions for birth are severed, the donkey’s hoof is extended;
When the donkey’s hoof is extended, the Buddha’s hand opens. To inform the Zen practitioners of the Five Lakes: Pass through each of the three barriers one by one."
There was a certain degree of uncertainty in his words.
Huanglong said, "The Way is like a mountain: the higher one ascends, the higher it becomes. It is like the earth: the further one travels, the further it extends.
Those who study it with shallow and limited minds stop as soon as they have exhausted their own strength. Only those who are resolute in their pursuit of the Way can fathom its height and distance."
"What else compares to this? (*Jiwen*). "What compares to it" (*shū yǔ*)—the final syllable is pronounced in the descending tone; it means "to reach" or "to equal.
Huanglong said: "The heaven, earth, sun, and moon of antiquity were like the heaven, earth, sun, and moon of today. The myriad things of antiquity..."
The nature and temperament [of the Way] are like the nature and temperament of the myriad things today. Heaven, Earth, the sun, and the moon are certainly not subject to change;

the nature and temperament of the myriad things are certainly not subject to alteration. Why then would the Dao alone be subject to change? Alas, those who have not yet attained it grow weary of the old and take pleasure in the new;
they abandon this and grasp that, like one traveling to Yue who goes north instead of south—truly, this may be called being at odds with [the Dao].
"Though he is a human being, he merely exhausts his mind and toils his body; the more diligent his will becomes, the further his Way remains from him.
(From the "Wall Inscription of Dun'an")
The place named Yue is located in Shaoxing Prefecture.

When he was traveling there, Huanglong said to Ying of Shaowu: "Your resolve must be focused on a single goal; persist for a long time without retreating, and in days to come you will surely know where the wondrous Way leads.
If, however, your mind harbors likes and dislikes and your emotions indulge in depravity, then even if your ambition and spirit are like those of the ancients,"
"I fear that in the end I shall not be able to see his Way" (from the Memorial Record).
Chan Master Hongying of Lestam in Longxing Prefecture, Shaowu: a native of the Chen family of Shaowu;
he was the dharma heir of Chan Master Huinang of Huanglong.

Master Baofeng Ying said: "The old masters of various quarters who critique the words of the predecessors and handle the public cases are like those who carry soil to build up Mount Tai or scoop up water to fill the Eastern Sea. Yet how could they rely on these acts to achieve loftiness or depth?
Observing their intent, they aim to increase [the merit], yet they do not realize that what they do is inappropriate. (From the *Guanglu*)
Regarding the term "gong'an" (public case): "Gong" refers to the track left by the sages and worthies during their tenure, the universal principle of the world.
"An" refers to the official records and documents of a government office.

Since there has never been a ruler of the world who lacked a government office, and there has never been a government office that lacked official records, these were taken as models to govern the irregularities of the world. Now...
The kōans (gong’an)—the records of the encounters between Buddhas and patriarchs—are likewise of this nature. [Yuanwu] remarks:

"Judgments, verses of praise, and critical commentaries serve to reveal the functional mechanisms of the ancients and to test whether a student’s understanding is correct or deviant; indeed, they are indispensable.
However, if one’s footing is not yet firm and one’s eye of the Way is not yet clear, and one instead relies on these as a means of livelihood, then one will fall into error."

Sentient consciousness stagnates; its obstruction of the Way is no small matter. Thus, Bao Feng’s words here represent the patriarchs’ method of untying the sticky and removing the bonds for the sake of others.
This is precisely the intention behind Miaoxi’s desire to enter Min and break the woodblocks of the *Biyán jí*.

If one were to discard public cases (*gōng'àn*) on this basis and suppress the *niàn* and *sòng*, then the true eye would not open and the distinctions between phenomena would remain obscure. To pierce through...
To dig up errors and confusion, and to face a wall whenever one encounters a matter—how can such a person serve as a teacher or model for gods and humans?
Whenever Master Ying of Shaowu saw students who were unrestrained and fearless of cause and effect, he would sigh for a long time and say:
"A weary life is like a temporary lodging; when staying, one follows conditions, and when departing, it vanishes. What can those people possibly achieve? You lot do not..."

One should recognize shame and propriety. To violate the boundaries of name and status, to defile and corrupt the teachings, and even to reach such extremes—this is not the way for a great man whose will is set upon expanding the ancestral Way and guiding future generations.
One ought not to privately indulge one’s own desires without restraint, plotting one’s own ruin and creating calamities that last for ten thousand kalpas.
That those suffering in the three miserable realms and the hells do not yet experience the true suffering is because they have not yet turned toward [the truth].
To lose one’s human form beneath the *kāṣāya* is truly a source of suffering (*Bìjì*).
"Traveling and lodging" means staying temporarily like a guest in an inn; how could one dwell there for long? "Lodging" is like a boat stopping overnight for rest.
At dawn they set out again; this was to signify that one does not abide permanently.
A great man cannot be led astray by wealth and honor, cannot be moved by poverty and low status, and cannot be bent by force or intimidation.
"This is what is called a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). This expression originates from the *Mencius*.
"Huī" means vast and great.
"Yòu" refers to leading and encouraging from the front; "yè" refers to supporting from the sides.
"Ji" means to dread; "mei" means to summon.

Ying of Shaowu said to Huītáng: "Generally speaking, those who are called 'good knowledge-holders' (shanzhishi) assist the Buddhas and Patriarchs in propagating the transformation [of beings], causing practitioners to turn their minds toward the Way and shifting customs and transforming social mores.
This is certainly not something that those of shallow virtue can accomplish. In the Dharma-ending age..."

"Qiu does not cultivate the Way or its virtue; he possesses little integrity or righteousness. He frequently engages in the exchange of bribes and presents, wagging his tail to beg for pity, and pursues fame and profit at the gates of those in power.
Once his karma is exhausted and his blessings have faded, the devas and humans will weary of him.
He defiles the True Lineage and brings disgrace upon his teachers and friends—is it not right that he should sigh with regret? Huìtáng nodded in agreement.
"Bhikṣu" is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "mendicant" (qǐshì).

This means that, above, one begs for the wisdom of all Buddhas to sustain the life of insight, and below, one begs for the food of sentient beings to sustain the physical body. A bhikṣu possesses five virtues:
namely, being a mendicant, destroying evil, terrifying Māra, maintaining a pure livelihood, and slaying the thief [of afflictions].
"Baoju" refers to parcels wrapped in bundles containing rare or exotic objects, presented as offerings by sycophants and flatterers to seek favors or recommendations.
"Angang" describes a corpulent or robust physique; the *Hanshu* states that those with arched brows were "angang," meaning they stood leaning against the side of a gate.
"Wagging the tail to beg for pity" means wagging the tail like a dog when seeing a person to flatter them, seeking nothing but compassion.
The sycophancy and insincerity of petty people is just like this:
they nod their heads to accept, and though their mouths say nothing, their hearts grant consent.
Ying Shaowu said to Pan Yanzhi, "Those who studied in ancient times cultivated the mind; those who study today cultivate outward traces.
Yet, the distance between the mind and its traces is as vast as that between heaven and earth."
Traces resulting from conditioned effort are called "traces.
Ying Shaowu said to Master Zhenjing Wen: "That which grows too rapidly will surely wither and die;
that which achieves success too quickly will surely be easily destroyed. To disregard long-term planning and instead create achievements through sudden means is never a path toward greatness."

This is the requisite foundation. Now, even Heaven and Earth—the most spiritual of entities—require three years and an intercalary month before their work is completed and their transformation perfected;
how much more so for the subtlety of the Great Way, which can certainly not be discerned in haste? It lies in the accumulation of merit and the building up of virtue;
hence it is said: "He who desires speed will not reach his goal. Through minute conduct one does not fail; beauty is achieved through long duration, leading to lifelong planning. Thus spoke the Sage.
It is said: "Trust it to maintain it; be diligent to practice it; be loyal to bring it to completion. Though a task may be great, it will surely succeed.
Formerly, the attendant Zhe sat through the night without sleeping, using a round log as a pillow. When he dozed off, the pillow would roll away;
upon waking, he would rise again and sit back down as before. He made this his constant practice. Some remarked that his application of mind was excessive, to which Zhe replied: "I am..."
One's affinity for Prajñāpāramitā is naturally meager; if one does not apply oneself with diligent effort and resolve, there is fear that one will be led astray by deluded habits.

How much more so when all is like a dream or an illusion and lacks true reality—how could it serve as a long-term plan? In the past, while I was in Western Hunan, I personally witnessed his conduct to be such as this;
therefore, the monastic community honored his reputation, revered his virtue, and praised him (as recorded in the *Lingyuan Shiyi*).
Chan Master Zhenjing Kewen of Baofeng in Longxing Prefecture was a native of the Zheng family from Minxiang in Shanfu.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Huanglong Nan and belonged to the eleventh generation under Mount Heng.
The *Erya* states: "In the Xia dynasty it was called *sui* (year), taking the sense of the sun completing one revolution through the zodiacal signs.

In the Shang dynasty it was called *si* (sacrifice), taking the sense of the completion of a single cycle of four-season sacrifices. In the Zhou dynasty it was called *nian* (harvest), taking the meaning of the ripening of grain.
In the Tang and Yu dynasties it was called *zai* (carrying), taking the significance of things ending and beginning anew. All of the above refer to the year.
The intercalary month is established again to fix the four seasons and complete the year. Zhang Chun said:

"An intercalation every three years makes the celestial influences slightly complete; an intercalation every five years makes them fully complete. This is because the intercalary months are insufficient while the days are excessive.
In antiquity, a year consisted of three hundred and sixty-six days, divided into twelve months."
Each month has thirty days, totaling three hundred and sixty days in a year; six days remain.
Furthermore, six months are short [by one day each], and subtracting these six days makes one year. Thus, twelve days remain in total. Over three years, this amounts to thirty-six days.
One intercalary month still leaves six days remaining, which carry over into the second year, making twenty-four days.
Including the preceding six days, there are thirty days in total. Furthermore, with the addition of an intercalary month, this constitutes three years.
Thus, the *I Ching* says, "In five years, there are two intercalary months," which signifies diligent application.
The attendant Zhè was Chan Master Mùzhè of Zhēnrú at Dàméi in Tánzhōu.
He was the son of the Wén family of Wénchúan in Fǔzhōu and succeeded Cùiyán Zhēn; he was the eleventh generation descendant in the lineage of Nányuè.
Regarding the teaching of Bodhiruci: "sleeping" is called "awakening" (jue). Prajñā is translated here as "wisdom.
Xiangxi refers to Xiangtan County in Changsha Prefecture, Huguang.
Master Zhenjing Wen had long studied under Huanglong. Initially, he maintained the vow not to appear before others;
later, however, having accepted an invitation from Dongshan, his path led him through the Western Mountains where he visited Master Shun of Yaocheng. Shun teased him, saying:

"Zhuge Liang of old claimed to be a recluse, yet the thatched cottage earnestly invited him to emerge from the mountains. If the pine blossoms are to be moistened by the power of spring, the roots must remain deep."
Yan’yo also manifested his opening [of realization]. Jinjeong declined the invitation and withdrew (*Sunnyu-rok*).
Hyangcheong Sun was Master Hyangcheong Gyeon-sun of the West Mountain school.
He was a native of Shuzhou and succeeded Chan Master Hwangnong Nang. He passed away while seated at Hyangcheong.
Zhuge Liang, styled Kongming, was a native of Langya. He ploughed his own fields on Sleeping Dragon Hill (Wolonggang) in Nanyang and was a friend of Xu Shu.
At that time, Liu Xuande was stationing his troops at Xinye; when Xu Shu saw him, he informed him, saying:
"Zhuge Kongming is a Sleeping Dragon. General, why not go to see him? This man is [worthy of your service]."
Because he could not be brought to submission through force, Xuande eventually went to Liang’s residence;
after visiting him three times and following his lead, he appointed him as Military Counselor. Later, he served as Chancellor of Shu-Han.
Zhenjing appointed Guang as the abbot. Guang resided at Wufeng; public opinion held that he was simple and clumsy, lacking the talent to respond to the needs of the age.

Yet, once Guang took up the abbacy, he disciplined himself with refinement and treated the assembly with broad magnanimity. Before long, all neglected matters were restored. Monks passing through the area vied with one another to spread the news.
Hearing this, Zhenjing remarked, "How easily do students engage in slander and praise! Whenever I visit a monastic community..."

Lin discussed it privately, saying: "That elder practices the Way and brings peace to the assembly; that elder does not misappropriate the permanent property of the monastery and shares both its bitterness and its sweetness with the community.
Truly, one who is called a 'Good Spiritual Friend' (Kalyāṇamitra) is the master of a monastery, practicing the Way and bringing peace to the assembly."

Not encroaching upon the permanent assets of the monastery and sharing both sweet and bitter experiences with the community is something one ought to do as a matter of course; what is there to say about it?
It is like a scholar-official serving in government: to provide security for the state and peace for the people, he simply says, "I do not accept bribes, nor do I harass the people.
Yet, refraining from accepting bribes and harassing the people—is this not merely doing one's duty? (From *Shantang Xiaocan*)

Guangdao was Chan Master Xiu Guang of Jiufeng in Ruizhou. A native of Zizhou in Western Sichuan, the Master was compassionate and kind toward all beings, never seeking out minor faults or scrutinizing others.
Consequently, the monastic community called him "Guang the Unconcerned.
He was a successor to Chan Master Zhenjing Kewen and belonged to the twelfth generation of the Nanyue lineage.
The term "yu" (carriage) signifies the multitude.
To manage affairs beyond one's station, receive rank from the state, herd the people, and rectify the nation—how could these be considered extraordinary?

Now, one who acts as a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend) presides over the monastic community (*saṅghārāma*), promotes transformation through teaching, brings peace to the assembly, and practices self-restraint; such a person does not interfere with the permanent endowments of the monastery. This is correct.
"It should be thus; how could it be anything beyond what is natural?
When Zhenjing resided at Guizong, every year the fundraising masters would submit their petitions, and bolts of cloth and silk arrived in great abundance.

Zhenjing looked upon them with a frown, and after a while, he sighed, saying: 'This is the blood and fat of those who have faith. I am ashamed that I lack virtue; how can I be worthy of this? (From Li Shanglao’s *Rishen Ji*)."
"Clouds accumulate and gather like a mass of clouds.
Zhenjing said: "In the Dharma-ending age, bhikṣus rarely possess integrity and righteousness. Whenever I see them engaging in lofty talk and grand discourse, they claim that no one can equal them.
Yet, when it comes to the kindness of a single meal, they first show disdain and only later assist the donor; they first disparage and..."
Later, he praised him, saying: "Those who seek what is right and call what is wrong 'wrong,' remaining upright and impartial without concealment, are few indeed" (from the *Biji*).
Zhenjing said: "The dharma of a bhikṣu is that one's enjoyments should not be excessive. If they are excessive, they will overflow. One should not scheme too much for matters to one's liking;
to scheme too much leads inevitably to ruin. Where there is something about to be accomplished, there must be something to cause its destruction. I have seen Huang..."

Master Longxian lived for forty years in this world. Whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, he never sought to ensnare the monastics of his time with his countenance, etiquette, or literary talent.
Rather, he was one who possessed a resolute realization of the ground and practiced the truth; he took great care to guide those who were sincere and earnest toward the authentic path.
His gravity and reverence truly embodied the style of the ancients, a quality rarely equaled by anyone else in all quarters. Therefore, today—
When facing the multitude, there is nothing that does not take the Dharma as its standard (from the *Risheri*).
He bends down and approaches them with meticulous care, for he employs skillful means (*upāya*) to bring their virtue to fulfillment.
"Tǐ" (pronounced *chí*) means accomplishment; "tǐcái" refers to structural form and style.
Zhenjing was serving as abbot at Baoning Temple in Jiankang. Prince Shu offered him a gift of plain silk for his vegetarian meal.

He asked an attendant monk, "What is this? The attendant replied, "It is spun silk gauze. Zhenjing asked, "What will you do with it? The attendant said, "It is suitable for making a *kāṣāya* (monastic robe).
Zhenjing pointed to the cotton *kaḷīra* he himself wore and said, "I usually wear this; those who see me do not find it particularly offensive. He then ordered [the attendant]—
[The items] were sent to the storehouse to be appraised and sold for the benefit of the community; such was his lack of concern for finery (from the *Ri-shek-ji*).
Regarding Prince Shu, Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty: he was promoted to the rank of Prince Shu by Lord Jing. Lord Jing had been appointed as Chancellor during the Xining era;
he implemented the New Policies which brought suffering upon the people. His son, Wang Pang, served as Grand Master of the Chongzheng Hall.
Because his father was intent on implementing the New Laws, Fan Pang died; subsequently, his father resigned from the相位 (Prime Minister).

During a moment of leisure and tranquility, as if in a dream, he saw a ghostly messenger leading Pang, who bore an iron cangue and wept before him, saying, "This is caused by your father's devotion to the New Laws.

The Duke asked the messenger for a way to be released from this retribution. The messenger replied, "Building a temple and providing meals for monks may exempt you. Thereupon, the Duke [proceeded to] in Jin...
He donated his fields and his residence to establish a temple, which was granted the name Baoning. He invited Zhenjing to preside over it.
"Jian" (縑) refers to silk; it is also written as "juan" (絹).
A *kāṣāya* (袈裟)—the full Sanskrit term being *kāṣāya*—is translated here as "improper color. It is also called the "dust-detaching robe."
*Kāṣāya* is the name for the "miscellaneous fragments" robe. Because it consists of many strips, the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) is divided into three grades:
those with nine, eleven, or thirteen strips are called the lower grade; those with fifteen, seventeen, or nineteen strips are called the middle grade;
and those with twenty-one, twenty-three, or twenty-five strips are called the upper grade.
"Estimate" means price; it also means that the matter is good.
Zhenjing said to King Shu: "In daily life, exert effort in what is right and firmly cease from what is not.
One should not allow one's resolve to waver because of ease or difficulty. If, because of today’s difficulties, you shake your head and disregard them, how can you know what will happen another day?"
"Is this not difficult to achieve today? (from the *Ri-she-ji*).
When Zhenjing heard that a man of the Way from one region had passed away, he sighed with deep compassion until his tears fell.

At that time, Zhantang was serving as his attendant and said: "When things are born within heaven and earth, they all receive a physical form; yet they eventually wither, die, and become decayed insects."
"It seems impossible to escape this. Why do you distress yourself so? Zhenjing said, "The flourishing of the Dharma depends on those of virtue to sustain it.
Now they have all passed away; the monasteries are in decline. By this, one may predict the future. (Recorded in the *Rishen ji*)
Chan Master Zhantang Wenzhun of Leshan Temple in Longxing Prefecture was the son of the Liang family of Xingyuan Prefecture.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhenjing Wen and belongs to the thirteenth generation under Mount Heng.
The meaning of the manifestation of omens:
withered and dead, withered and aged, extinguished; incomplete, damaged, and decayed.
*Chanlin Baoxun Heyizhu*, Scroll One.
