Judging by my craft as a wheelwright: if I turn the wheel too slowly, it will be smooth but not firm; if I turn it too fast, it will be strained and not fit.
When I am neither slow nor fast, I grasp it with my mind and respond with my hands;
my mouth cannot describe it, for there is a numerical principle (a subtle knack) inherent in it. I cannot explain it to my son, and my son cannot receive it from me. Such is my age.
"At seventy, one grows old at the wheelwright's bench. Of those ancient wheelwrights, many died before their craft could be transmitted.
Thus, what Your Majesty has been reading is but the dregs. Duke Huan was greatly delighted and produced the *Zhuangzi*.
A skilled person is like one who drives horses. A master horseman adjusts his efforts according to the horse.
"Nú" and "jì" refer respectively to a dull horse and a fine horse. "Shàng" refers to the dull horse, while "xià" refers to the fine horse.
Those who have lost their original nature each attain what is appropriate for their own pace—whether slow or fast—so that they do not lose what was originally bestowed upon them.
The line and the square are the tools used by the carpenter; if the wood attains them, then its curves and straightness become clearly manifest.
Lingyuan said: "A capable abbot takes the minds of the assembly as his own mind; he never treats his own mind as private.

He takes the ears and eyes of the assembly as his own ears and eyes; he never treats his own ears and eyes as private. Thus, he is able to communicate the will of the assembly and exhaustively fulfill the sentiments of the assembly.
Now, if one uses the minds of the assembly as one's own mind, then one's own likes and dislikes are, in fact, those of the assembly."
Thus, what is liked will not be perverse, and what is disliked will not be erroneous. Furthermore, why rely on private confidants as one's own heart and mind, and willingly submit to their flattery?
Since one uses the eyes and ears of the multitude as one's own eyes and ears, then the intelligence and wisdom of the multitude are all one's own intelligence and wisdom.
Therefore, there is nothing clear that is not reflected, and nothing sharp that is not heard. Moreover, why rely on private eyes and ears?
This inevitably invites obscurity, delusion, and depravity. Now, those who entrust their innermost thoughts and rely upon others as their eyes and ears should be virtuous and enlightened men;

they must strive to seek out their own faults, share the desires of the multitude, and remain free from partiality or private bias. Thus, there is no one among the people to whom they do not turn their hearts.
It is only natural that their Way, Virtue, Benevolence, and Righteousness should spread far and wide. Yet, the minds of the ignorant and unworthy strive only to...
When a person’s faults run counter to the desires of the multitude and they are immersed in partiality and self-interest, all people will naturally become alienated from them.

Thus, it is only natural that their ill repute and perilous conduct should spread far and wide. From this we know that a monastic administrator who shares the same desires as the community is called a worthy sage;
one who runs counter to the desires of the community is called a commoner. In general, one should lay bare one's innermost heart.
The intentions behind entrusting them to the eyes and ears differ; yet the resulting good and evil, or success and failure, are as opposed as this.
Is it not because the sentiments in seeking out faults vary, and the methods of delegating authority to others differ?
The minds of common people do not harbor the rules for a careful end; their mouths do not utter words of instruction or rectification.
They do not choose with whom to entrust themselves, nor do they establish conduct by which to stabilize themselves. Upon seeing a petty scholar-official, they do not know what to pursue.
Flowing along with external objects, one does not know what is being grasped; hence it is called the "ordinary flow. Lingyuan said:

"In recent times, those who act as elders encounter two kinds of conditions. For the most part, their wisdom and cognition are not clear, and being struck by two winds, they lose the essence of the Dharma.
First, encountering adverse conditions, they are frequently struck by the wind of decline. Second, encountering favorable conditions, they are frequently [struck by the wind of attachment]."
When one encounters the winds of profit, being struck by these two winds, the vapors of joy and anger intermingle within the heart, and a look of brooding resentment floats upon the face.
This leads to a gateway for receiving humiliation and being ridiculed by the worthy and enlightened.

Only the wise are well able to transform this into a means of gathering and transforming others, providing a beautiful guidance for those who come after, such as when the Monk of Langye went to Suzhou to visit Fan Xi.

The text continues: Having received offerings from the faithful and over a thousand strings of cash, he subsequently dispatched people to secretly count the number of monks in the various monasteries within the city.
He sent money to them all in secret, arranging for a communal vegetarian feast on the same day. He then took his leave of Lord Fan in advance;
that morning he set sail, and by dawn the public realized he had already departed. Some pursued him as far as Changzhou and were able to see him there. He accepted [the offerings].
He turned [the offerings] toward the benefit of the Dharma. Behold this one act of an elder, which caused both the clergy and laity of Gusu to give rise to faith and deepen their seeds of the Way.
This is what is called a method for converting and gathering [disciples];
it is truly as different from those who pilfer the position of the Dharma, seek only gain and sustenance, and plot for their own sake as heaven is from earth. (Letter to Master De)
"Bó" (勃) refers to a change in facial expression.
"Qiào" (誚), pronounced with the initial *cái* and the final *xiào*, means to reproach one another with words.
The Chan Master Huìjué of Guǎngzhào in Lángyá, Xūzhōu, was a native of Luòyáng and succeeded Fényáng.
Chan Master Zhao was the tenth generation descendant of Nanyue.
Fan Xiwen’s surname was Fan, his given name Zhongyan, and his courtesy name Xiwen.
A native of Runan, he was appointed as a Participant in State Affairs during the Qingli era of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty and was posthumously honored with the title Wenzheng.
*Mǐn* (pronounced as in "min") refers to a string of cash.
When Wen Zhenggong addressed Langye, he said, "Last year when I arrived here, I thought of finding a man of the 'groves' with whom I might converse.
I once asked an official whether there were any fine monks among the various mountains. The official named two monks from Beisi, Ruiguang and Ximao, as such."

"Excellent," I said. "Is there no one else like this among the various Chan masters and Vinaya masters? The official replied to me, "The Confucians honor the conduct of the scholar-officials, while the monks discuss virtue and achievement.
As for those such as Xi and Mao, for thirty years they have not stepped beyond their doorsteps; their clothing consists only of plain cloth and undyed silk.
They are entirely unattached to fame, profit, or sustenance. Therefore, the people of the land hold their integrity in high esteem and revere them as teachers."

If one ascends the Dharma seat to preach the teachings, acting as the Buddha’s representative to propagate the transformation of beings, possessing spontaneous eloquence and being acclaimed as a *kalyāṇamitra*, this is not something a dull-witted official can understand.
On a day of leisure, I visited the two venerable masters Xi and Mou and observed their long-standing conduct; it was exactly as the official had described.

I reflected on my departure, thinking that Suzhou and Xiu County were once renowned for their fine customs; yet now, observing even this aged official, he is still able to distinguish between a gentleman and an ordinary man.
If this is the case for petty men, how much more so for those with true discernment? Langya said, "What the official has spoken is indeed a profound discourse.
I request that you record it so that those who have not yet heard it may understand. (From the *Langya Bielü*)
Ruiguang Temple had four auspicious omens: namely, the bells and drums rang spontaneously; the jeweled pagoda emitted light; auspicious bamboo grew intertwined;
and a white tortoise listened to the Dharma. For these reasons, it was called Ruiguang (Auspicious Light), which is the present-day Wofosi (Reclining Buddha Temple).
To "tread" means to practice. A "gate threshold" (kūnmen) is the lintel of a doorway.
An "upper person" (shangren) possesses wisdom and virtue within and superior conduct without; because they stand above others, they are called an upper person.
"Xiù" refers to the Prefecture of Jiāxīng.
Língyuán said: "Master Yuán of Zhōngshān never associated with high officials throughout his life; he did not seek fame or profit and cultivated himself through humility, finding joy in the Way.
When scholars and gentlemen first urged him to engage with the world, Yuán said: 'If one possesses good fields...'"
"What is so late about his achievement? I only fear he lacks the requisite talent. When Lord Jing heard this, he said:
"He takes flight at the sight of color; he soars before he settles. Yuan Gong has captured this essence. (Zhouyou Ji)
"Using humility to cultivate oneself. The Image says: "The humble and humble gentleman uses humility to cultivate himself. Humility is the ultimate expression of modesty.
This refers to the gentleman’s way of cultivating himself through self-effacement and self-abasement; "to cultivate oneself" means to dwell within oneself in this manner.
"The bird takes flight at the mere sight of color; such is the nature of birds. When they perceive that a person's countenance is not benevolent, they soar away with grace.
They wheel and hover, observing closely, until they find a place where they will not be startled by bows or slings, only then do they descend.
When people of the world perceive the subtle signs of opportunity, they should likewise act in this manner."
Lingyuan said: "The ancient sages have stated that it is difficult to attain awakening through the study of the Way; once awakened, it is difficult to maintain it;
and once maintained, it is difficult to practice it. Now, when it comes to the time of actual practice, the difficulty exceeds even that of awakening and maintenance.
This is because while awakening and maintenance require only diligent, steadfast effort applied to one's own person, practice necessitates a vow of equal-mindedness and the mortification of oneself."

Taking the benefit of others as one's primary responsibility, if the mind is not impartial and one’s vows are not firm, then benefit and harm will be inverted, and one will fall into the ranks of a worldly master.
Thus, Zhiwei Lingyuan said:
"Brother Dongshan possessed an exceptionally gifted nature; whether speaking or remaining silent, he was always within the middle way. He habitually revealed his words..."

The principle of his phrasing was naturally superior; those in various quarters who wished to emulate it found that anything other than being unconventional led to vulgarity, and they could never reach his level.
Even among the ancients, such a style could not be found. Yet, he remained humble and radiant in guiding others, as if driven by hunger and thirst.
He once said: "I have no dharma; how can I be so diligent? You disciples are truly sinners within the gates of the Dharma."
Lust is the transgression of dissipation.
As for humility and radiance: the higher one’s position, the lower one’s heart becomes; thus one is both honored and radiant.
Lingyuan’s Daoist learning, conduct, and righteousness, his pure sincerity, profound virtue, and the style of the ancients—his composure and reticence were especially remarkable.
He was revered by scholars and officials. He once said: "What the common people neglect, the sages regard with caution.

How much more so for one who is the master of a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) and assists in proclaiming the Buddha’s transformation? If one's practice and understanding are not in accord, how can one possibly fulfill this role?

The essential point is to examine oneself at all times, ensuring that fame, profit, and sustenance do not sprout within the mind. Should there be anything regarding the precepts and regulations that has not yet been fully realized... [The text continues: *nà*... (monk’s robe).

If you have something you have not yet mastered, you should withdraw to reflect and cultivate virtue, awaiting what is to come. I have never seen one whose own person was upright yet whose monastic community was not well-ordered.
As it is said: "Observing the countenance of a man of virtue causes the contentious intentions of others to dissolve.
This is truly the point (Recorded Sayings).
"Pure" (*chún*) means being single-minded and without admixture; "sincere" (*chéng*) means being true and without falsehood.
These are terms used to express being manifestly trustworthy.
Linyuan said to Yuanwu: "Although a monk may possess the potential for insight into the Way, if he does not store it deeply and nourish it richly..."
If one acts upon this, it will inevitably be abrupt and violent; not only will it fail to benefit the gates of the teaching, but it may even invite calamity and disgrace.
Master Yuanwu said: "The study of the Way depends on faith; establishing faith depends on sincerity. When sincerity is maintained within, the multitude will be free from delusion.
When faith is maintained within oneself, one can teach others without deception. Only through faith and sincerity does one gain benefit and avoid failure."
Thus we know that if sincerity is not unified, the mind cannot be preserved; if trustworthiness is not unified, words cannot be put into practice. As the ancients said:

"Food and clothing may be dispensed with, but sincerity and trustworthiness must not be lost. Therefore, a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) should teach people through sincerity and trustworthiness.
Furthermore, if one’s mind is not sincere and one does not believe in the matter, can they be called a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra)? The *I Ching* says:
"Only the most sincere in the world is able to fully realize their own nature. Being able to fully realize their own nature, they are then able to fully realize the nature of others.
Now, if you yourself cannot fully realize your own nature, yet desire to realize that of others, the multitude will surely deceive you and not follow you; for you yourself are not sincere.

If one speaks of sincerity first and then of truthfulness later, the multitude will surely doubt and fail to believe. This is what is meant by the saying: "When shaving the hair, it is better to reach the skin;
when clipping the nails, it is better to slightly invade the flesh. It is truly because if sincerity does not reach its limit, things will not be moved;
if self-sacrifice does not reach its limit, benefit will not arrive. Thus, it is clear that sincerity and trustworthiness must not depart from oneself for even a moment. (Letter to Censor Yu)
Chanyuan Wuguo Keqin, Chan Master Foguo of Zhaojue Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture, was the son of the Luo family of Pengzhou.
He succeeded Chan Master Wuzu Fayan as his dharma heir.
His given name was Baocun, and he was styled Baoquan.
Sincerity in the mind is called *cheng* (sincerity); this is the substance of faith. Speaking with reality is called *xin* (faith);
this is the function of sincerity.
Only one who possesses the utmost sincerity in the world can fully exhaust their own nature; thus they can fully exhaust the nature of others. Being able to fully exhaust the nature of others...
If one can fully exhaust the nature of things, then one can assist in the transformative nourishment of Heaven and Earth.
If one can assist in the transformative nourishment of Heaven and Earth, then one may participate alongside Heaven and Earth as their third.

The commentary states: As for "nature" (*xing*), its virtues are without anything unreal, and its principles are without anything lacking. Therefore, it is devoid of the private biases of human desire.

One who can fully realize this possesses knowledge that is without obscurity and acts in a manner that is never inappropriate. That "Heaven and Earth possess ultimate sincerity" refers to the virtue of the Sage;
none in the world can surpass it. "To praise" (*zan*) means to assist. "To participate" (*can*) means to be equal to Heaven and Earth.
"To stand up and act as three [is] to deceive, cheat, and be arrogant. 'Sishu' means for a brief moment.
Yuanwu said, "Who among men is without fault? To err and yet be able to reform—no good is greater than this. Those of antiquity all praised such reform."
To be free of faults is to be truly virtuous; it is not the absence of faults alone that constitutes beauty. Therefore, in the conduct of human beings, errors and excesses are frequent;

even those of superior wisdom and those of inferior folly cannot avoid them. Only the wise are able to reform their faults and turn toward goodness, whereas the foolish mostly conceal their errors and gloss over their transgressions.

To reform and turn toward goodness causes one's virtue to renew itself daily, and such a person is called a gentleman (*junzi*). To gloss over and conceal one's faults causes one's evils to become ever more manifest.

This is what is called a petty person. Therefore, to hear of righteousness and be able to shift toward it is difficult for ordinary feelings; to see goodness and joyfully follow it is what the virtuous esteem.
It would be appropriate for you, sir, to forget these words beyond their literal meaning (addressed to Wen, the Assistant Administrator).
Transgressions and evils: to lose the principle unintentionally is called a transgression; to harm the principle intentionally is called evil.

When a person conceals their faults, they harbor both transgressions and evils; fearing that others may know of them, they adorn themselves with clever speech, wishing to avoid blame while praising their own goodness.
"Being able to shift toward what is righteous" means to move away from it. Confucius said:

"That virtue is not cultivated, that learning is not discussed, that one cannot shift toward righteousness when hearing of it, and that one cannot reform what is not good—these are my worries. Master Yin said: "Virtue must be cultivated before it is perfected;
learning must be discussed before it becomes clear. To see righteousness and be able to shift toward it, and to reform one's faults without regret—" this [is the way].
The fourth is the essential of daily renewal. If one is unable to achieve this, even the sages remain concerned; how much more so for those who study? Yuanwu said:
"My late teacher spoke of how there are those who move others through their virtue and conduct as elders, and those who subdue others through their power and influence.
These are like the flight of the phoenix, which all birds love, or the gait of the tiger and wolf, which all beasts fear. Its...
In their sense of reverence and submission, they are one and the same; yet the difference between their categories is as vast as that between heaven and earth (*Zhuōyòu jí*).
Yuánwù said to the Abbot Lóng: "If one wishes to manage the monastic community (*cónglín*) but does not strive to grasp the sentiments of its people, then the community cannot be managed.
If one strives to grasp the sentiments of the people but is not diligent in receiving those below, then the sentiments of the people cannot be grasped."
It can be achieved. If one strives to welcome subordinates without distinguishing between the worthy and the unworthy, then subordinates cannot be welcomed.

If one strives to distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy while loathing the speaking of their faults and delighting in conforming to oneself, then the worthy and the unworthy cannot be distinguished.
Only the sagely and enlightened person does not loathe the speaking of faults nor delight in conforming to themselves; they follow only the Way. This is how one attains the hearts of others.
The monastic community was thus settled (*Guanglu*).
Chan Master Shao隆 of Mount Huqiu served as the Abbot of Pingjiang Prefecture. He was a native of Heshan in Huzhou and succeeded Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin;
he belonged to the fifteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage.
Yuánwù said: "The abbot takes the wisdom of the assembly as his own wisdom and the mind of the assembly as his own mind.

He is constantly apprehensive that even a single thing may not have its true nature fully expressed, or a single matter may not accord with principle. Thus he diligently seeks out and receives counsel, seeking only what is good. One should inquire into whether a principle is correct or not;
why should one deliberate over whether a matter is large or small? If the principle is correct, even if it involves great expense, why should it not be undertaken?"

It is regrettable. If a matter is improper, even if its expenditure is small, what harm is there in eliminating it? For the small is the precursor to the great, and the subtle is the sprout of the manifest;
therefore, the worthy are cautious at the beginning, and the sages maintain their vigilance. If a tiny stream is not dammed, it will eventually transform a mulberry field;
if a blazing fire is not extinguished, it will ultimately consume the plains and wilds. Once the spreading flames have become intense, the calamity is already complete; though one may wish—
To rescue him, it was truly too late. As the ancients said, "If one does not take care of minor details, they will eventually bring ruin to great virtue.
This is precisely what that means (from the Letter to Fozhi).
To discern right from wrong through wisdom is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*). It is also "to know. It is to master all principles and govern all things.
It is to be diligent and earnest; it is to be zealous; it is to restrain and stop.
The appearance of a small, flickering fire is called *yuan*;
it refers to the spreading of a great fire.
Regarding "not being heedless of minor conduct," the Book says: "Alas! Morning and night, there must be nothing that is not cautious. One must not be heedless of minor conduct."
"In the end, this will bring trouble upon the Great Virtuous One. When a mountain reaches nine *ren* high, its work is undone by one basketful of earth.

The commentary states: "The word 'or' (*huo*) may mean 'perhaps' or 'at some point. Lüshi says: "This refers to the practice of diligent virtue. The single character 'or' is most full of significance;
if one ceases for even a moment, it is no longer the practice of diligent virtue. "Self-conceit" (*jing*) means to maintain or hold fast. "Trifling conduct" (*xi xing*) refers to minor matters.
The character "lèi" (累) is pronounced with a departing tone (*shēng*).
It refers to matters that extend and reach one another. Yuanwu said to Yuan Budai: "In all matters concerning the office of an Elder, you must assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s transformation.
Always contemplate benefiting and saving others as your primary concern. If you act without self-conceit, then those reached will be vast and those saved will be many. However, first—
If there is a mind that prizes itself and displays its own abilities, then thoughts of seeking advantage through luck will arise, and the heart of the unworthy will be born.
(From the *Yunmen An Ji*, following the Shuanglin Stone Inscription)
Master Ciyun Jingyuan of Yuanpudai, the Huguo Temple in Taizhou, was the son of the Zhang family of Nanci in Yongjia.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yuanwu and belonged to the fifteenth generation under Mount Heng.
Yuánwù said to Miàoxǐ, "In all matters of conduct, one must be careful from beginning to end. Therefore, those who excel at the undertaking will surely excel at the completion;
those who excel at the start will surely excel at the finish. To be as careful at the end as at the beginning ensures that no failure occurs. As the ancients said:
'Alas, the robe was not finished when it was turned into a skirt,' and 'The last ten li of a hundred-li journey are equal to the first ninety. These are all lamentations for having a beginning..."
There is no end to this. Thus it is said: "There is none who does not have a beginning; few are able to reach the end. Long ago, the old master Huìtáng said:

"The monk Hángbò Shèng was also an extraordinary seeker of the Dharma; it was only that in his later years he went astray. When one observes his beginnings, can he not be called worthy? (From the *Yúnmén Ān Jí*).
Huangbo Sheng: Chan Master Weisheng of Huangbo Mountain in Ruizhou. A native of the Luo family of Tongzhou, he was a dharma successor of Chan Master Huanglong Nan.
He belonged to the twelfth generation under the lineage of Mount Heng.
"How could this not be so? Yuanwu said to Fojian, "Master Baiyun’s every movement and action was invariably modeled after the ancients.

He once said, 'If a matter does not consult the past, it is called a lack of lawfulness. I have extensively studied the words and deeds of former sages, and thus I have fulfilled his aspiration. However...

"It is not merely that I am fond of antiquity; rather, it is because people of the present day are insufficient as models. My late teacher often said, 'The Master holds fast to antiquity and does not recognize the changes of the times.
The Master replied, 'To change the old and alter the constant is the great affliction of people today; I shall never do so.
(From *The Daily Record of Chan Master Xian*)
Fojian of Taiping Temple in Shuzhou. Chan Master Fojian Huiqin was the son of the Jiang family of his native prefecture.
He was a successor of Chan Master Wuzu Faian and belongs to the fourteenth generation under the lineage of Nanyue.
Regarding the hexagram Dà Xū (Great Accumulation), the Image says: "Heaven within the mountain is Great Accumulation.

The superior man extensively recognizes the words and deeds of the past in order to accumulate his virtue. The Commentary states: "The 'words and deeds of the past' refer to the speech and conduct of the ancient sages.
By observing their words and examining their conduct, one completes one's virtue; this is the meaning of 'Great Accumulation. As for 'accumulation' (xù)..."
It is that which has been accumulated and formed.
Thus, it is the eternal, unchanging Way of the ancients.

The Buddha-insight Master Qin moved from Taiping to Zhihai. When the Prefectural Governor, Master Ceng Yuanli, asked who was worthy [to succeed him], [the Master] replied: "The one who has accumulated [this Way] is the one."
Upon the succession of the abbotship, Fojian proposed the head seat Mingben for the position. The Duke wished to meet him once;
Fojian said, "Mingben is a man of rigid integrity who remains aloof from the world and has no worldly attachments. Even if you were to invite him, I fear he would not comply;
how much less would he come of his own accord? The Duke pressed his invitation firmly. Mingben replied, "This is what is called 'the elder who reveals his body'. He ultimately fled to Sikong.
Master Shan turned to look at Fojian and said, "No one knows a son better than his father. He immediately commanded the various mountain monasteries to make a firm request;
with no other choice, [Fojian] finally accepted the command. (From the *Daily Record of Attendant Xian*)
Chan Master Zhibing of Nanhua in Shaoyou was the Head Seat Bing. He was a native of Yongkang in Shu. By nature he was stern and severe;
at the time, he was known as "Bing the Iron-Faced. He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fojian Qin and belonged to the fifteenth generation under Nanyue.
Chengshen first beheld his physical form and later served as the abbot.

"Elder" (*zhǎnglǎo*) is a title for one of venerable virtue; having thoroughly realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he possesses internal wisdom and virtue, causing students to revere and follow him;
thus, he is called an "elder."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "suppressed and aroused" (*yīfā*):
Fojian said to Xun Fudeng, "A person of lofty character does not take fame or rank as a source of honor;
a person who has realized the truth is not distressed by suppression or frustration. Those who accept favor and exert their strength, or see profit and offer their sincerity—all such individuals..."
[Recorded by] Zhongren yixia (Below the Average Man).
Inquiry concerning Fodeng of Anji County, Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang Province: Chan Master Shou Xun Fodeng of He Shan was the son of the Shi family of this prefecture.
He was a successor of Chan Master Fojian Qin and belongs to the fifteenth generation under Nanyue.
*Cuò* (挫) means to crush or break. *Xiào* (効) means to offer or exhaust.
It describes the appearance of offering one's sincerity and exhausting one's reverence.
Fojian said to the Head Seat, Ming: "In all matters concerning those called 'Elders,' one must have nothing to which they are attached. If there is even one thing..."
When one has preferences, one is harmed by external things. When one craves desires, the mind of greedy attachment arises.
When one craves gain and sustenance, the thought of vying for competition arises. When one craves compliance and obedience, flattery and sycophancy flourish.

When one craves victory and defeat, the mountain of "self" and "other" becomes high. When one craves exploitation and oppression, the sounds of lamentation and resentment arise. To investigate these exhaustively, they do not depart from this single [principle].
Mind. If the mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas naturally vanish. Nothing that you have attained throughout your life exceeds this. You should exert yourself in this;
it is for the purpose of correcting those who come to study [you]. (Southern Huayan Stone Inscription)
Thieves cause harm and invasion.
"Love" (*ālaya*) refers to the incessant entanglement of affectionate attachment.
"Flattery" (*kuhana*) means being base and submissive toward superiors; "deceit" (*lapanā*) means being sycophantic and fraudulent toward inferiors.
"Exploitative and grasping" refers to the carving away and plundering of the people's wealth.
To "encourage this" means to promote such behavior.
Fojian said: "My late master was frugal; his single bowl-bag and shoe-sack had been patched a hundred times and mended a thousand times, yet he could not bear to discard them."
[The Master] set them aside and once said: "These two items have accompanied me out of the pass for barely fifty years; how could I ever be willing to abandon them midway?

There was a monk named Wuzhe from Quannan who presented him with a coarse hemp robe, saying he had obtained it overseas; he claimed that when worn in winter it was warm, and when worn in summer it was cool.
The former master [Zhaozhou] remarked: "For this old monk, when cold there are firewood, charcoal, and paper quilts; when hot there is the pine wind."
"What is the purpose of hoarding this? [The Record of Daily Life] says:
"It is for mending and patching robes.
'Hé' refers to coarse hair-cloth; it is cloth woven from the fur of two types of mice: the ice-mouse and the fire-mouse. The fire-mouse... [text fragment].
Entering fire, they are not burned; their fur grows to about one chi in length. This is what is known as "fire-washed cloth" (*huobanbu*). As for the "ice-rats":
in the north there is ice a hundred chi thick, beneath which live rats that feed only on ice. Their fur grows several cun long and can be made into cloth.
When these two things are combined, it is warm in winter and cool in summer. This is recorded in the *Shenyiji* (Records of Divine Marvels).
Fojian said: "When my late master heard that Zhenjing had passed away, he prepared a seat and offerings for him and wept with excessive grief. He sighed, saying:
'Such a person is hard to find—one who has seen the very root of the Way, devoid of branches and leaves. It is a pity he died so young; I have not yet heard of anyone who can succeed to his path.
From this point on, the monasteries of Jiangxi will fall into silence. (From the *Rilu*).
Fojian said: "Our late master remarked that Master Baoyun was throughout his life open and unreserved, without the guile of a citadel.

Whenever he perceived a matter that accorded with righteousness and could be done, he would leap forward and take the initiative himself. He delighted in drawing forth and promoting the worthy and capable, and took no pleasure in sycophancy or fickle association."

He sat upright on a single mat in a state of serene detachment all day long. He once said to the attendant Neng, "To maintain the Way and remain content in poverty is the natural lot of a patch-robed monk.
Those who allow their success or failure, their gain or loss, to shift what they uphold may not yet be spoken of as having realized the Way" (Daily Record).
His erudition was so thorough that he could comprehend ancient texts. Furthermore, his mind was as vast as a mountain range with deep valleys;
like the ocean receiving all and the mountains containing everything, he harbored no thoughts of "self" versus "other.

Regarding the meaning of "fortified walls and inner chambers" being obscured—this signifies having no outer city-walls and no inner treasuries, such that there is no distinction between exterior and interior.
This refers to the embankments [of the heart].
To "leap for joy" means to perceive righteousness and accord with principle; it is to advance with vigor.
"Adhering and separating" means to attach oneself when there is profit and to depart when there is harm. Those who "adhere and separate" do not follow [the Way].
Principle and righteousness. To merely seek a hasty accommodation is not the way.
*Xiāo* (pronounced xiào) refers to a bird flying alone; it also implies being as one is. Fojian said:
"If one does not worry for the sake of the Way, then the mind’s application will not be far-reaching. If one dwells in constant ease, then the will’s purpose will not be realized."
Great indeed! The ancients underwent hardships and experienced perils before they could enjoy lifelong peace.

For when tasks are difficult, the will becomes sharp; when one endures austerity, reflection deepens. Thus, they were able to transform calamity into fortune and transform material things into the Way.

Yet I often see students who pursue external objects while forgetting the Way, turning their backs on light to cast themselves into darkness. Consequently, they gloss over their own inadequacies and deceive themselves.
People consider this to be wisdom. They force others to follow what they cannot reach and treat others with contempt to appear superior.

By means of this, they deceive others, yet they do not realize there are those with prior awakening whom they cannot deceive; by means of this, they conceal their faults, yet they do not realize there is public opinion which cannot be suppressed.

Therefore, those who consider themselves wise are regarded as foolish by others, while those who consider themselves lowly are regarded as high-minded by others. Only the truly virtuous are not [thus deceived].
However, phenomena are dispersed and infinite, while the human capacity to fathom them is limited and finite.
To attempt to encompass infinite phenomena with finite wisdom results in the intellect becoming biased and the spirit becoming exhausted;
thus, there will inevitably be deficiencies regarding the Great Way (Letter to Xiu Zizhi).
"Rui" (銳) refers to the appearance of a sharp point penetrating deeply.
[The saying] "If one's deliberation does not penetrate deep into the tiger's den, how can one obtain the tiger's cub? implies that a student must not allow worldly affairs to preoccupy their mind.
Only after they have wandered at ease within the realm of the subtle and profound, and roamed leisurely in the land of "having nothing," will they necessarily—
One treads upon the realm of non-action and peaceful bliss;
yet, if one's cognition is biased or deficient, then phenomena and principle cannot be harmoniously integrated,
remaining obstructed and unpenetrated.
Fojian said to Master Longya Cai, "If you wish to reform the defects of former practitioners, you must not attempt to eliminate them too hastily.

You must reform through specific circumstances so that the common folk do not become suspicious; in this way, they will likely remain free from resentment. I have often said that there are three essentials for a *zhuchi* (abbot):
discernment, capability in action, and decisiveness. If one lacks any of these three, then one's discernment will be clouded, and in the end, one will fail."
If petty people become negligent and disrespectful, the abbot’s authority will not be sustained.
Chan Master Zhicai of Longya Temple in Tanzhou, whose secular surname was Shi and who hailed from Shuzhou, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fojian Qin.
He belonged to the fifteenth generation under Mount Heng.
Fojian said: "In general, as the head of a monastery, what is most valued is pure conduct. One must maintain great integrity to welcome monastics from all quarters.
If even the slightest trace of vulgar or improper behavior remains within oneself, one will be scrutinized by petty people;
even if one possesses the virtue and realization of the ancients, students will harbor doubts and fail to place their trust. (From *Shantang Xiaocan*)
"Vei-xie" (猥媟) means vulgar and base; "xia" (下) means lax and negligent.
"Kui-shu" (窺覷) describes the manner of peering and looking with a narrow gaze.
Fojian said: "Among the disciples of the Buddha-eye [Foyan], only Ga'an was resolute and upright, not conforming to worldly sentiments. As a person, he had no personal attachments."

"Excellent. In his actions, he was without factional alliances; he was pure, austere, reverent, and conscientious. From beginning to end, he established himself through integrity and reputation, possessing the spirit of the ancients.
Among the monastics of recent times, few can compare to him" (Letter to Geng Longxue).
Foyan Chanyuan, the Zen Master of Longmen in Shuzhou, was a native of the Li clan from Linqiong.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Wuzu Faian and belonged to the fourteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage.
"Stout and upright" means to be supremely impartial and without private interest.
"Factionalism" (*dǎngyuán*) refers to forming cliques with superiors; "pulling up from below" refers to drawing others upward.
Master Foyuan Yuan said: "The demeanor when presiding over the assembly must be solemn even on days of leisure. When facing guests..."
Discourse: When one is engaged in private intimacy, a forest-dweller (aranyaka) must deliberate before speaking, acting, or undertaking any deed.
Only after careful consideration should they proceed; do not act with haste or recklessness.

If you are unable to reach a decision on your own, you ought to consult the elders and extensively inquire of the ancient sages to broaden your knowledge and experience, thereby supplementing what you have not yet mastered and illuminating what you do not yet understand.
"How can one vainly display an air of grandeur and solely indulge in arrogance, thereby manifesting one's own ugliness?
If even a single action is lost at the outset, then a hundred subsequent virtues cannot conceal it. (From *A Letter to Zhenmu*)
"Presiding over the multitude" (*lì zhòng*) means "to face them from above. This refers to the way one establishes oneself: inwardly firm and outwardly supple.

The demeanor of one presiding over the multitude is to receive from above and yield to those below. If one is not harmonious, one cannot engage with others; if one is not solemn, one cannot govern subordinates.
"Ni" means to draw near or associate with.
The Buddha-eye says: When humans are born between heaven and earth, they receive the qi of yin and yang to form their bodies.
Unless one is a true sage who appears in the world through the power of compassionate vows, it seems impossible to suddenly eliminate the mind of desire and profit. Only the Sage...

People know that one cannot eliminate another's desires for profit and pleasure; therefore, one first rectifies their mind through the Way and its Virtue (*Dao-de*), and subsequently uses benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and wisdom to instruct and restrain them.

Through this gradual progress day by day and month by month, one ensures that their desires for profit and pleasure do not overcome benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and wisdom, thereby preserving their integrity of the Way and its Virtue. (Letter to Geng Longxue)
Foyan said: "A student must not be mired in words and language. For words and language are interpretations based on others;
they obstruct the gate of self-awakening and prevent one from transcending the realm of speech and symbols.
In the past, Daguan Ying initially saw Master Shimen Cong, and while he was displaying his verbal eloquence within the meditation hall, Cong said: 'What you have been saying is merely paper.'"
The Master said: "As for the subtle and profound essence of the mind, one has not yet beheld its depths; one must seek wondrous enlightenment.
Once enlightened, one stands preeminent and transcendent, neither riding upon words nor being hindered by phrases.

Like the roar of the lion king, which strikes terror into all beasts, when one looks back at the study of mere letters, it is not merely a matter of ten to a hundred or a thousand to ten thousand. (Record of Dragon Gate)
*Ni* (second tone): To stagnate.
Daguanying, Chan Master Tanyi of Mount Jinshan in Runzhou, was a successor of Chan Master Shimen Cong.
Fuyan said to Gao'an: "The *Baizhang Qinggui* generally aims to distinguish the correct from the deviant and to provide a model for regulating things and harmonizing the assembly."
Thus, one establishes regulations according to the times to govern the sentiments of later generations. Human sentiment is like water; ritual rules and laws serve as its embankments.
If the embankments are not firm, there will inevitably be flooding and breaches. If human sentiment is not restrained, it will run wild and cause disorder.
Therefore, to eliminate sentiment, cease delusion, prohibit evil, and stop depravity, one cannot for a single moment dispense with ritual rules. Thus, ritual rules and...

How could the Dharma possibly exhaustively restrain human emotions? It is nevertheless a stairway that assists one in entering the Way. The establishment of rules and regulations is as clear as the sun and moon;
those who look toward them will not be lost. They are as expansive as the Great Road; those who walk upon them will not be confused.

Although the institutions established by the former sages differ, they are no different in their ultimate source. In recent times, the monastic communities have established labor regulations and rules.
Among them, there are those who strictly adhere to the rules and regulations, and there are those who hold them in contempt.
Both of these states result from turning one's back on the Way and losing propriety, following one’s passions and pursuing evil.

They never consider that the former sages established these [rules] to remedy the defects of the Final Dharma, to restrain licentious emotions, to block the sources of craving and desire, and to cut off the paths of depravity. (From the *Donghu ji*)
"Jie-chou" refers to the steps of a terrace; "xia-dan-chou" refers to the lower part of the vermilion steps. This means that what is shallow appears deep.
"Mie" means to slight or disregard. Foyan said to Gao'an: "One who can see the tip of an autumn hair cannot see his own eyelashes; one who lifts three thousand jin [of weight]..."

As for those who are heavy with responsibility yet cannot lift themselves up, they are not much different from students who are clear in their criticism of others but ignorant in showing leniency toward themselves (from the *Zhenmu ji*).
Chan Master Ga’ān Shànwù of Yúnqū in Nánkāng Commandery was a native of the Lí clan of Bàn Prefecture.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fǎyǎn Yuǎn and belonged to the fifteenth generation below Nányuè Huáì.
Regarding the "autumn hair," Zhuangzi said that it refers to the extremely minute hair grown by animals in autumn. Mencius said:
"One's clarity is sufficient to discern the tip of an autumn hair, yet one does not see a cartload of firewood."
*Jie* (pronounced "jie") refers to the eyebrows. A *jun* is thirty *jin*. Master Gao’an Wù said:
"When I first traveled to the ancestral mountains, I attended a small public discourse by Master Fojian, who said:
'Greed, desire, anger, and hatred are as harmful as enemies; one must oppose them with wisdom. Wisdom is like water: if it is not used, it stagnates; if it stagnates, [it becomes turbid]. "
He did not flow [with worldly attachments]. When one does not flow, wisdom does not function.

As for what to do with greed, desire, hatred, and anger—at that time, although I was young, I knew in my heart that he was a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). I then requested to be admitted as a resident monk (according to the *Yunju Shilu*).
Gao’an said: "If a student maintains a state of centrality and rectitude, even if they undergo a hundred setbacks and humiliations, they will remain vast and free from anxiety.

Should their orientation, however, be biased or deviant, and they spend their days and nights busily scheming for profit and status, I fear that this noble body will find no place within heaven and earth" (*Zhenmu ji*).
The designation "lowly and petty" (*qūqū bēixiǎo*) is synonymous with being "mediocre" (*lùlù*).
Gāo'ān said: "Virtue, morality, benevolence, and righteousness are not possessed by the ancients alone; people of today also possess them.

It is because their knowledge and insight are not clear, their learning is not broad, their spiritual capacity (*kengqì*) is not pure, their will and spirit are narrow and inferior, and they do not practice with vigor."

Consequently, one is shifted by sounds and forms, rendered unconscious of this process. This is because deluded thoughts and emotional attachments have accumulated through long habituation and cannot be eliminated all at once;
for this reason, one fails to reach the state of the ancients. (This letter to Gentleman Geng Longxue is found in the *Zhenmu ji*).
When Gao’an heard that Cheng Kumu was residing at Jinshan and living in luxury and splendor, he sighed for a long time and said:

"The dharma of a bhikṣu prizes purity and frugality. How could it be appropriate to act like this? It merely increases the insatiable desires of those among the younger generation who habituate themselves to light food and fine clothing.
Are they not ashamed before the ancients?"
Chengkumu (成枯木), Chan Master Facheng (法成) of Jingguo Monastery in Dongjing (東京).
A native of Heshuo (何朔), he was a successor to Chan Master Furong Kai (芙蓉楷) and belonged to the twelfth generation of the Qingyuan (清原) lineage.
"Extravagance" (*chi-mi*) refers to wasteful luxury.
"Light and fat" means riding on fat horses and wearing light furs. An ancient poem says: "Riding fat horses and wearing light furs, they stroll leisurely through the neighborhoods;
though they may gain the pity of market-goers, they are still despised by those who truly understand."

Gao’an said: "The fundamental principle of a *zhuchi* (abbot) is to treat the monastic community as his home. He must distinguish roles appropriately and entrust responsibilities to those who are worthy.
His conduct determines the principles of security and peril; his success or failure concerns the very source of the teaching and transformation.

As a model for others, how could he afford to be casual? I have never seen a *zhuchi* who, while being lax and negligent himself, can cause his monks to submit, nor one whose legal regulations decline..."
To restrain the wild arrogance of the monastic community: in the past, King Śrī Harṣa sent away his head seat monk, and Yangshan Wei dismissed his attendant;

these accounts are recorded in the classical texts and serve as sufficient models for emulation. Today, however, everyone pursues their own private desires, causing the regulations of Baizhang to fall into great ruin.

They are negligent in rising early, frequently failing in the etiquette of formal assemblies, sometimes indulging in greed and gluttony without restraint, and at other times acting for the sake of profit.
They were nurtured until they gave rise to clamorous strife; even such things as sycophancy and ugliness came to exist in every way. Alas!
To hope for the flourishing of the Dharma-gate and the prosperity of the religious teachings—how could this ever be possible? (From the *Longchang ji*)
To distinguish; to involve; to hinge upon;
to concern; to neglect and abandon; for the bowstring to loosen;
to wither and decay through slow torture.
Chan Master Wushi Jiechen of Yuyang Monastery in Qingyuan Prefecture was surnamed Chen and was the son of the Zhang family of Wenzhou.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Changling Zhuo. By nature he was stern and resolute; when presiding over the assembly, he adhered strictly to ancient regulations.
At that time, he was known as "Chen the Iron-Faced One."
Yangshan Wei, the Chan Master Xingwei of Yangshan in Yuanzhou, was a native of Heshuo. He was a successor of Chan Master Huanglong Nan.
By nature he was stern, yet he possessed a disciplined method in managing affairs. When he assigned someone to perform a specific task, no one dared to disobey.
Once, he gave the names of twelve individuals to the *weina* (administrative officer) and instructed him to have them all arrive at the abbot’s quarters the following day.
He suffered a public rebuke. Furthermore, at the time of the tea ceremony, one person was missing. Daowei asked who it was. The attendant replied, "Yongtai of Suizhou.
The head seat said, "Tài has not yet returned from his mountain tour; I have invited another monk to take his place. Daowei approved of this.
Suddenly, someone reported that Tai was indeed there. The head seat had hidden him; Wei, with a solemn expression, ordered a search and found him.

Tai confessed his own inadequacy, fearing he might lose what he had received [in instruction], and stated that the head seat truly did not know [of his whereabouts]. Wei ordered the bell to be struck to assemble the community and declared:
"To deceive the assembly while obscuring one's own conscience is something others ought not even to do, let alone for the head seat to do so by virtue of his position."
The position of Seat-Holder (Śayanāsana) is an office honored by senior teachers; yet [you] have destroyed it yourselves. Both men were punished and expelled from the monastery.
Consequently, the assembly submitted to his impartiality. Later, Daoyi succeeded to the Dharma and resided at Huangbo Mountain; the Head Seat resided at Mt.
Gui and succeeded Chan Master Huanglong, producing the *Sengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha).
*Huī* means to destroy or ruin. *Sùxìng* means to rise early.
*Cānhuì* refers to the evening *xiǎocān* (small session) for reflection and assembly.
To seek after things with insatiable desire is called *tān*; to crave them with insatiable appetite is called *tāo*.

Whenever Gao’an resided at Yunju and encountered a monk in his quarters whose realization did not accord with his own, he would immediately seize him by the sleeve and, with a stern countenance, rebuke him, saying:
"Your parents raised your body; your teachers and friends have fulfilled your aspirations. You are not beset by the hardships of hunger or cold."
"Without the toil of conscription and labor, if you do not now cultivate the path with firm and resolute diligence, what face will you have to show your parents, teachers, and friends on another day?
When the monks heard these words, some wept incessantly.
Such was the strictness and order of his commands (from the *Qian'an Yishi*).
*Mì* (pronounced *méi*) refers to the sleeves of a garment.
Military conscription is called *zhēng*; civilian labor service is called *yì*.
When Gāo'ān was residing at Yúnjū, he heard that a monk was ill and moved him to the Yánshòu Hall; he sighed with deep lamentation as if [the monk] had emerged from his own body.
He visited him morning and evening to inquire after his health, even going so far as to personally prepare his food. He would not eat until he had first tasted it himself.

If the weather grew slightly cold, he would pat the man’s back and ask, "Are you not wearing too few clothes? If it was hot, he would examine his complexion and ask, "Are you not suffering from the heat?

When the man passed away, he did not inquire whether the deceased had any property; rather, he exhausted all the courtesies of the monastery to escort the body to its final resting place. The administrative officials...
Or, when others spoke disparagingly, Gao’an rebuked them, saying, "In the past, Baizhang established the permanent endowment for those who were aged or infirm;
you are neither old nor ill. Those from the four quarters who recognized his character held him in high esteem.
When he retired to Yunju and later passed through Tiantai, there were barely fifty disciples following him; some who were unable to go with him wept as they parted. Indeed, his...
Virtue moves people in such a way (from the *Sandang Sāmcān*).

The *Yanshou Hall* (*Yǎnshòu Táng*) is the place for comforting the elderly and the infirm. In ancient monastic communities (*cónglín*), elderly monks were sent to the *Ānlè Hall* (*Ānlè Táng*), while the sick were sent to the *Yanshou Hall*;
this is what the present-day *Nirvāṇa Hall* (*Nièpán Táng*) is.
That his misfortune could not be averted was because his heavenly mandate was coming to an end, and thus it could not be saved.
When Gao’an retired from Yunju, Yuanwu wished to renovate Foyin’s Wulong Hermitage as a place for him to rest and relax.
Gao’an said, "For one who has left the secular world, if there is the joy of the Way and righteousness, the physical form may be cast aside. As for me, I follow my heart's inclination."
It was like the morning moon at Changgeng; how long can its light and shadow last?

Furthermore, the Western Hills and Mount Lu have forests and springs that connect one after another—all are places for my retirement in old age. Why must everything be possessed by oneself before it can be enjoyed?
Not long after, he took up his staff and traveled to Tiantai, where he eventually passed away on Mount Huading (from the *Zhenmu ji*).
Foyin (Buddha-Seal) succeeded Chan Master Liaoyuan of Yunju in Nankang Commandery; he was the dharma heir of Chan Master Shixian of Kaiyuan.
The *Yanju* (Seclusion at Ease) states: "To 'seclude' means to dwell alone. As the *Analects* says: "When you, Master, dwell in seclusion..."
Regarding "Following the Heart," Confucius said: "At fifteen, I set my heart upon learning. At thirty, I became established. At forty, I was no longer confused.
At fifty, I knew the mandate of Heaven. At sixty, my ears were attuned to all sounds. At seventy, I could follow the dictates of my heart’s desire without overstepping the bounds of propriety.
The commentary states: "To 'follow' means that in all matters one acts according to the desires of the heart, yet does not transgress the law."
It is "crossing over. The star Chang-geng (Long-geng) is bright. To the east is Qi-ming, called the planet Venus; to the west is Chang-geng, called the planet Mercury.
Venus appears when the sun rises while it is in the west; Mercury appears when the sun sets while it is in the east. Furthermore, first...
That which rises before the sun is called *qīmíng* (the Illuminator); that which sets after the sun is called *chánggēng* (the Long-Tailed Star).
Regarding the "morning moon," this refers to the moon on the twenty-seventh or twenty-eighth day; as soon as it appears, daybreak has already arrived.
Thus, its radiance and duration are as brief as this.
Gao’an said: "Among the *zhendi* (patch-robed monks), there is no distinction between the worthy and the foolish;

it depends solely upon the *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend) to cultivate their virtue and deeds through patient guidance, to develop their capacities and talents through successive trials, to honor their words with commendation, and to preserve their integrity through generous affection.

As years and months accumulate, both reputation and substance flourish together. For all people possess the spiritual spark; it is only through diligent encouragement that they are brought forth, like jade hidden within its ore."
A raw gem, if cast aside, is but a piece of pottery or stone; yet when polished and refined, it becomes a jade scepter or a ceremonial tablet.
It is like water at its source: if obstructed, it becomes mud; if dredged and cleared, it becomes a river or marsh.

Thus we know that in this age of the semblance-dharma (xiangji), it is not only that the worthy are neglected and left unused, but that the way of nurturing and encouraging them has also failed to reach its full potential. During the time when the monastic forests were flourishing, all were...
In a declining age, talent is discarded; in such a time, one is deemed ignorant. When an era flourishes, one is deemed wise. Thus it is said: "All humans possess the spirit of enlightenment;

it is only through diligent cultivation that it is brought forth. From this we know that the talents of scholars rise and fall with the times: if they are cherished, they arrive; if they are encouraged, they flourish.
"Suppressed, it declines; cast aside, it is severed. This is how the moral character, virtue, and talent of scholars wax and wane" (Letter to Li, the Commissioner of Transport).
"Jingjiang" (旌獎) means to manifest excellence above; it also means to encourage and reward below.
"Puo" (璞) refers to the stone in which jade is hidden. "Dizhuo" (抵擲) means to cast away or discard.
"Zuozhuo" (琢磨) refers to the treatment of jade and stone; having first carved it, one further polishes it, meaning that once it has already been refined, one makes it even more so.
This is to seek their essence.
The *gui* and *zhang* are auspicious jade vessels; they are round at the top and square at the bottom. The Duke holds the *huan-gui* nine inches long;
the Marquis holds the *xin-gui*, and the Earl holds the *gong-gui*, both seven inches long.
*Yēn* (pronounced *è*) means to block or obstruct. *Jùn* (pronounced *jùn*) means deep.
*Yīn* means great. Gāo Ān said:
"In the greatness of transformation and instruction, none takes precedence over morality (*dào*), virtue (*dé*), propriety (*lǐ*), and righteousness (*yì*). If the abbot honors morality and virtue,"
When scholars esteem reverence and practice ritual propriety and righteousness, then scholars feel shame at greed and competition.

When monastics harbor pride that leads to a loss of dignified demeanor, then scholars suffer the弊 (calamity) of arrogance and violence. When monastics harbor disputes that cause their countenances to change with emotion, then scholars suffer the禍 (calamity) of assault and strife.
The former sages, perceiving these things before they occurred, consequently selected men of wisdom and sagacity to preside over the monastic groves.
They caused all to look up to them with full regard; even those who did not understand were transformed.

Thus, during the time when the Way of Shitou and Mazu flourished, men of outstanding talent emerged, their deportment gentle and refined, harmonious and solemn. Whether issuing commands or speaking, they would communicate through a glance of the eyes or a raising of the eyebrows.
That all these may serve as models for future generations is indeed only to be expected (from the Letter to Sishin).
Reverence is manifested outwardly; reverence is maintained inwardly.
He lost his composure and displayed an air lacking in reverence, manifesting the signs of arrogance.
This was to admonish and instruct him.
Regarding Master Xituan (Stonehead) of Nanyue during the Tang Dynasty: he was a native of the Chen family of Gaoyang in Ruizhou.
He succeeded Chan Master Xingxi of Qingyuan. Later, to the east of Hengye Temple, there was a rock shaped like a platform;
he built a hut there and resided within it.
"Shun" means to blink the eyes.

Gao’an said: "My late teacher once remarked that when traveling on pilgrimage beyond the mountain passes, one often encounters many unpleasant circumstances at the small monasteries visited along the way.
He reflected that when Fayan went to study under Dizang and Mingjiao met Shending, they no longer experienced any such afflictions.
(Recorded Sayings)
Master Wenyi of Qingliang Monastery in Jinling was known as Fayen. He was the son of the Lu family from Yuhang.
Once, while traveling on pilgrimage with the mountain master Xuwu, they reached the region outside Lake Fu. Encountering a sudden downpour, the mountain streams surged like cascades.
They took temporary lodging at Dizang Monastery west of the city to rest briefly during the snow. As they sat by the brazier, Zhen said, "The Master..."
"Where are you going? The Master said, "I am traveling on pilgrimage. [The monk] asked, "What is the matter of traveling on pilgrimage? The Master said, "I do not know.
[The monk] said, "Not knowing is most intimate. At these words, the Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment, whereupon he succeeded to his Dharma.
He was the one who later founded the Fayan school.
Chan Master Guichen of Dizang Luohan Monastery in Zhangzhou was the son of the Li family of that mountain.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xiansha Shibei. Later, the Prefectural Governor of Zhangzhou invited him to reside at Dizang Monastery, and subsequently he moved to Luohan Monastery.
There, amidst dilapidated buildings and ruined walls, the Master remained serene and contented.
When Mingjiao saw Chan Master Shending Song, Song was seated in the hall. Song spread out his sitting mat and paid respectful obeisance.
Song pointed to two small jars on the hall floor and said, "The time for you to come has arrived; this year the temple will finally have sauce for food.
Until next year, we shall eat gruel. He then saw a lay attendant (jingren) carrying a basket to gather things and throw them away.
In the midst of the monks' alms bowls, Huìsōng observed that some were chewing their food while others left it as it was, appearing unconcerned.

Huìsōng tucked his sleeve under his arm and went down to the hall to look; he found them eating broken rice cakes and biscuits. Huìsōng questioned the senior monks, who replied, "This monastery has never cooked porridge since its founding.
On days when a donor invites us for a meal, we dispatch the monks one after another to attend, leaving behind these dry remnants."

The remnants were collected and stored in the treasury. On days when there was no *zhāi* (fasting/retreat), he ordered them to be crushed, toasted, and evenly distributed, manifesting his sharing of both sweet and bitter experiences.

Gao’an was upright and firm both inwardly and outwardly; his demeanor was majestic and imposing. Whether in motion or stillness, he never forgot the rules of propriety. During his time among the assembly, he repeatedly...

Even when he witnessed acts of aggression or encroachment, he took no offense. Throughout his life, he maintained a life of simplicity and frugality. Within his quarters, he did not grant permission for anything frivolously;

if others did not accord with his views, he would invariably respond with a stern countenance and direct speech to resolve the matter. His fellow monks all submitted to him with faith and respect. He once said, "In the study of the Way, my learning is no superior to others';
it is simply that throughout my life, in all I have done, I have had no cause for shame before my own heart."
Style, majesty, and measure; a solemn countenance and reverent demeanor—these are extraordinary.
They are states of integrity, movement, and regulation.
This means leading students to a state where there is neither excess nor deficiency, thereby ultimately bringing them to completion.
He was a man of great virtue.
When Gao’an was residing at Yunju, he saw some monastics who sought out the hidden faults of others; he immediately spoke to them with composure, saying: "The matter is not as you think.

For those of us beneath the forest, the cultivation of the Way is our urgent task. Harmony is the means by which one cultivates the self; how can we allow ourselves to indulge recklessly in attachment?"
Hatred ruins a person’s conduct; such are its devious workings. When the Master first declined the invitation to Yunju, Foyan sent a letter urging him, saying:
"Yunju is preeminent in the region east of the Yangtze River; it is a place where you may settle the assembly and practice the Way. It seems you need not persist in your refusal."
The Master said, "Since the beginning of the monastic communities, there have been no few scholars who, because of such designations, have ruined their integrity and righteousness.
Upon hearing this, Fojian remarked, "Gao'an’s sense of propriety in his coming and going is something that other patch-robed monks cannot match" (Recorded Sayings).
"Jia" (Shell) signifies the head. When speaking in terms of ten thousand, "jia" occupies the foremost position; thus, Yunju was the preeminent among the ten monasteries of Jiangnan.
"Qu" (Departure) and "jù" (Arrival) refer to the locus of realization and to one's conduct.
The "Exhortation for Elderly and Ailing Monks" by Gao’an states: "I, this poor monk, have often perused the Tripitaka and carefully examined the Buddha’s intent.
He did not permit bhikṣus to sit and receive food without labor, lest they give rise to a mind of indolence or conceive the view of self.

Every morning, the Buddha and his disciples carry their bowls to beg for food, making no distinction between the noble and the lowly, and harboring no sense of superiority or inferiority, so that [the donors] may obtain merit."
It is distributed equally to all. That which is later termed "permanently established" was originally intended for bhikṣus who were aged or infirm and unable to go begging;
it was not something that those in the prime of youth could obtain to eat. This continued until after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the era of the True Dharma.

Those who currently occupy the abbot’s quarters do not merely scrape away the contents of the alms bowls of the multitude to gratify their own appetites; they even use these means to cultivate personal favors beyond ordinary human relations.

In the worst cases, they go so far as to gouge out treasures and purchase rare curiosities to distribute widely as favors, hoping thereby to be transferred to a great monastery. One can only fear that in the future...
"The Iron-Faced Old Man Yan calculates it" (from *Nianya Manlu*).
Zen Master Zhongshan Ruyan of Jinling was styled Zhe’ung; his dharma lineage is unknown.
"Shè" (pardon) means to fully release those who have committed offenses. As for [Master] Càn, his seclusion in the mountain is not well-documented.
The ancient [master] Dòng of Rìzhōu originated from Chán Master Bǎo. He was a native of Lúzhōu and succeeded Chán Master Jiè of the Fifth Patriarch.
He belonged to the ninth generation under Qīngyuán. By nature he was grave and meticulous; he once served as the head of the storehouse at Wǔzǔ. When Jiè fell ill, [he attended to him].
He ordered an attendant to go to the storehouse to fetch fresh ginger for decocting medicine. Baoshou scolded him. The attendant informed Baoshou of the precept [against taking life].
Baoshou then ordered money to be taken back to trade for it; only then did he take the ginger and give it to him. Later, there was a vacancy for the abbotship at Dongshan in Junzhou.
The Prefect entrusted him with a letter of recommendation and appointed the one he designated as the abbot. The letter of appointment read: "Han Zhude is capable of selling fresh ginger.

He subsequently entered the world and resided at Dongshan; later, he moved to Guizong Temple. One day, as he was leaving the gate, he saw an official riding a horse toward him. The Master asked, "What official is this?
The attendant replied, "It is the County Magistrate, who has ordered us to clear the way. Baofu stood to one side by the roadside.
He tried to avoid it, but the horse suddenly saw him and knelt down, refusing to move. Ba said, "Even a beast recognizes a man.
The magistrate realized this was Ba, bowed again, and departed. Later, when Ba moved to Yunju, one night a mountain deity carried his sedan chair around the temple.
Ba said, "Carry your father and mother up to the Abbot’s quarters. When Ba first traveled as a wandering monk, he once stayed overnight at an inn.
Harassed by a courtesan, he yielded his bed to her so she might sleep. Bao sat upright in meditation through the night until dawn.
When the courtesan demanded payment for the lodging, Bao gave it to her; then, going outside, he took fire and burned his own mat before departing.

The courtesan told her mother the truth, whereupon she invited the Master to hold a vegetarian feast and seek repentance, declaring him to be a true son of the Buddha. He once composed the *Damo* [treatise].

Praise! This has been most widely disseminated throughout the monastic forests. Master Langye Jue understood this; it is now included within the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma).
He sat upon the great throne, dwelling in majesty. "Fàn" means much; it means floating.

*Kṣatra* is a Sanskrit term; here it means "pole," referring to the flagstaff. Whenever a śramaṇa attains the Way, they erect a banner to announce [their achievement] to the four quarters. (From the *Chuyao lan*).
Combined Commentary on the Jewel Instructions of the Chan Forest, Scroll Two.
