*Combined Commentary on the Precious Instructions of the Chan Forest*, Scroll Three.
Collated by the Layman Zhang Wenjia (style name Zhongjia) of Hulin and Jinghui.
When Master Xuedang Xing was residing at Jianfu Monastery, one day he asked a newly arrived monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "Fujian."
At Zhoulai, Xuetang asked, "Did you see any good elder monks along the way? The monk replied, "Recently I passed by Master Ben, the abbot of Boshan in Xin Prefecture.
Although I did not pay my respects, I recognize him as a good elder. Xuetang said, "How can you know he is good?
The monk replied, "The paths leading to the monastery were cleared and opened; the corridors and eaves were well-maintained; and the incense and lamps in the halls were never extinguished."
The morning and evening bells and drums were distinct; the twice-daily offerings of gruel and rice were refined and pure;
and the monks showed courtesy when meeting people. By this, it was known that he was a fine elder. Xuetang laughed and said, "Ben is indeed virtuous, yet you also possess the eye of discernment.
He then conveyed these words directly to the District Magistrate, Lord Wu Gong Fupeng, saying: "This monk’s adherence to his principles is quite remarkable."
Regarding the matter of Fan Yanling’s recommendation of Zhang Xiyan: Your Excellency’s virtue is no less than that of Lord Zhang Zhongding.
As this old monk is advanced in years, I beg for the favor of appointing you as the current abbot; this would surely be a great event for those among the forest [of monks].
Lord Wu was greatly pleased, and on that very day, Ben was promoted to the post of Abbot of Jianfu Temple (the account of Fan Yanling is from the *Rangchao Leyuan*, in the *Donghu Ji*).
Xuetang traveled to Wugu Mountain in Quzhou. Chan Master Xuetang Daoheng was the son of the Ye family of Xunzhou;
he was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fuyan Yuan and belonged to the fifteenth generation under Nanyue.
"Along" means following the current downstream; here it refers to following a single path.
Basan was originally Chan Master Wuben of Jianfu Temple in Rengzhou. A native of Jiangzhou, he previously resided at Boshan.
He succeeded the Great Wisdom Chan Master (Dahui). He is the sixteenth generation descendant of Nanyue.
Upon entering the temple, the six paths are wide and open; the dwellings are excellent. The corridors and eaves are well-maintained;

the construction is magnificent. Incense and lamps burn without ceasing; the repayment of gratitude is admirable. The bells and drums are distinct; the monastic regulations are excellent. The rice gruel and meals are pure and refined.
"May the assembly be well. The monks' conduct is exemplary, and their decorum is excellent.
As for Zhang Xiyan—who served as the Magistrate of Pingxiang during the Song dynasty—and Fan Yanling, who was a Palace Attendant (*dianzhi*) leading troops through Jinling:
when Zhang Yong was appointed by imperial decree to govern Jinling, he asked [Fan]: 'Are you the Celestial Envoy?'"
“Did you see any good officials along the way? He replied, “Yesterday I passed through Pingxiang. The district magistrate, Zhang Xiyan, is a good official.

Yong asked, “How do you know he is good? He answered, “From the moment I entered his jurisdiction, the bridges and roads were in excellent condition, the fields and gardens were wide and well-cultivated, there were no idle farmers in the wilds, and no gambling in the markets. At night, the sounds of the watch-drums were clear and distinct.”
Knowing that there were indeed men of excellent governance, he praised them, saying: "Xiyan is certainly a worthy man; the Heavenly Official is also a fine officer.
On that very day, they were jointly recommended to the court: Xiyan was appointed as the Commissioner for Grain Transport (Fayunshi), and Yanling was appointed as a Court Gentleman (Gemenhou).
Zhang Yong, courtesy name Fuzhi, was later posthumously enfeoffed as the Duke of Dingguo.
Regarding the form of address "Gexia" (Your Excellency), his *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) states: "The Chancellor, the Three Dukes, and the Prefectural Governor all address one another as 'Gexia.'"
Xuetang said: "A golden embankment spanning a thousand li may collapse from the breach of an ant; the beauty of a white jade璧 (bi) may be marred by a single flaw.
How much more so for the unsurpassed, wondrous Way, which is not merely like a golden embankment or a white jade璧! Furthermore, greed, desire, anger, and hatred are not merely like ants or flaws.
It depends on the rectitude and prudence of one's will, the diligence of one's practice, the firmness of one's maintenance, and the perfection of one's cultivation."
Only after it is beautiful can one benefit oneself and others (from the "Letter to Yu Wupeng").
"Golden Embankment" (*Jindī*) takes the sense of solidity; below it refers to the banks of a pond.
[The text] is fragmentary.
Xuetao said: "When I was at Longmen, Tiewei Ben was residing at Taiping.

Someone remarked that not long after Ben had departed from his hometown on pilgrimage, he heard that his home monastery had been destroyed by fire one night, leaving nothing but ashes. Upon receiving this letter, Ben threw it [aside]."
Di said, "This merely disturbs the human mind" (*Donghu ji*).
The reading for *weijin* (煨燼) is *jin* (盡); it refers to the remains of fire.
Xuetang said to Master Guang of Huicang, "In my early twenties, I heard the words of the 'Man Who Dwells in Solitude' regarding the Middle Way."

Without a master, one does not stand; without external rectitude, one does not act. These words should be practiced throughout one’s life. The undertakings of the sages and worthies are fully contained therein.

I wear these words upon my person: whether remaining at home to cultivate the self or leaving home to study the Way, even down to leading oneself and presiding over the multitude, they remain my guide.
It is like a scale and stone for determining weight, or a compass and square for forming squares and circles; to abandon these would cause every matter to lose its standard.
(According to the *Guanglu*, the "Gentleman Who Dwells in Solitude" was the father of Xuetang.)
Master Huiguang of Huicang at Guifeng in Xinzhou: Master Huiguang of Huicang was a native of Jianning.
He was a successor of Chan Master Xuetang Xingji.
"At the age of twenty" (ruogan)—in ancient times, capping took place at twenty; here, "fifteen or sixteen" refers to the period before one has been capped.

This refers to wearing the great sash. Furthermore, every sash must have pendants. Whenever the ancients encountered virtuous deeds or admirable words, they would immediately record them upon their pendants to demonstrate that they would not forget them.
It serves as a standard for measurement. Furthermore, "standard" (zhun) refers to that by which one levels and rectifies. The commentary states:
"One sets up water to observe the plumb line; taking water as the level constitutes the instrument for leveling."
Xuetao said, "When Gaoyuan presided over the assembly, he would invariably say, 'Among you, there must be those who possess true understanding.
I asked him the reason for this, and Gaoyuan replied, 'Have you not seen how Guishan said, "Observe the conduct of those who are superior; do not vainly follow the vulgar and base"?
Throughout my life, those who did not sink into the ranks of the ignorant while in the midst of the assembly have all spoken these words. [This occurred] in the midst of a vast and crowded multitude.
Those who are base are many; those with true insight are few. The base are easy to associate with; those with insight are difficult to approach.

If one can indeed exert one's own will amidst this, it is like a single person facing ten thousand enemies. When the power of vulgar habits is exhausted, one becomes a truly outstanding man of boundless capacity.
I have practiced these words throughout my life, and only then did I succeed in not failing the resolve for which I left the household life. (From the *Guanglu*).
It is both empty pretension and deception. To stand firm, uphold the Way, and transcend while remaining independent—this is the mark of a true master.
Xuetang said to Qian’an: "In performing your duties, you must weigh matters according to their relative importance. Before speaking, you must first reflect;
ensure that your words accord with the Middle Way and do not lean toward partiality. If you act impulsively and recklessly, it is rare that anything will succeed. Even if success were achieved,"

In the end, it can never be entirely successful. While among the assembly, I have fully observed both its advantages and its defects; only those possessed of virtue can win people over through broad-mindedness.

I constantly hope that those of future generations with the will and strength to practice this will examine it carefully before putting it into action, for only then will it become a source of sublime benefit.

Lingyuan once said: "Ordinary people, when at ease, are often able to understand things through inward reflection; yet as soon as they engage in affairs and their minds scatter outwardly, they lose their harmonious integration."
Having lost the essence of the Dharma-body, if one truly desires to succeed to the task of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and to enlighten future generations,
one must constantly examine and reproach oneself (from the *Guanglu*).
Furthermore, Chan Master Qi’an Shouren of Changlu in Zhenzhou was a native of Shangyu in Yue.
He succeeded Chan Master Xuedang Xing and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Nanyue.
There was a certain person of improper appearance. To "open and guide" means to instruct and lead.
When Master Huayan Hua resided at Mingguo, Xuetang never failed to visit him for even a single day. Occasionally, there were those who spoke of him privately;
Xuetang said, "My nephew Hua is a man who does not delight in profit or seek fame; he does not praise first and later slander."

"Āróng’s union was merely a superficial fit; he lacked integrity, relying instead on a clever countenance and flowery speech. Yet, his realization of the Way was clear and lucid, and he moved with effortless ease whether staying or departing—a quality rare among monastics.
I certainly held him in high esteem. (From *The逸事* of Qiān’ān)
Chan Master Ying’an Tanhua of Tiantong in Mingzhou was a native of the Wang family of Qizhou.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Huqiu Long and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Nanyue.
Xuetao said: "In a student, if spirit (qi) overcomes will (zhi), one becomes a petty person; if will overcomes spirit, one becomes an upright man.
When spirit and will are equal, one becomes a sage or worthy who has attained the Way. There are those who are fierce and stubborn, refusing correction and admonition; this is caused by their spirit.
Upright men, even if forced at gunpoint to do evil, would rather die than waver; this is caused by their will" (Guanglu).
"Zhi" (will) refers to the mind above; "qi" (vital energy) refers to the blood and energy below. By nourishing the mind through principle, the will does not become clouded.
By leading the energy with the will, the energy does not fall into degradation. The Discourse says: "He whose energy obeys the commands of the mind is a worthy person;
he whose mind obeys the commands of the energy is a petty person. Now, energy is the culmination of the will, and the will is the..."
The mind is the commander. If the mind merely follows the fluctuations of the vital energy (*qi*), then *qi* will instead become the commander of the will.
When *qi* acts as the commander, the will of one's mind declines; this is what it means for the mind to be enslaved by *qi*.
Sages and noble gentlemen govern *qi* with the mind rather than being governed by *qi*; they direct *qi* with the mind rather than being directed by *qi*.
Xuetao said: "When Gao’an resided at Yunju, Puyun Yuan was the Head Seat; Yicai Seng was the Secretary; Baiyang Shun was the Librarian;
Tong Wutou was the Guest Master; Xian Zhenmu was the Rector; Huarui was the Assistant Steward;
and Yongrui was the Prior—all of whom were men of virtue and accomplishment. Yongrui was always frugal and disciplined."
He did not light the oil for the permanent lamp. His nephew Hua teased him, saying, "If you wish to become an elder in the future, you must have a straight nose;
how can you consider this sufficient? Fayong’s nephew remained silent. Although Fayong was frugal in his own conduct, he was extremely generous toward others.
He received those coming from all directions without the slightest sign of weariness. One day, Gaofeng saw him and said:

"It is truly difficult to find a Jiansi (Superintendent) who applies himself with such diligence. Furthermore, he must look after the monastery’s permanent assets (changzhu) and ensure they are not neglected or lost.
The Jiansi replied, "Any failure on my part is but a minor transgression. It is for you, Master, to honor the worthy and treat scholars with respect;

to be as vast as the sea and as accommodating as a mountain, taking no account of trivial matters—this is truly the mark of a Great Virtuous One. Gao'an simply smiled. Thus, there arose in the monastic community the nickname "the one who uses the large bowl" (an anecdote).
Chan Master Ziyuan of Puyun in Nankang Commandery: a native of the Yong clan of Mianzhou;
he was a dharma successor of Chan Master Nan’an Wu and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Heng.

The Head Seat (shouzuo) serves as a model for the monastic community; he is the eye and mirror for humanity and the heavens. By taking his seat to preach the Dharma, he opens the way for future generations;
hence he is called the Head Seat.
As for the monk Yicai, his identity is not clearly known; some identify him as Shuian.
The Secretary was in charge of literary correspondence; all matters concerning temple notices, petitions, letters, and prayers were under his jurisdiction.
Baiyang Shun, the Chan Master Baiyang Fashun of Fuzhou, was the son of the Wen family from Mianzhou and succeeded the Buddha [in the Dharma lineage].
Chan Master Yuanyan was the fifteenth generation descendant of Nanyue. One day, the Master ascended the hall and said: "Good things arrive one after another in great abundance;
there is no need for fabrication or contrivance. Yellow leaves falling in the woods are swept away by the water."
Horizontal valleys and white clouds are swept back by the wind; a single cry from a cold wild goose severs all lingering thoughts. As soon as the frost-chilled bell tolls, my mountain crumbles.
Yet the white poplar has a quality that surpasses others: throughout the night, it stirs the dead embers in the cold hearth.
The Librarian was in charge of the Sūtra Collection and was concurrently proficient in its doctrinal principles. He constantly supervised the cataloging and verification of the cases and volumes;
those that were missing he restored to completion, and those that were torn he mended with paste.
Fǎtōng, the Chan Master of Běishān in Zhēnzhōu, was a successor of Chánmèi Liǎoqīng.

As the Guest Master (zhīkè), he was responsible for receiving guests; whenever monastics or laypeople met him, he would attend to them with incense and tea, ensuring that all matters of reception and invitation were conducted with meticulous order.
Chan Master Zhengxian Zhenmu of Guizong in Nankang Commandery: a native of the Chen family of Tongzhou;
he was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fuyan Yuan and belongs to the fifteenth generation under Mount Heng.

The *vinaya-dhara* (weina) serves as the administrative leader of the monastic community, exhaustively managing their discipline and harmony. There is no internal or external monastic affair that he does not oversee;
the term "vinaya-dhara" combines both the Chinese and Sanskrit designations, corresponding to what is today known as the *yuèzhòng* (joyful assembly).

The Assistant Administrator was in charge of the monastery’s permanent assets, including gold, grain, money, and silk, as well as the receipts and disbursements of rice and wheat, maintaining a calendar for these matters at all times.
He was appointed by Chan Master De-yong of Shuanglin in Wuzhou, whose secular surname was Dai and who was a native of that same prefecture;
he was a dharma heir of Chan Master Gao-an Shan-wu.
The term for *jian-si* (monastic supervisor) in Sanskrit is *karmadāna*, which here means "abbot" (*si-zhu*). This refers to the present-day *jian-si*.

For this office, one must be diligent in attending to the incense and lamps morning and evening, receive officials, and have a record of integrity, capability, and public conscientiousness; only those who harbor no grievances among superiors or subordinates shall be appointed to it.
The ocean’s capacity for inclusion is like that of the great sea; there is no water it does not receive. The mind is like a mountain valley;
there is nothing it cannot contain. Xuedang said:
"If a student does not know where the Way is directed, they must seek out teachers and friends to inquire and investigate it. This is good."
Knowledge cannot be realized through solitary transformation; therefore, it relies upon students to provide assistance and support.

For this reason, there must be masters of the Way and virtue presiding over the *caitya* (monastery) to establish the Dharma-society, and there must necessarily be worthy and wise monastics (*śramaṇas*) to serve as its members.

This is like the tiger’s roar that brings forth a biting wind, or the dragon’s leap that causes clouds to rise. In the past, Mazu of Jiangxi became manifest through the influence of Baizhang and Nanquan.
With great capacity and great function, Nanyue and Shitou attained Yaoshan and Tianhuang, thereby manifesting their great wisdom and great capability;
thus, they were united as once in a thousand years, of which there is no doubt in this discourse.

It was as if wings met with the wind, or as if a giant fish leaped through a deep ravine—all of which was the natural course of events. Consequently, they established monastic groves and increased [the Dharma].
The radiance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is brilliant. When our former master was residing at Longmen, one evening he said to me, "I possess no virtuous achievements;

I cannot return to the vast seas of the monastic community with a grand presence. In the end, I shall feel ashamed before the old man of Dongshan. Having finished speaking, his voice choked with tears. I have often reflected upon this.
Nowadays, those who act as teachers of the Way are separated from the ancients by a factor of ten thousandfold (a letter to Zhuanan).
"Zanyou" means to assist and aid; "shexi" means a gathering or assembly.
"Xiào" (rhapsodic blowing) is the sound of exhaling breath; it conveys a piercing coldness.
"Xiáng-téng" (leaping upward) describes the manner of soaring and ascending far.
This refers to the line on the fifth nine of the Qian hexagram in the *Yì*: "The flying dragon is in the heavens; it is advantageous to see the great man. Why?
This is what it means. The Master said: "Sounds of the same pitch respond to one another; breaths of the same quality seek one another. Water flows toward moisture; fire moves toward dryness.
Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. When the Sage arises, all things behold him. That which is rooted in Heaven is closely related to that which is above."
That which originates from the earth is closely related to what is below; thus, each follows its own kind.
Master Yaoshan Weiyen of Dingshui, in Liuzhou, was a native of the Han clan of Jiangzhou and was a dharma successor of Master Shitou Xiqian.
The Emperor of Jingzhou was Chan Master Daowu. He was a native of the Zhang family of Dongyang in Wuzhou and succeeded Chan Master Shitou.
His appearance was like that of a soaring bird; he was as grand and majestic as a wild goose.
"Pai" (沛) describes the rapid flow of water downward. "Shan" (潸), pronounced like the character for mountain (山), describes the falling of tears.
Xuetang said: "When I was at Longmen, Lingyuan resided at Taiping. The authorities disturbed him with improper intentions."
Lingyuan wrote in a letter to his late master: "To walk the Way straightforwardly may well be impossible;

to serve as an abbot by compromising one's integrity is truly not my aspiration. It would be better to let my mind roam among a thousand crags and ten thousand gorges, daily satiated with fodder and grain."

To fulfill the remainder of his life—how could he have been weary of it? Within less than ten days, there came the command of the Yellow Dragon (the Emperor), whereupon he followed his inclination and returned to Jiangxi (as recorded by the Head Seat Cong).
"To walk uprightly while serving others with an upright path—wherever one goes, one will be dismissed three times.
To serve others by walking crookedly—why must one necessarily leave the state of one's parents? This is the speech of Liu Xiaohui from the *Analects*.
"Chu-su" refers to rice made from grass seeds. "Juan-juan" denotes earnest concern and inquiry.
Regarding "xun-jie": ten days constitute a "xun," while twelve days constitute a "jie."
Xuetang said: "Lingyuan compared the 'categorized patch-robed monks' to the words of the ancients, who said: 'It is like making figures out of wood or earth.

When making a wooden figure, one first desires the ears and nose to be large, and the mouth and eyes to be small. If people criticize this, the ears and nose can be made smaller, and the mouth and eyes can be made larger.

When making a figure out of earth, the ears and nose [first...]"* *(Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at the end of the sentence regarding the ear and nose of the earthen figure.)*

When the ears and eyes were small, they first wished for them to be large; when people criticized this, they replied that while the ears and nose could be made larger if small, the mouth and eyes could be made smaller if large.
Although these words concern a minor matter, they can serve as a metaphor for great principles.

When scholars face matters requiring choice between alternatives, they should not disdain reflecting three times over their decisions; thus they may become persons of loyalty and integrity. (Recorded Sayings)
"To model the form of a person is called 'puppet' (ou).
Xuetang said: "When Wanan sent Gaowan to visit Tiantai, he returned and told me:

'The Head Seat Deguan has remained hidden at Xingyan for thirty years, his shadow never leaving the mountain. When Lord Geng of Longxue served as the Prefect, he specifically [sought him out] with auspicious..."
Wang Yan received him. Wanguan declined with a verse, saying: "For thirty years I have closed my door alone; How could an imperial decree reach these green mountains?
Cease bringing trivial matters from the human world To exchange for my lifelong leisure beneath the forest trees. When the mission arrived a second time, he still did not comply.
Master Geng sighed and said, "Today’s Yishan [Hanshan Deqing] is here! Wanguan said, "He has an old..."

One who could recall their words from the previous night said: "Failing to realize the root of the Way, you are submerged in birth and death; your mind arises in response to objects, and your thoughts move according to emotions.
With the heart of a wolf and the intent of a fox, you practice flattery to deceive others; you curry favor with those in power and seek fame at the cost of integrity."
"To deviate from the truth and pursue delusion, to turn one's back on awakening and align with the sensory dust—this is something a man of the Way beneath the forest trees would never do.
I said, "Guan is also one who possesses the vital breath of a monk" (anecdote).
Chan Master Wanan Daoyan of Donglin in Jiangzhou was a native of the Xie clan from Tongzhou.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Dahui Zonggao and belongs to the sixteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage.
Guanshouzu’s origins are unknown.
The *shifu* (official tally) follows the Han system: it consists of a piece of bamboo six inches long, split and then rejoined to serve as a token of authentication.
A *lang* is so called because it is greedy and harms living creatures.
"Interval energy" (*jiānqì*) refers to that which appears not every generation; it denotes individuals such as Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou.
It is also said to refer to those who transcend the ordinary, being beyond the concerns of the mundane world.
Xuetang was born into a family of wealth and nobility, yet he never displayed an air of arrogance. He lived a life of frugality and simplicity.
While residing at Wugu Mountain, a monk presented him with an iron mirror. Xuetang said, "The mountain stream is clear and pure;
even a hair can be reflected in it. What is the use of keeping this? Ultimately, he declined the gift (from his *xingshi*).
To possess wealth is called "rich"; to possess emolument is called "noble.
*Cǐ* (泚) is pronounced with the *qiān* and *lǐ* finals; it means clear water.

Xuedang was benevolent, compassionate, loyal, and forgiving. He honored the worthy and respected the capable. He seldom uttered frivolous words or vulgar speech from his mouth, nor did he maintain any haughtiness.
He was steadfast and never gave way to violent anger. At the critical junctures of departure or remaining, he was extremely principled and pure. He once said:

"When the ancients studied the Way, they were indifferent toward external things and had no personal preferences, even to the point of forgetting rank and position and renouncing fame and beauty; it seemed as though they could do this without effort.
Yet those who study today exhaust every skill and artifice and ultimately achieve nothing. What is the reason for this? It is because their resolve is not firm."
Firmness. The matters are not uniform; they are merely similar in kind (Xing-shi).
Loyalty (*zhong*) is defined as exhausting one's own self; benevolence (*shu*) is defined as yielding to others.
The vulgar and base words [of others] cannot shift the integrity of one's principles; they remain firm and upright.

For ten nights, his feet swelled like heavy cocoons, yet he did not rest. This means that his feet were so injured that the skin peeled away, appearing like heavy cocoons.
"Zhugong" (渚宮)—the first character pronounced as "zhǔ"—is the name of a location; it refers to the present-day province of Jingzhou.
Regarding the Epitaph for Chan Master Miaoxi: Following the passing of Zantang, [Miaoxi] requested Juefan to draft a record of his life and deeds.
Furthermore, having obtained a letter of introduction from Chan Master Zhaoran of Longan, he traveled specifically to Jingzhou to visit the Layman Wujin and seek an epitaph for his stupa.
Upon first meeting Wujin, [Miaoxi] was asked: "Why have you come such a long distance on foot wearing straw sandals?"
The Master said, "I have come from several hundred li specifically to see you, sir. The official asked, "How old are you? The Master replied, "Twenty-four years.
He asked again, "How many water buffalo do you have? The Master replied, "Two.
The official said, "Where did you learn such empty talk? The Master replied, "Today I saw you, sir, in person. Wujin laughed and said, "For now..."
He sat down to drink tea. As soon as he was seated, [the Master] asked again, "What is the purpose of your journey from afar?
The Master stepped forward and said, "Venerable Teacher Zhantang has passed away and been cremated; his eyes, teeth, and prayer beads remained unburnt, and countless śarīras were obtained."
The venerable elders of the mountain gate all wished for a great master’s hand to compose an inscription for the pagoda, in order to inspire the younger generation.
They had come from afar specifically for this purpose, venturing to trouble your esteemed hearing. Wujin said, "I am here because I have been punished for my offenses;
I have never composed writings for others. Now I have a question: if you can answer it, I shall write the pagoda inscription; if you cannot answer it, I shall [give it to someone else]."
[The Master] gave five strings of cash, wrapped his feet, and returned to Tuṣita to practice Zen. The Master said, "Please ask the Excellency [a question].
The Excellency said, "I have heard that Old Zhun’s eyesight is unimpaired—is this true? He replied, "It is. The Excellency said, "I am not asking about those eyes.
The Master asked, "Which eyes are you asking about? The Excellency said, "The adamantine, true eye. The Master—
[The Master] said, "If this is the true eye of the Vajra, it resides upon your Excellency’s pen.
The Official said, "If that is so, I shall provide for him the illumination, enabling him to shine upon heaven and earth.

The Master then stepped forward and said, "Our late Master was most fortunate; thank you, Excellency, for the stupa inscription. Wujin merely responded with "Wei-wei" and smiled. This is a brief account.
He said: "Śāriputra, there is no mention of śarīras in the books of Confucius and Laozi.

After the World-Honored One, the Buddha, entered parinirvāṇa, his disciples collected his śarīras and erected stupas to make offerings to them. Chan Master Chouzhou Congshen had as many as ten thousand grains of śarīras.
In recent times, wherever the smoke from the incense of Longqing Xian and Baizhang Su reached, it all turned into śarīras. Great!
As one who has left the household life, your primary concern should be the great matter of birth and death.
If, when birth and death arrive, you do not know where they lead, then you are no better than a simple man from a village of three households who knows exactly what to do at the end of his life.

He leaves clear instructions that this physical body of the four elements is a temporary confluence of conditions; from the very beginning, how could the *śarīra* (relics) possess any inherent nature? If [it were] Brahma...
One's conduct is pure, one's wholesome karma is firm, and one’s spiritual clarity is vast and penetrating. Foreknowing the transition of the retribution, one is neither startled nor terrified;

thus, the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—will not deviate by even a hair’s breadth. If, however, one harbors a mind of worldly attachment toward these fundamental matters, [the consequences will follow].
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you have never maintained watchfulness; as subtle, continuous currents flow, great conceit arises.
This is like a masterless ghost coming to borrow a dwelling. Under such conditions, how could you hope to cast off the flowing pearl and keep the sense faculties unimpaired?
It would be impossible.
Master Miaoxi Gaoruo said: "Whenever Tanzhang obtained calligraphic works by former sages, he would invariably burn incense to read them.
He would sometimes have them engraved on stone, saying, 'How could I bear to cast aside the profound virtue and illustrious names of the former saints? Such was his refined appreciation.
Thus, at the time of his death, he did not possess a single gold coin; he had only the ink-traces of various worthies from the Tang and Song dynasties, which filled barely two bamboo baskets."
The disciples vied with one another in composing verses in response, obtaining over eighty thousand coins to assist in the rites of cremation (*Ke’an ji*).
One *jin* here refers to ten *liang*.
"Calligraphic traces" (mòjì) is synonymous with "traces" (jì); it refers to books and calligraphic models.
"Chāpí" is a Sanskrit term; here it means "cremation. Miaoxi said:
"The Buddha-nature resides at Dayue. The practitioner and the local guest were scuffling (the character yóu is pronounced as in kǒu, meaning to strike). The Buddha-nature...

When they wished to discipline the estate workers, Master Chao Ran remarked, "If you allow the estate workers to humiliate and insult the practitioners, it will not only result in the loss of the proper distinction between superiors and subordinates, but I fear that petty people will take advantage of the occasion to act with arrogance, and thus the matter will not be carried out.
Fóxìng did not listen. Before long, as expected, an estate worker indeed murdered the administrator (from the *Kānán jí*).
Chan Master Foxing Fatai of Da Mei in Tanzhou was a native of the Li clan of Hanzhou.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin and belonged to the fifteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage.
"Di-ke" refers to tenant farmers.
Zu Chaoran was from Lin’an Prefecture. Chaoran was Zen Master Wenzu, who was a successor of Zen Master Tianyi Huai and belonged to the eleventh generation of the Qingyuan lineage.
To kill one of lower rank by means of one of higher rank is called "shishu" (弒).
Miaoxi said: "When Chan Master Chaoran was residing at Mount Yang, a temple servant stole the monastery's grain.

Chaoran had long resented this servant and intended to dismiss him. He ordered the storekeeper and an attendant to provide a written confession on his behalf. The attendant wished to protect the servant..."
The guest observed that Chao-ran’s demeanor was aloof; he suppressed his intention to provide for [the monk's] departure from the monastery and instead sent someone back to shout at him.
When Chao-ran refused to provide the required supplies, the messenger grew angry, claiming that the practitioner had usurped authority, and both men were merely struck with bamboo rakes.
It appears that Chao-ran did not realize he was being secretly plotted against by the practitioner. Alas! Such is the cunning of petty men (from the *Ke’an ji*).
"Suppression" means to constrain and oppress. "Cunning, deceitful, and obstinate" refers to those who are full of such traits. Miaoxi said:
"Liking and disliking, difference and sameness—these are the common sentiments of humanity. Only the wise, the accomplished, and the highly enlightened are not turned by them.
Formerly, when Yuanwu resided at Yunju and Gao'an retired from the East Hall, those who loved Yuanwu detested Gao'an. Regarding "sameness":
Gaofeng was at odds with Yuanwu; consequently, the monastic communities were thrown into a state of confusion. There arose factions of Yuanwu’s followers and Gaofeng’s partisans.
Observing these two great beings, one sees that they spread their illustrious names throughout the land like the sea, far beyond what ordinary people can emulate.

It is a pity that they were clouded by the light-minded trust placed in the sycophantic words of petty men, which deluded their intelligence and led them to be ridiculed by those of true discernment. Therefore, it is only fitting that they be held accountable.
The lineage of the Seat-Master (Zuozhu) Yinshan consists of those who are men of lofty character (*zhílín jí*). "Great Being" (*dàshì*) is a title for one possessed of virtue;
it refers to the eminent and worthy of the present age who intend to rise above the common herd and whose wisdom transcends the ordinary sentiments of the masses.
Because they propagate the Way and benefit sentient beings, they are called "Great Beings."
Master Liang was a native of Western Shu. He had extensively lectured on the sutras and śāstras, but upon meeting Mazu, he realized the Great Matter.
He subsequently lived in seclusion at Mount Xi in Hongzhou, and no further news of him was heard.
During the Zhenghe era, a scholar named Xiong traveled through the western mountains and passed by Cuiyan. Elder Simen was from Poyang, as was the scholar; therefore, [the elder] sent two...

The strongman lifted the sedan chair and escorted him along. As they passed through the woods and valleys, where trees and shrubs cast deep shade, he happened to see a monk whose appearance was ancient and whose spirit was pure.
With bushy eyebrows and a snow-white head, he wore a garment woven of leaves and sat upon a flat rock like a Buddha depicted in a mural—perfectly serene and translucent.
Xiong said to himself, "In these times, there are no such monks as this. I have often heard of Daoliang..."

The Abbot had been living in seclusion on the Western Mountains; as people suspected he was still there, Xiong Fang went out to meet him, stepping forward with trepidation and saying, "Could this be Master Liang?
The monk pointed his hand toward the east, and Xiong Fang, along with his two attendants, turned their gaze in that direction as he did.
He lost sight of where the monk was. At that time, the light rain had just ceased. The bear climbed onto a rock to look; the place where [the monk] had sat was still dry.
Pausing and looking back, he sighed and said, "My past karmic conditions were not profound; though I encountered him, I did not truly meet him."
Chan Master Yinshan of Longshan in Tanzhou had, upon visiting Mazu, attained realization of the essential point of the mind. Later, he lived in seclusion at Longshan in Tanzhou.
One day, while Wuben of Leishan and his senior companion, Master Mi, were wandering the mountains, they saw vegetable leaves floating down a mountain stream.
Thinking, "Could there be a practitioner dwelling here? they pushed aside the grass and followed the stream for six or seven li. Suddenly—
Seeing Mount Yin in front of the hermitage, he asked, "This mountain has no path; from where did you, Reverend, come?
Dōng said, "Setting aside for a moment the matter of there being no path, from where did you, Master, enter? The Master replied, "I do not come from among the wandering clouds and waters."
Dong said, "How long has the Master resided on this mountain? The Master replied, "Neither spring nor autumn.
Dong said, "Did you reside on this mountain first, or did the mountain reside here first? The Master said, "I do not know. Dong said, "Why do you not know?
The Master said, "I have not come from the realm of humans or devas. Dong said, "What principle did the Master realize that you then came to reside on this mountain?"
The Master said, "I see two clay oxen fighting their way into the sea; until this very day, there has been no news of them.
After a long silence, Dongshan assumed his formal demeanor, prostrated himself, and asked, "What is the master among masters?
The Master replied, "He never leaves his door for all his years. Dongshan asked, "What is the guest within the master? The Master replied, "Green mountains shrouded by white clouds. Dongshan—
Dongshan asked, "How far apart are guest and host? The Master said, "Waves upon the waters of the Long River.
Dongshan asked, "When guest and host meet, what words are spoken? The Master said, "A clear breeze brushes past white clouds.

Dongshan took his leave and composed this verse: "I have always dwelt in a thatched cottage of three bays; A single ray of divine light leaves all phenomena at rest. Do not take up right and wrong..."

He came to refute the self, saying, "The frivolous speculations of floating life are irrelevant. Thereupon, he burned his hermitage and withdrew into a secluded and remote place deep in the mountains, where his whereabouts became unknown;
consequently, he was given the name Yinshan (Hidden Mountain).
Miaoxi said: "The ancients would shift toward the good upon seeing it and reform when they had faults; they led themselves by virtue and followed right conduct, seeking to avoid blame.
Nothing is more grievous than not knowing one's own evils, and nothing is more admirable than delighting in hearing of one's own shortcomings.

Yet, was it truly because the wisdom and talent of the ancients were insufficient, or their insight and vision unclear, that they were like this? It is surely because [the Master] wishes to cause those who come after..."

The world is vast, yet it is narrowed for the individual by means of the precepts (*śīla*). Now, the breadth of the monastic groves and the multitude of the four seas cannot be known by one person alone;
they must rely upon the ears, eyes, thoughts, and deliberations of those around them before they can fully comprehend their principles and master human affairs.
If one merely dwells in honor and self-importance, attending only to minor details while neglecting the grand scheme, even a worthy person will not [be able to fulfill this task].

I understand. The unworthy do not examine things; they do not reform their wrongdoings, and they may even refuse to follow what is right, acting recklessly according to their own whims without any sense of restraint.
This is truly the foundation of calamity; how can one not fear it? Even if there are no individuals by your side with whom you may consult, you should still take the ancient sages as your model.
How could you possibly act like one who has fortified his city and strengthened his troops, leaving himself with no way out?
To enter [the Way]—this is hardly what is meant by "gathering the hundred rivers to form the great ocean" (a letter to Master Baoshan).
It is simply to follow and cultivate [the teachings].
Miaoxi said: "When various quarters nominate an Elder, they must nominate one who upholds the Way and has withdrawn in tranquility.

By nominating such a person, their will and integrity will become even firmer; wherever they go, they will not destroy the permanent property of the monastery but will instead establish the monastic groves.

They are also those who uphold the Dharma and can remedy the evils of today. Furthermore, as for those who are deceitful, sycophantic, and crafty, they know no shame and naturally flatter those in power."
As for holding official rank, why should one seek patronage at the gates of the powerful and influential?
(Letter to Zhuan-an) It is better to withdraw with equanimity and joy, refusing to serve as a man of state.
Miaoxi said to the Layman Chaoran, "Public opinion cannot be abolished in this world.

Even if one suppresses it so that it does not prevail, what can be done about public opinion? Therefore, when a monastery promotes a man of the Way, everyone who hears of it will surely rejoice and offer congratulations;
yet if they promote someone who is not truly qualified, everyone will surely sigh with sorrow. In truth, there is no [other way]."
He judged whether public opinion was being followed or not. Alas! By this, one may divine the flourishing or decline of the monastic community (from the *Ke'an ji*).
The Layman Chao’ran, Prince Zhao Lingjin, styled Biao zhi and titled Layman Chao’ran, was a native of Nankang in the capital region.
He was a dharma heir of Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin.
"Yi" means restraint; "qi" means sorrowful anxiety.
Miaoxi said: "Frugality and letting go are the foundation for cultivating the self and the essential requirement for entering the Way. Observing the ancients throughout history..."
There are few who do not fail to practice frugality and relinquish their attachments. In recent years, monks traveling through Jingzhou and Chu have purchased woolen mats;
those passing through the region east of Zhejiang have sought spun silk. Are they not ashamed when compared to the ancients? Miaoxi said:
"In the past, virtuous abbots did not personally manage the monastery's assets, but entrusted everything entirely to the administrative officers. Recently...
The current incumbent, relying on his own superior talent and strength, ensures that matters—whether great or small—are all brought before the abbot’s quarters;
thus, those in charge of affairs possess nothing more than empty titles. Alas!

If one wishes to govern the affairs of an entire monastery with the resources of a single person, one must ensure that petty people do not obstruct, that the regulations remain orderly, and that the most impartial judgment prevails. Otherwise, it is impossible.
It is also difficult [to explain] (in the letter to Mount Tang).
To be deceived, obscured, and shielded is called "obscuration" (*mōng*).
Miaoxi said: "When Yang reaches its extreme, Yin is born; when Yin reaches its extreme, Yang is born. Prosperity and decline multiply one another; this is the way of Heaven and Earth."
This is the natural order of things: abundance and prosperity are appropriate only at midday. Therefore it is said, "When the sun reaches its zenith, it declines; when the moon is full, it wanes.
The waxing and waning of heaven and earth correspond to the rhythms of time—arising and subsiding with the seasons—how much more so for human beings?

Thus, in ancient times, when people were in the prime of their physical vigor, they were mindful that the passage of time was swift; they contemplated this morning and reflected upon it evening, remaining ever cautious and reverent.
Be ever more cautious; do not indulge your passions, do not give rein to your desires, but seek only the Way. Thus you will be able to preserve your good reputation.
As for those who ruin themselves through dissipation and desire, or bring about their own downfall through indulgence in passion—such states are perilous and beyond remedy.
To then beat one's breast and wring one's hands would be too late. The opportune moment is difficult to find and easily lost. (Written by Xianglin.)
Zhen (Thunder) above and Li (Fire) below:
*Feng* (Abundance), signifying "abundant prosperity. *Feng* means "greatness. To act with clarity is the momentum of great abundance;
therefore, its divination indicates a way of prosperity. Yet, when abundance reaches its peak, decline is imminent, and thus there is also a way of anxiety. The Sage—
People consider such anxiety to be useless. One should simply maintain the ordinary and avoid excess. The *Tuan* commentary says: "When the sun reaches midday, it declines;
when the moon is full, it wanes. Heaven and earth wax and wane in accordance with the seasons; how much more so for humans? How much more so for ghosts and spirits?
This speaks of the difficulty of maintaining abundance and serves as a warning. Midday represents the ultimate height of prosperity.
It should then be dark at midnight. When the moon reaches its fullness, it inevitably suffers a waning;

since even the waxing and waning of heaven and earth depend on the timing of their increase and decrease, how much more so for human beings born between heaven and earth? Ghosts and spirits are the vital mechanisms of the qi of heaven and earth.
During times of abundance, one takes this as a warning, desiring that people maintain the Mean and avoid excessive prosperity. Thus one dwells in *Feng* (Abundance).
The Way is by no means easy to master.
"Xiao" (消) refers to the death of Yin; "xi" (息) refers to the death of Yang.
"Lingwen" (令聞) means superior goodness; "shangqu" (上去) [is pronounced] as a level tone, meaning that one's fame reaches far and wide.
"Opportunities are difficult to encounter; achievements are difficult to accomplish and easy to ruin. Opportunities are difficult to encounter and easy to lose.
'Ah, the moment! Ah, the moment! It will not come again'—these were the words spoken by Han Kuai Che to persuade Han Xin."
Miaoxi said, "In antiquity, those who were advanced to positions of authority first selected for moral integrity and virtue, and secondly for talent and learning.

If one was not a vessel of excellence yet placed themselves before others, their reputation was often slighted upon being seen or heard. For this reason, monks reflected upon themselves to polish their own reputations and principles as they stood firm.
Lately, however, I have observed that the monastic communities are in decline; students disregard moral integrity and virtue, possess little sense of principle and righteousness, and lack—"
Regarding integrity and shame: they deride the pure and simple as vulgar and crude, while they prize the clamorous and superficial as brilliant and quick-witted.

Consequently, the younger generation’s insight becomes clouded; they engage in mere browsing and transcription to fuel their verbal sophistry. As this grows day by day and month by month, it eventually results in a degenerate and corrupt style.
When it comes to discussing the Way of the Sage, they are as bewildered as one facing a blank wall. This situation is perhaps beyond remedy. (With)
(Han Zicang’s commentary):
"Grinding and polishing" refers to refining one's skills.
"Superficial study" (*shèliè*) means a broad survey or a cursory observation; the term is like crossing water or hunting wild animals—it implies that the intent is not focused or specialized.
In the end, they were unable to perceive its profound and abstruse meaning.
As for the "Wall-Facing" [ignorance], the *Analects* states: The Master said to Bo Yu, "Have you studied the *Zhou Nan* and *Shao Nan*?"
If a person does not study the *Zhou Nan* and *Shao Nan*, is it not as if they are standing facing a wall?
This means that they see nothing of any single object and cannot take even a single step forward.
Miaoxi said: "In the past, Huítáng wrote the 'Record of the Engraved Names at Huánglóng,' stating: 'In ancient times, those who studied lived in mountain caves;
they ate earth and wood; they wore skins and grass. They did not set their hearts on fame or profit, nor did they register their names with government offices.
It was only from the Wei, Jin, Qi, Liáng, Sui, and Táng dynasties onward that monasteries were first established to gather students from all quarters. He then selected...

The worthy provide counsel for the unworthy; thus, the wise lead the ignorant and deluded. From this, the distinction between guest and host is established, and the hierarchy of superior and subordinate is divided.
Now, when the multitudes of the four seas gather within a single monastery, the task of one who holds such responsibility is truly difficult to accomplish.

The essential point lies in grasping the great while relinquishing the trivial; prioritizing the urgent while deferring the slow; refraining from private schemes, and benefiting others rather than oneself. This...
Those who are busily occupied with schemes for their own persons alone differ from the former by as much as heaven and earth.

Now, Huanglong has had the names of successive abbots inscribed upon this stone, so that those who come in the future may see them and observe: "Who possessed virtue and wisdom? Who possessed benevolence and righteousness?
Who was impartial toward the multitude? And who sought only their own personal gain? Alas! Is it not cause for alarm? (Stone Inscription)

His name was registered [in the registers of the dead], yet his body remained detached from the mundane world; his traces were lodged among the mists and clouds. Therefore, the officials in charge of the registers could not include his name.
*Chàng* (剏) is pronounced with the initial *chǔ* (楚) and the final *làng* (浪); it means "to begin" or "to create."
Small people are so preoccupied with profit that they have not even a moment’s leisure.
When Attendant Zhang Zishao said to Miaoxi, "The position of Head Seat in a Chan monastery is a rank for selecting the worthy;
yet nowadays, regardless of whether one is worthy or unworthy, all quarters treat this as a shortcut to fortune. He also [said] to the Master...
The Dharma has declined. Thus, it is indeed difficult to find such persons during this age of semblance (*xiangji*).

However, if one selects those whose conduct is somewhat superior, whose talent and virtue are somewhat complete, and who possess a sense of shame, integrity, and righteousness to occupy these positions, they will still be a marked improvement over those who advance through treacherous means (from the *Ke'an ji*).
A place where one crosses water on a journey is called a *jin* (ford); a place for traveling by land is called a *tu* (path).
Miaoxi said to Zishao, "Among those who preside over the Dharma in recent times, none equals Zhenru Zhe;

in skillfully assisting the monastic communities (*conglin*), none is like Yangqi. Critics, however, maintain that Ciming was straightforward and impulsive, negligent in his affairs, and utterly lacking in restraint.
Yangqi served him with such selfless devotion that he feared nothing would be overlooked and worried that nothing would be accomplished.

Even when braving the cold and enduring the heat, he never allowed his own needs to take precedence or permitted himself a moment of indolence. From Nan’uan until Xinghua, this continued for nearly thirty years;

he held the reins of discipline throughout the entire lifetime of Ciming before finally passing away. As for Zhenru, from the time he first packed his belongings to begin his travels as a wandering monk...
When leading his disciples in the world, he forgot his own body for the sake of the Dharma, much more so than one who is parched with hunger and thirst.

Whether in moments of haste or distress, he never showed a hurried countenance nor spoke with ill-tempered words. In summer he did not open the windows; in winter he did not use fire. His single room was serene and secluded, with layers of dust covering the desks.
He once said: "If a monk lacks lofty insight within and lacks the guidance of a master or the companionship of virtuous friends without, it is rare that he can achieve anything."
Those who have become vessels are like Fu’s iron-legged staff, stubborn and unyielding; they are like Xiu Yuan-tong, headstrong and defiant.
All others bow before their reputation. Alas! These two elders are truly the mirrors for the monastics of a thousand years to come (from Ke’an’s *Jiwen*).
"Assisting and supporting" means to aid and bolster. Just as when a court has ministers who serve as its limbs, the world is well-governed;
so too, when a monastic community has wise and virtuous monks, the Dharma-gate flourishes.
Regarding "braving the cold," this refers to times of intense winter or scorching summer heat.
Whether engaged in strenuous labor, he would leap forward to take the lead with his own body, never once displaying an expression of laziness upon his face.
It began with Yang Dainian of Nanyuan, who sent a letter to Huang Shoudan, the Governor of Yichun, requesting that he invite the Master to take up a monastic position and preach the Dharma.
Because Nanyuan had made this request, the Governor subsequently went to visit Shending, who sighed in admiration and said:
"Fenyang has such a son! From this point on, the Master’s reputation spread throughout the four quarters.

The śramaṇa Benyan of Dinglin possessed noble conduct and was highly respected and trusted by the scholar-officials. Upon seeing Ding, he praised him, saying that Ciming’s insight and realization were capable of reviving the Way of Linji.
At that time, the seat at Daowu was vacant; Benyan petitioned the Prefect to request that he take charge of it. Thus, the Dharma...

He brought order and solemnity to the community, even to the point of sacrificing his own life for the sake of the assembly. Later, he moved to Shishuang, then resided at Foyan, and finally stayed at Xinghua.
He took charge of the fundamental regulations and exercised authority over the monastic administration.
This meant presiding over the monasteries, weighing the appointments of monks, establishing the governing framework, and setting forth the disciplinary rules to rectify the deficiencies of the times.
For the sake of the Dharma, one knows only that there is the Buddha-Dharma, yet does not know that there is one's own body.
Even in moments of haste and urgency, or during times of negligence;
even in states of distress, collapse, or wandering in exile.
Suddenly, his expression changed abruptly; he was ill-tempered.
He was perverse, rigid, and haughty, lacking any approach to human sentiment.
Chan Master Yongfu Tiejiao Changlu Yingtian succeeded Letan Huicheng. As for his travels...
Upon arriving at an inn, he was pressured by a courtesan but remained unswayed. The woman informed her mother, who sighed and said, "He is a true son of the Buddha.
Thus, the monastic communities say: "Throughout his life he was as steadfast as an iron foot; the value of his Way resounded through the universe."
*Yanfu* means to fall prostrate; it is synonymous with *dào* (to topple). In the *Analects*, Confucius said: "The virtue of the gentleman is like the wind;
the virtue of the common people is like grass. When the wind blows over the grass, the grass must surely lie prostrate."
The tortoise knows the fortune or misfortune of the future; the mirror reflects the beauty or ugliness of the present.
Zishao, along with Miaoxi and Wan’an—the three of them—went to the front hall to inquire after the health of the Abbot at the Head Seat’s quarters.
Miaoxi said, "Only when the body of one in the forest [of practice] is at ease can one study the Way. Wan’an directly disagreed, saying, "It must not be so..."
"One who studies the Way ought not to look back upon their own body. Miaoxi said, "You obstructive fellow, you are even more deluded!
Although Zishao held Miaoxi’s words in high regard, he ultimately considered Wan’an’s words to be the correct ones (*Jiwen*).
"Ben" (本) refers to Boshan Wuben; it is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùshēng*).
It signifies the "proper measure" (*zhōngjié*) in the delivery of speech.

Zishao asked Miaoxi, "What comes first for one currently serving as abbot? Miaoxi replied, "Accommodating and settling the Zen practitioners. Not— [the text here implies a negation or further qualification].
"It is merely a matter of managing money and grain. At that time, Wan’an was seated in the assembly and disagreed, saying:

"If one calculates what the monastery’s permanent endowment (changzhu) receives and is able to exercise restraint over superfluous expenses, using them according to the Way, the money and grain will be beyond counting; why should they be a cause for concern?
However, for a current abbot, the foremost priority must be to find a monk who embraces the Way. Even if an abbot possesses strategic wisdom, he can [only succeed]..."
"Store ten years' worth of grain. Under my seat, there is not a single monk who truly embraces the Way.

As the former sages said, 'Sitting and wasting away the offerings of the faithful,' I am ashamed before the dragons and devas; what benefit is there for the abbot? Zishao said, "What the Head Seat has said is most appropriate.
Miaoxi looked back at Wan’an and said, "Every one of you is just like you," whereupon Wan’an withdrew. (All of the above is found in the *Kekan ji*).
One should exercise restraint by measuring income and assessing expenditures; being frugal, modest, and economical, one must not allow for extravagance.
To "store" (chǔ) means to accumulate. It is like a crown prince succeeding to the throne; therefore, it is called "storing" (chǔ).

Master Wanan Yan said: "When our late teacher Miaoxi first resided at Mount Jing, during a night assembly he spoke extensively on the various schools and the principles of the Caodong tradition without ceasing.
The following day, Head Seat Yin said to our late teacher: 'Entering the world to benefit sentient beings is by no means a trivial matter.
If you truly intend to uphold and revitalize the religious teachings, you should address current defects as they arise; it is not necessary [to exhaust yourself with exhaustive discourse]. "
