It was not Biao. As an aide to a true king or hegemon, he indeed obtained Jiang Shang on the northern bank of the Wei River.
Conversing with him, [the King] was greatly pleased and said, "Since my late father, Duke Tai, used to say that a sage would surely come to Zhou, Grandfather Tai has long looked forward to you.
Thus he was titled Taigong Wang (Grandfather Tai, the One Who Waits) and appointed as his teacher. He was enfeoffed as the Lord of Lü. Later, he assisted King Wu in the campaign against Zhou.
It is a step on the ladder of the stages; it is also the sequence of succession.

Zhu’an said: "Xuanyuan An often remarked that Master Nanyuan Huanglong was broad-minded and generous, loyal and trustworthy, reverent yet compassionate, profound and far-reaching in his discernment, and widely learned with vast erudition.
He frequently traveled through Huxiang with Yunfeng Yue, once taking shelter from the rain under a tree."
Fayue sat with his legs spread out in a relaxed posture, while Nan alone sat upright and alert.

Fayue glared at him and said, "The wondrous Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not the earth-spirit of some ancient temple in a village of three households. Why do you assume such a deathly expression?

Nan bowed his head in thanks, yet he sat even more upright than before. Thus, Imperial Historian Huang Tingjian (Luzhi) praised him, saying: "Master Nan never forgot reverence, whether in motion or stillness."
He was truly the master of the monastic community (*Huàn'ān jí*).
Sitting with his legs spread wide and extended, he placed both hands upon his knees; his posture resembled a winnowing basket (*jī*). A Tang poem says:

"The shade of green trees is thick enough for all four neighbors; the blue moss grows ever thicker, naturally free of dust. [This refers to] sitting with the head bared and the legs spread like a *jī*.
Sitting beneath a tall pine tree, he looked upon the people of this world with white eyes.
Zhu’an said: "To lead oneself and face the multitude, one must rely on wisdom; to dispel delusions and eliminate attachments, one must first possess awakening.

If one turns one's back on awakening and unites with the dust of the senses, the mind will become obscured. If wisdom and folly are not distinguished, affairs will fall into disorder. (Written by Chan Master Zhui).
Zhu’an said: "When Fojian was abbot at Taiping, Gao’an served as the *karmadāna* (rector). Gao’an was young in years and bold in spirit;

he looked down upon those from all quarters, finding few who could satisfy his mind. One day during the midday meal, when the *khakkhara* (wooden gong) was struck, he saw an attendant set aside a separate vessel of food for Fojian.
Gao’an stepped out of the hall and said in a loud voice: 'A spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of five hundred monks—'"
Zhao Ban was departing, yet how could he serve as a model for later students? When Foguan did not hear or see him, he went down from the hall to inquire;
it turned out that Zhao was carrying vegetables in his water vessel because Foguan had long suffered from spleen ailments and did not eat oil. Gaoyuan felt ashamed.
He went to the abbot’s quarters to take his leave. Fojian said, "What the rector says is quite appropriate.

Since Huiqin has been so ill, I have often heard the words of the sages that one should resolve all obstacles through principle. Since his food was not excellent, there should be no cause for suspicion among the assembly.
The rector’s spirit and character are bright and far-reaching; he shall one day serve as a pillar for our school. I hope you will not harbor resentment over this matter."
When Fodian moved to Zhikai, Gao’an succeeded Longmen; he was thus a successor of Foyan.
A *gāndī* is any object that produces sound when struck, such as bells, chimes, wooden boards, or fish-shaped drums—all things that make a sound upon being struck are termed *gāndī*.
Tian Yan’nan, a pillar of the Han, said to Huo Guang: "General, you are a pillar of the state.
Now, when one speaks of a 'pillar,' it is intended to support the ancestral lineage and cause the Dharma to endure for a long time."
*Jièdì* (芥蔕): The upper character is pronounced *jiè*; the lower character is pronounced *cā*. It refers to someone hoping for another’s magnanimity, saying:

"I hope you will not feel resentment. It also refers to a thorn or a splinter. A "thorn" (*gěng*) is a bone that cannot pass down the throat. In antiquity, those who spoke with blunt and upright integrity were called "bone-thorns" (*gǔgěng*).
Straightforward speech is difficult to accept, much like a thorny bone remaining stuck in the throat.

Zhu’an said: "In general, when discussing the Way with officials or engaging in social exchange, one must strip away all intellectual understanding so as not to let them remain ensnared in conceptual traps.
One must directly clarify the single point that transcends the ordinary. My late teacher Miaoxi once said: 'When gentlemen meet, if there is a question, one should respond;
if there is no question, one should not speak. Furthermore, one must be someone who stands within the midst of this."
This person has finally attained it. These words will be beneficial for the present time and will not damage the integrity of the abbot’s office;
you should reflect upon them carefully. (Letter to Xinghua Puan)
"To eradicate" means to remove one's doubts and attachments, and to sever one's worldly sentiments and thoughts.
Zhu’an said: "The fertile soil is good at nurturing things; a benevolent ruler is good at nurturing scholars.

Nowadays, those who hold the position of abbot often do not take the interests of the community to heart. They are anxious for their own desires, loathe hearing virtuous words, and delight in concealing their faults."

It is evil. To act wantonly according to perverse conduct, following one's own momentary whims, and then to have petty people seize upon those actions according to their own likes and dislikes—how could the way of maintaining the Dharma not be placed in peril? (Letter to Old Man Hong)
Zhu’an said to Ye’an: “The Prime Minister, Layman Ziyán, remarked that our late master Miaoxi throughout his life prioritized moral virtue, integrity, and courage.
He was one who could be trusted but not distanced; who could be approached but not pressured; who could be killed but never humiliated.
In his private life he was neither licentious nor gluttonous; when facing death or calamity, he regarded them as nothing.”
As the saying goes: "Even Ganjiang and Moye find it difficult to contend with [such a foe]; one merely fears injury or loss.
Later, this was just as Ziyuan had said (as recorded in the *Huanchan Jiwen*).
The last three phrases of "ke qin" (may be intimate with) are derived from the "Ruxing pian" (Chapter on the Conduct of the Confucian) in the *Kongzi Jiayu*.

Regarding "yinru" (excessive indulgence and dampness), the *Liji* states: "In one's private life, one should not be excessive; in eating and drinking, one should not be gluttonous. The commentary explains: "Yin" means to be dissolute or profligate.
To indulge excessively in the taste of flavors is called *ru* (moisture).

*Gānjiāng* and *Mòxié* are the names of two fine swords. According to the *Biographies of Filial Sons*, the consort of the King of Chu became pregnant while embracing an iron pillar during the summer to seek coolness;
she subsequently gave birth to an iron mass. The King of Chu then commanded Gānjiāng to forge a sword from it.

After three years, the two swords were completed—one female and one male. Gan Jiang secretly took the male sword and hid it, while presenting the female sword to the King, who placed it in a secret casket.
It frequently let out a mournful cry. The King questioned his ministers, and they replied, "Swords have both male and female aspects;
that which cries is merely longing for its mate. The King was greatly enraged. Gan Jiang, knowing he would surely die for his crime, concealed the sword...
Within a pillar of his house, he entrusted his wife, Mo-xie, saying: "When the sun rises over the northern door, there will be a pine tree on the southern mountain.
The pine grows upon stone, and a sword is within it. Later, the wife gave birth to a son named Mei-jian-chi. When he was fifteen years old, he asked his mother, "Where is my father?
His mother recounted the previous events; he then contemplated splitting the pillar and indeed found the sword therein. Desiring to...
The father had sought revenge. When the King of Chu learned of this, he issued an edict to find the man, promising a generous reward to whoever did so.
Mei Jian Chi then fled. Shortly thereafter, a guest arrived and said, "Are you not perhaps Mei Jian Chi? He replied, "I am.
The guest continued, "I am a man from Zengshan who can avenge your father's death for you. Mei Jian Chi said, "My father was formerly innocent, yet he was unjustly subjected to such bitter torment."
"Your Majesty has now granted me this favor; what else do you require? The guest replied, "I must have your head along with your sword. Thereupon, Chi took his own life by cutting off his head.
The guest obtained the head and the sword and presented them to the King of Chu. The King said, "This is a great fortune! The guest said:
"I wish to cook this head with oil. The king then cast his head into the cauldron along with it. After boiling for three days, it did not decompose.
The guest requested that the king look at it; the guest then struck the king's head with a sword, causing it to fall into the cauldron. The two heads gnawed at one another.

The guest feared that his own head would not withstand the pressure as the space between its brows turned red; he therefore cut off his own head to assist it. The three heads bit one another, and in a brief moment, they all rotted away.
"Yu" signifies anxiety and concern; "que" signifies loss and deficiency.
Zhu’an said: “Master Yuan’an, as abbot, understood the beginning and end of human relations and was clear regarding the fundamental principles of the monastic community (sōrin).
He once said to me: ‘One who serves as the leader of a region must select monks of aspiration and integrity to assist him.
This is like having a comb for one’s hair or a mirror for one’s face; then, benefits and harms, beauty and ugliness, can no longer be concealed. Thus it is.
Cimeng attained Yangqi; Mazu attained Baizhang. It is like pouring water into water—nothing can obstruct it (from the *Huanchan ji*).
Zhu’an said: "Those of later learning receive only the superficial; they value what they hear while despising what they see, and thus are ultimately unable to fathom its profound mysteries.

Therefore it is said: 'The mountain does not weary of being high, for within it lie layered cliffs of accumulated emerald green; the ocean does not weary of being deep, for within it lie the four seas and nine rivers.'"
Yuan: "If one wishes to investigate the Great Way, the essential point lies in exhausting its heights and depths;
only then can it illuminate the subtle and obscure, responding to changes without limit" (Letter to Master Jin).
"Superficial learning and skin-deep reception. The *Dongjing fu* states: "Superficial learning and skin-deep reception; they value what is heard and despise what is seen. Commentary:
"Fū" (skin) refers to the surface layer of the skin. Because the reception is like that of the skin, it is called "skin-deep reception" (*fūshu*).
This refers to external reception that is shallow and thin, rather than internal, substantial reception; thus, they value what is heard and despise what is seen.
"Beyond the abysses (mingyuan) lies the blackness of the waters. Taking the four seas of the east, west, south, and north as the four abysses, their depth below is profound.
The sea undergoes nine revolutions; the waters swirl and eddy, reaching a depth so extreme that they constitute the nine abysses."
Zhu’an said to Minister You: “The intent of the sages and worthies is conveyed with gentleness and clarity; it is leisurely and its principles are manifest.
As for the practices they employ, they do not expect rapid accomplishment but allow for long-term persistence; they do not require inevitable progress.”
Yet, by allowing for the possibility of "near-attainment" (shujī), one can infer the intention of the sages and worthies; thus, they have been able to maintain this through ten thousand generations.
That there has been no error or failure is precisely because of this (from the *Huàn'ān jí*).
It is hoped that you will examine this with composure and deliberation.

"Jian" (亘) means to penetrate through. Lord You, the Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, said: "Before the time of the Patriarchs, there was no office of abbot. Later, when they appeared in the world to practice the Way, they were driven by necessity.
Yet, as for their dwelling, they used thatched huts merely to shield themselves from wind and rain; as for their food, they took coarse grains merely to satisfy hunger."

He was so arduous and emaciated that there were those who could not bear his distress; yet among kings, dukes, and great officials, there were even those who desired to see him but could not obtain the opportunity.
Therefore, what he established was all磊磊落落 (lofty and magnificent), startling heaven and shaking the earth. Later generations were not like this:

living in high halls and spacious mansions, wearing fine clothes and eating sumptuous food, they had their every whim satisfied by a mere gesture of the chin. It was then that the followers of Pāpīyas began...
His mind was moved by this vast and profound [teaching]. Yet, he hesitated at the gates of power, wagging his tail and begging for favor;
worse still, he practiced crafty seizure and violent plunder, like someone plucking gold in broad daylight, no longer aware that there is such a thing as cause and effect in this world.

This letter from Miaoxi was not written solely for the sake of Boshan; it exhausts the habitual tendencies of all quarters from time immemorial, leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind—like drinking from a granary.
The water of the Upper Pond reflects the Duke’s liver and intestines with perfect clarity. If you can believe, accept, and practice this, what need is there to seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere?
(Seen on a stone inscription at Lingyin Monastery).
"Peng-bi" refers to weaving thorn branches to form a gate. The "Ruxing" (Conduct of the Confucian) chapter of the *Liji* states:

"The Confucian may have an estate of one mu, a room with walls of one zhang on each side, a gate of woven thorns with a small square opening, a door of wild grass, and windows made from overturned jars."
"Emaciated and withered" refers to one who is worn by anxiety and toil.
"磊落" (leiluo) means as when a multitude of rocks collapse and fall, yet without obstruction; these are all the marks of a great man.
Nothing remains obstructed within his breast, like passing straight through amidst a thicket of spears and halberds, or leaping over brambles in a thorny forest.
The hand simply acts; there is no five-colored thread beneath the heels. There is no "ten-character barrier" upon the tip of the tongue.
There are no traces of mud on the bridge of the nose. And there are no golden specks within the eyes. This is why.
"To point with the chin" means to direct by merely moving the chin; it requires no exertion of force, and everything is accomplished as desired.
"Yangyang" describes an appearance of drifting and wandering. "Zejū":
the first character is pronounced *zī* (upper tone) and the second is pronounced *zū* (lower tone); it refers to the state of wishing to move forward but being unable to do so.
"Seizing gold" (jué jīn). "Jué" means to grasp with the claws. *Liezi* says: "Formerly, there was a man of Qi who desired gold.
At dawn, he dressed in his cap and robes and went to the marketplace, arriving at a place where gold was being sold.

He stole the gold and departed. The owner of the gold caught him and said, 'Everyone else was present; why did you seize someone else's gold? He replied, 'At the time I took the gold, I did not see the person.'"
Yet one sees only the gold; this speaks of how people covet profit and forget their shame, seeing the benefit while forgetting the harm.
Regarding the "Upper Pond Water," ancient records state: To the east of Luoyue there was a man named Bian Que, surnamed Qin and given name Huan.
He was a native of Bohai Commandery. In his youth, he served as a head of a lodging house.

When he hosted the Guest Lord Changsang, he found Bian Que uniquely extraordinary and treated him with constant diligence for over ten years. One day, he called Bian Que aside to sit privately and spoke to him in confidence, saying:
"I possess a medicinal formula. As I am approaching old age, I wish to transmit it to you. You must not let it leak out. The magpie respectfully agreed.
He then took the medicinal formula from his breast and gave it to him, instructing him to take it with water collected from the upper part of a pool;
he said, "In twenty-one days, you shall see things. He gave him the entire formula and suddenly vanished. The magpie followed these instructions.
Take it with medicinal water. After twenty-one days, look at people in one direction beyond the wall;
subsequently, examine the patient, and you will see all the nodules and obstructions within the five viscera. This is merely what is called "taking the pulse. (Note:
Before the rainwater has reached the ground, collect dew from bamboo and wood; thus it is named "Upper Pond Water.")
Minister You said to Zhuo’an, “In the past, Miaoxi revitalized the Way of Linji during a time of decline.

His nature was naturally humble and open; he never sought to display his realization of the principle. Throughout his life, he did not pursue power and influence, nor did he seek profit or sustenance.
He once said: ‘In all matters, one must not act with negligence or indolence, nor should one maintain an air of extravagance. This was because there is benefit [in such restraint].”
Regarding those who act upon things at the proper time, there may be faults without merit; if one indulges in luxury and indolence, then one will not succeed.
I, the unworthy one, have taken these words to heart and made them a lifelong admonition. As for what the Master said yesterday:
It is truly a blessing for the Buddha-Dharma that you, our Lord, have stayed overnight at the meditation hall.
We earnestly hope that your compassionate vows will remain tireless, so that the path toward goodness may be illuminated and the way for all beings may grow ever greater.

By this, we pray that future generations and those of later years will not seek only immediate or superficial gains, but each harbor far-reaching aspirations. Would this not be a source of benefit and salvation for the monastic community? (Recorded by the attendant).
To restore what has declined and bring about renewal is called "restoration" (*zhongxing*). Examples include King Xuan of Zhou and Emperor Guangwu of Han;
they were those who restored the great enterprise of emperors.
To act with ease and indulgence, following one's whims and gratifying one's desires, constitutes the state of aesthetic refinement and intention.
It is convenient; it is a strategic plan.
Master Miyun Yuanwu said: "The flourishing or decline of the monastic community depends upon ritual and law; the excellence or deficiency of practitioners depends upon their habits.
If one were to practice the ways of the ancients—dwelling in nests or caves, drinking from mountain streams, and eating from trees—in this present age, then..."

It is not possible. To cause people of the present day to wear richly patterned garments and eat fine rice with fatty meats—if this were practiced in ancient times, it would likewise have been impossible.
What is the reason? It is simply a matter of whether one is accustomed to it or not. For what a person sees morning and evening becomes the norm.
One must say that worldly affairs ought naturally to be thus.

If one were suddenly to drive them to abandon this and pursue that, not only would they harbor doubts and fail to believe, but it is feared they would likewise refuse to comply. Judging from this, human nature finds comfort in what it is accustomed to.

"It is only natural that they were startled by what they had not seen; why should this be considered strange? (From "A Letter to Imperial Censor Shi"). Master Mian Xianjie of Tiantong in Qingyuan Prefecture was a native of the Zheng family of Fuzhou. His style name was Miaoxing. He entered the monastic order at the age of twelve under Master Wuxue Zuyuan of Mount Jingshan. At twenty-one, he received full ordination at Mount Jiuhua and subsequently traveled to study under various masters. He visited the Dharma seat of Master Shouzhuo at Mount Yunju in Jianyang, where he attained great realization. Later, he resided at Mount Jing in Yuezhou, where he established the Way and transformed disciples. In the second year of the Zhishun era, he was invited to serve as the abbot of the Great Bao'en Monastery in the capital. In the first year of the Chunyou era, he was appointed as the abbot of the Great Yongming Monastery. In the third year of the Chunyou era, he was summoned to the imperial court, where he was granted the title of Chan Master Miaoxing. In the first year of the Qianyuan era, he was again summoned to the capital and appointed as the abbot of the Great Huayan Monastery. In the second year of the Qianyuan era, he retired to Mount Tiantong. In the second year of the Baoyou era, he passed away at the age of seventy-four. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Miaoxing. His remains were enshrined in the eastern pagoda on Mount Tiantong. His dharma heirs numbered over three hundred. He succeeded Chan Master Huayan Ying’an. He was the seventeenth generation descendant of Nanyue. Miyuan said to the Head Seat Wugu:
"Among those in the monastic communities, only the people of Zhejiang are weak and lack firm resolve.
Your talent and capacity are vast and great; your temperament is profound and dignified; your aspirations are upright and resolute; furthermore, your realization is stable and secure. In the future—"
The *I Ching* says: "Simply remain concealed and obscure; do not expose your sharp edges. Break your square corners and blend with the tiles; maintain this through the Middle Way.
Do not yield even slightly to the influence of power or profit—this is precisely to perform the work of a Buddha without leaving the realm of worldly toil" (Letter to Xia’an).
It means being humble and yielding.

"Tao-hui" (concealing and hiding) refers to setting aside empty fame and discarding superficiality to pursue substance; it means obscuring one's traces and harmonizing with the light of the world while sharing in the dust of the mundane.
Regarding "breaking the square to join like roof tiles," the *Liji* (Book of Rites), in the "Conduct of the Confucian" (*Ruxing*) chapter, states:

"The Confucian is one who studies extensively without weariness and practices earnestly without fatigue. He admires the worthy yet is tolerant of the masses; he breaks the square to join like roof tiles.

One who is magnanimous is like this. A brief commentary notes: "Breaking the square to join like roof tiles refers to the craft of making pottery. At the beginning, the clay is round; it is [then] split..."
It is divided into four, its shape being square. It destroys its roundness to become square, and unites its squareness to become round.
Thus, within its capacity for inclusion, there has never been a lack of discernment. Therefore it is said: "Broadness is such as this."
Mimian said: "Our late master Ying’an once remarked that the worthy and the unworthy are opposites and must be distinguished.
The worthy establish themselves by upholding morality, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness; the unworthy employ power, profit, deceit, and flattery in their affairs.

When the worthy attain their ambitions, they surely put into practice what they have learned; when the unworthy occupy positions of authority, they mostly indulge in private interests, envying the worthy and being jealous of them."
It is possible. When one indulges in desires and craves wealth, there is nothing one will not do. Therefore, when one obtains the worthy, the monastic community flourishes;
when one employs the unworthy, it falls into ruin. If either of these conditions exists, one will certainly be unable to maintain tranquility (as seen in the letter of Master Yue).

Envy is sacrificing oneself for fame and profit. To be unable to endure the prosperity of others is called envy; furthermore, to harm the virtuous is called *ji* (envy), and to resent the beauty of others is called *du* (jealousy).
Miman said: "A monastic has three 'do nots': when affairs are many, do not fear them; when there are no affairs, do not seek them out; and as for right and wrong, do not discriminate between them."
If an abbot understands these three matters, he will not be deluded by external things (as recorded in the notes of Attendant Hui).
Miman said: "When a monk’s conduct is crooked and depraved, and he has long possessed traces of unwholesome behavior, this is mutually known throughout the monastic community."

Yet, once others understand what I employ, their eventual slander is simply a matter for them; in time, the truth will manifest of itself without the need for further clarification.
Nor is it necessary to insist on one's own correctness to provoke or attack others; in this way, one may perhaps be considered a true recluse beneath the forest trees (Letter to Shui-an).
"Partial views" and "narrow views" are like looking at the sky through a tube; one can see only a small portion.

Devious, biased, unjust, and sycophantic speech.

At the end of the Shaoxing era, there were still mature elders within the monastic forests who could maintain the established traditions and protocols, never daring to leave their side for even a moment.
In recent years, however, the lineage has lost its core; the mainstays are no longer mainstays, and the guiding principles are no longer principles.

Even if such frameworks exist, how can they be rectified? Thus it is said: "If one mainstay is raised, all the meshes will open; if one mechanism is slackened, ten thousand things fall into disorder."

Matters have fallen into ruin; it is perilous that the fundamental principles are not being sustained and the monastic communities are not flourishing. Only the ancients understood how to rectify the branches by attending to the root.
They were concerned solely with whether the legal statutes were not strict, rather than worrying about scholars losing their proper place. Their focus on what was essential lay in impartiality.
Nowadays, those who hold positions of authority in various quarters confuse the private with the public and subvert the fundamental with the derivative. Those above seek profit regardless of the Way;

those below pursue gain regardless of righteousness. With superiors and subordinates in disarray and hosts and guests in confusion, how can monastics turn toward what is correct, and how can the monastic communities flourish? (Letter to Minister You)

One who learns the Way well first governs the internal to resist the external, and does not covet the external to the detriment of the internal. Therefore, the essential point in guiding others lies in purifying the mind.
